## 18.508 A message's facts, kept in requests the disk takes

On the M700, once Diego's Gmail account was restored (18.499), 107 of its
messages showed "?" in the list, and `maild` said "107 worked out again" at
every look. Since M8 a message's facts carry the start of its text,
`words`, for search (18.496): with a newsletter's sender, subject, preview,
recipients and a thousand bytes of words they come to about 1,460 bytes, and
a request to the disk carries 1024 (`DISK_DATA_MAX`). Every such `setattr`
was refused - "more than one request to the disk carries" - and nobody
looked at the answer. While the facts the messages had from before stayed,
the list read them and nothing showed; the loss took them, and the rows
went blank. The test's messages were all short.

`keep_facts` writes them in three requests - the list's, then whom it went
to, then the words with the version last, so facts that did not all arrive
are worked out again - each long one kept to 900 bytes, cut at a whole
character; a refusal is said. `x86-mail-2` 15: a newsletter of sixty
recipients and three thousand accented characters delivered, its sender,
subject and version kept and its words there, and nothing refused.
**Control**: the facts in one request, and the letter has no subject in the
list and `maild` says it could not keep them. Mail's seven suites and
`host` pass.

## 18.509 Astra D3a: the desktop composed in C

`docs/astra-display.md` D3a. **`gfx.scene`** (`user/kits/gfx/scene.c`),
compiled inside `gfx.c`: the window manager describes, before each pass,
everything it composes - the look, the desktop's colour, wallpaper and
version stamp (a picture, made when it changes), each window in drawing
order with its place, flags, picture, menu bar and lights' state, the
menus, the resize outline, the volume display and the pointer's picture -
a call a window and no tables; the scene composes each damaged rectangle
into the back buffer as `compose.lua` and `drawwindow.lua` did: which
windows show, the desktop under the rest, shadows, each window copied,
blended or stretched, its grip, its three lights and rounded corners, the
menus, the outline, the volume display and the arrow. A drag's label is
drawn after it in Lua, and the screen is the window manager's. The kit's
primitives became C functions on surfaces - `fill_on`, `blit_on`,
`blend_on`, `blit_round_on`, `fill_round_on`, `frame_round_on`,
`triangle_on` - which the Lua methods call, so the scene draws with them
rather than a copy.

**`wm compose-check`** composes each pass by the scene and again by the Lua
over it and counts the pixels that differ in what was damaged - the part a
pass puts on the screen; the Lua drew the stamp and the arrow past the
rectangle, where nothing is shown, and the scene clips them. Two controls
did not bite at first: shadows are off in the default look, and the back
buffer kept the last frame where the scene drew nothing; each rectangle
now starts magenta in the check, and the suite turns shadows on.

`x86-scene` 3: the Deskbar, the desktop, Calculator, Preferences, a cube
turning, a menu, a window moved, 150 per cent and back - 1500 passes, not
one pixel different. **Control**: the scene casting no shadow, and
10,867,485 pixels differ over 1446 passes. `frames` before and after, under
QEMU: a composing pass 1.35 to 1.01 ms idle, 0.80 to 0.47 with one window
animating, 3.53 to 1.59 with four stacked; the window manager's busy time
347 to 293, 955 to 714 and 2121 to 1423 ms. The whole gate, 62 of 62.

## 18.510 Astra D3b-1: the primitives and the scene with no Lua

For the window server, which is C and has no Lua, to compose with the same
code the window manager's scene does. `draw.c` holds the kit's primitives -
fill, copy, blend, stretch, a rounded copy, rounded fills and frames, a
triangle - moved out of `gfx.c` as they were, behind `draw_primitives.h`;
`surface.h` holds a surface's shape and the inline helpers every loop over
pixels uses (`row_of`, `clip`, `over`); `scene_core.c` holds the scene and
its composing, and `scene.c` is the Lua binding over it. `gfx_draw.h` still
keeps the shape from every other kit. `check_lanes.py` reads `blend_row` in
`draw.c` now: since 0.11.114 the lanes it meant were no longer in `l_blend`,
which it was still reading.

`test_draw` 14, on this Mac: a fill and a copy clipped at the edges, a blend
at half, a stretch, a triangle's rows; a scene of two windows overlapping, a
menu over them and a hidden one, composed - the desktop, each window where
it shows, the menu on top, the hidden one not drawn, a corner rounded - and
the same pixels composed again over magenta. **Control**: the menus not
composed, and it fails. The AArch64 image builds. The whole gate, 61 of 62:
`x86-film`'s sound, which has failed under load before, passes alone.

## 18.511 Astra D3b-2, step 1: the window server, started at boot

`user/servers/windowserver.c`, a role of the init image (27), started by
init at boot with the screen and the console's endpoint (Diego, 10
October: option (a)). Its manager door is `windowproto.h`, a greeting for
now that answers the screen's size; the shell lends the door only to
`/Kosmos/Programs/wm.lua`, which declares `needs windowserver` and finds it
at `/Windowserver`. The window manager greets it as it starts; the desktop
is still composed in its process.

The whole gate stopped eight suites at boot - every machine without a
display: init asked to hand the server a screen it did not have, was
refused, and `start` ends init when a spawn fails. It starts only where
there is a screen now, and a failure is a line in the log, as the power
button's is; the eight pass. `x86-scene` 4: `windowserver: the screen,
1920x1080` and `wm: the window server answers, the screen 1920x1080`.

## 18.512 The launcher opens without waiting for the Deskbar

Diego, 10 October: "when clicking the kosmos button in the dock, the app
launcher takes like a full second to show". Measured, under QEMU, from the
press: the launcher's process started at 37 ms, the kit loaded by 98, every
application listed by 200, and then **840 ms reading where the dock is** -
`/Running/Deskbar/anchor`, a question to the Deskbar, which a kit window
answers only between its waits for events, and the Deskbar's wait is its
clock's second. Its window opened 50 ms after, and its first frame 20 after
that. Loading the applications was a tenth of it.

The window manager answers it now (`dock`): the middle of the dock window's
top edge, in points, which is what the Deskbar published - every window's
place is known there, and the window manager answers as it runs. The
launcher says how long the question took. `x86-dock` 54: the launcher
learnt where the dock is in at most 100 ms. **Control**: the Deskbar asked
again, and 872 ms. The whole gate, 61 of 62: `x86-maps` waited for its
machine's Telnet under load and passes alone.

**What this showed is wider** (`roadmap.md`): anything that asks a running
application through `/Running/<name>` waits for that application's next
turn, up to its tick - a second for the Deskbar, whose writes Preferences
makes as a slider moves.

## 18.514 Astra D3b-2, step 2: the window server composes

`docs/astra-display.md` D3b-2 step 2. The window manager hands the window
server, each once and as a region, the back buffer, a region the scene is
written in, and every picture the scene names under a slot it chooses: a
window's two buffers (`gfx.wrap{ region = cap, offset = }`), and its own
wallpaper, version stamp, menu bars, level bar, arrow and a drag's label -
each now `gfx.surface{ shared = true }`, which `s:region()` names. A pass
is described by slot, `scene:wire` writes it with the damage into the
shared region (`windowproto.h`'s `ws_scene_head`, windows, menus and
rectangles), and one `WS_OP_COMPOSE` composes it into the back buffer and
puts it on the screen; the watcher's copy (VNC) is still taken here. A
drag's label is a picture of the scene's now, composed last, rather than
drawn by the window manager after it. A picture whose surface is freed or
collected is forgotten on the next pass; a window's buffers are freed with
their region. The server holds every count to its region, every slot to
the pictures it has, every picture to the region it came in and a source
rectangle to its picture. Without a window server the window manager
composes in its own process as before.

`x86-scene` 6: the window server greeted and composing, and every picture
in a region of its own; 1950 passes composed by the window server and again
by the Lua, and not one pixel differs; a window shown for three seconds and
closed - 20 pictures held before it, 22 while it was open, 20 after.
**Controls**, in one run, three failures: the server's desktop colour off by
one bit, and 18,830,786 pixels differ; the forgetting switched off, and the
pictures held went 54, 56, 56; the stamp made private, and "a 503x18
picture with no region of its own". `test_draw` 16: a drag's label drawn
last and only inside the rectangle composed; **control**: the label not
drawn. The whole gate, 62 of 62, in 7:00.

**Measured, and it costs a round trip.** `frames`, 0.11.118 against this,
under QEMU on one processor: a composing pass 0.97 to 3.54 ms idle, 0.48 to
0.95 with a cube turning, 1.59 to 2.37 with four stacked; the window
manager's busy time 336 to 382, 744 to 1041 and 1377 to 1607 ms - because
it waits while the server composes. Timed inside, with a cube turning, in
counter ticks a pass: composing and showing 757,000 in the window manager's
process, 740,000 in the window server's - the same work at the same speed -
and 1,160,000 for the call around it, so the round trip is 420,000 a pass,
about a quarter of a millisecond, and writing the scene 43,000. That is
QEMU switching address spaces, where every switch empties its whole
translation cache and both sides walk their pages in again; the number
that decides is the M700's (D6). What takes the window manager out of the
wait is D4, where commits go to the window server and a pass is not a call.

**On the M700** (i7-6700, eight cores, 1720x1440), `frames 8`, 0.11.118
against 0.11.119: a cube turning, a composing pass 0.14 to 0.16 ms and the
window manager's busy time 220 to 239 ms over 3100 passes, the worst pass
1.19 to 1.26 ms; idle, 0.71 to 0.91 ms over the 25 passes that composed
anything. **The round trip is about 20 microseconds on the machine**,
against a quarter of a millisecond under QEMU - the emulator's number was
the emulator's, as `CLAUDE.md` says they are.

## 18.515 Astra D3b-2, step 3: the screen given back when the window manager goes

`docs/astra-display.md` D3b-2 step 3. The window manager greets the window
server with an endpoint of its own (`WS.alive`), which goes when its process
does. The window server takes the screen from the console when it is handed
the back buffer - the window manager no longer takes it itself when there is
a window server - and while it has a manager it waits for requests at most a
fifth of a second before asking whether that endpoint still names anything.
When it does not - the window manager ended or crashed - the server lets go of
every picture, the scene and the back buffer, hides the display's pointer and
gives the screen back, and the console clears it and prints from the top.
Before this, a window manager that crashed left its last frame on the screen,
since only it could give the screen back.

`x86-scene` 7: `kill wm` from Telnet, "the window manager is gone; the screen
is the console's", and the screen 100% one colour where the desktop was 31%.
**Control**: the server not looking at the endpoint, and the screen is never
given back. Starting the window manager again is not checked: from Telnet it
is not lent the door, which is right, and the console's shell does not answer
after the kill - on 0.11.118 as well, so older than this; `roadmap.md`, *Known
and unexplained*. The whole gate, 62 of 62 in 6:35 - after a first run that
failed 17 suites on a full disk, 600 MB free, which a baseline build of mine
in the scratchpad had taken.

## 18.516 Astra D3b-2, step 4: the window manager composes nothing

`docs/astra-display.md` D3b-2 step 4. The window manager's Lua composing is
gone: the passes in `compose.lua` (what each window shows of a rectangle,
then the desktop and the windows back to front), `drawwindow.lua`, the Lua
drawing of the desktop, the arrow, a drag's label, shadows and kept corners,
the strips' own composing, `wm compose-check`, and the fallback to composing
in its own process. `compose.lua` describes the scene, makes one call, and
copies the damage to a watcher. The window manager no longer maps the
screen: its size comes from the window server's greeting, and with no window
server it says so and starts no desktop. It says how many pictures the
window server holds whenever that changes. 1046 lines out, 113 in.

`x86-scene` 7, reworked now that there is no Lua composing to compare
against (`test_draw` holds the scene on the Mac): the window server greeted
and composing, every picture handed over and no pass refused, through the
same desktop as before; the desktop on the screen, 31% one colour; a window's
pictures 20, 22 and 20; the screen the console's after `kill wm`, 100% one
colour. **Controls**, in one run: the server never putting what it composed
on the screen - 96% one colour with the desktop up, and the give-back check
fails with it; the forgetting off - the pictures held climb from 43 to 59
and never come down.
The whole gate, 61 of 62: `x86-display-4` read a screendump shorter than
its size (`IndexError` in `_colour_area`) with 1.7 GB free on the disk; alone,
79 of 79 in 3:08.

## 18.517 TCP sends a window of segments, not one at a time

The M700 sent a whole VNC frame, 1720x1440 and 9.9 MB, in 7.2 s: 1.4 MB a
second over a gigabit card (`roadmap.md`, remote 8). Timed from the Mac,
the request was answered in 44 ms and the bytes took 7.04 s - so the time was
the sending, and `net.c` said why in its own words: "one segment in flight,
retransmitted on a timer". One 1460-byte segment a round trip of about a
millisecond is exactly 1.4 MB a second.

Now a window: as many segments as the congestion window, the far end's
window and the ring allow; RFC 5681's slow start from ten segments, then a
segment a round trip; on three repeated acknowledgements everything from
`snd_una` goes again at once and the window halves; on the timer, the same
with the window back to a segment. Two things the loss suite found on the
way: QEMU's network shrinks its window while it holds segments past a gap,
so repeated acknowledgements are counted whatever the window (RFC 5681 asks
it unchanged, and no loss was seen before the one-second timer); and after
going back, the far end acknowledges past where `snd_nxt` has got to again,
which was refused as impossible and stopped the connection - so `snd_max`,
the highest byte sent, bounds what is taken.

**QEMU cannot show the speed**: its network acknowledges at once, and a frame
takes 0.47 s with one segment in flight or many. What it can show:
`x86-servers` 35 now has the stack's own line - "has sent 4 MB, at most N
bytes in flight" - say more than a segment: 9368 bytes. **Control**: the
window held to one segment, and "at most 1460 bytes in flight" fails it.
**`x86-tcploss`** (new, 4 checks, 40 s): booted with `opt/kosmos/net_drop=37`,
which leaves one data segment in 37 unsent as if lost, three whole frames by
VNC arrive in 8 to 11 s each and match the screen, with 107 segments lost.
Its controls were the two faults above, each found by it: a frame that never
finished, and frames past a minute. The whole gate, 63 of 63 in 6:55.

What bounds it next is the ring: 16 KB each way (`tcpring.h`, whose comment
says its size was never measured), so at most 16 KB in flight - about 16 MB a
second at a millisecond. The M700 is the measurement.

## 18.518 Datagrams, and a multicast group joined (N11a)

`docs/sharing.md` N11a, the first step of finding SMB servers on the network.
The stack had UDP "as far as DNS and DHCP need it, and no further". Now
`NET_OP_UDP_BIND` binds a port - any free one for 0 - and joins a multicast
group when one is named, and answers like a connection made at once: a
handle and a region of the two rings in `tcpring.h`, in which whole
datagrams travel, each a `struct net_datagram` (who sent it, or where it
goes, its port and length) and its bytes, published once all of it is
there; `PUSH`, `WAIT`, `POLL` and `CLOSE` mean what they mean for a
connection. A datagram that finds its ring full is dropped, as UDP may; one
to an address whose Ethernet address is not known yet waits a second for
the answer. A group joined is reported with IGMPv2 (to the group, a time to
live of one) and left on close when nobody else here is in it; a router's
query - which carries the Router Alert option, so IP options are taken for
IGMP alone - is answered for each group still joined. Datagrams to a group
go to its own Ethernet address (01:00:5e and its low 23 bits) with a time to
live of 255, multicast DNS's. The Intel card takes every multicast frame
(RCTL.MPE) and the stack keeps those of a group joined. `opt/kosmos/net_address`
gives a machine its address at boot where no DHCP answers. The network kit's
`net.udp`, the namespace's `fs.udp`, and `udp`, a program: `send`, `listen`
and `echo`.

**`x86-udp`** (new, 6 checks): QEMU's user network carries no multicast, so
the machine is put on a wire of its own - `-netdev dgram`, each frame a UDP
datagram between two ports on the Mac's loopback - with `10.9.0.2/24` from
the boot, running `udp echo 5353 224.0.0.251`; `tools/run_udp.py` is the
other machine on it, answering ARP and speaking IPv4 and UDP in Python: the
IGMP report for 224.0.0.251 seen; the hello to the group on the group's
Ethernet address, with a time to live of 255; a datagram to the group said
by the program and echoed to its sender after an ARP question; one to the
machine's address echoed to port 7777; one to 224.0.0.252, not joined, left
alone. **Controls**, in one run: no report on joining, and every group taken
as joined - "no IGMP report" and "a datagram to a group the machine did not
join was taken". `-netdev socket,mcast=` was tried first: QEMU's own
recording (`filter-dump`) showed the machine sending, and on this Mac none
of it reached a listener on the group.
The whole gate, 63 of 64: `x86-film`, whose sound gaps under load are carded,
failed once alone as well (1300 samples, a run of zeros at 1.62 s) and then
passed twice alone.

## 18.519 The DNS message in one place (N11b)

`docs/sharing.md` N11b. The resolver's names - written as labels, stepped
over - leave `net.c` for `user/servers/dnsmsg.c`, which multicast DNS will
share, and grow what `mdnsd` needs: a name read back with its compression
pointers followed, a header, a question and a record with its data held
inside the message. **A pointer must point backwards**, to a name before it,
which is how every encoder writes them and which makes a loop impossible to
read rather than something to count.

`tools/test_dnsmsg.c` (host, 19 checks): a name written and read; a
multicast DNS answer as a printer or a Mac sends one - PTR, SRV, TXT and A,
each name compressed against another - read record by record to the
message's last byte; and refused: a pointer onto itself, one forward, one
back to its own name's start, a label past the end, a reserved label type, a
name of 320 bytes, a record that says it is longer than the message.
**Control**: the 255-byte limit taken out - which first did *not* bite,
since the test's 256-byte buffer refused the long name before the rule
could; the check now reads into room enough, and fails without the rule.
The whole gate, 62 of 64: `x86-film`'s carded flake, and `x86-kernel`'s "smp:
a new thread avoids a loaded core", a placement test that reads the load;
both pass alone, the kernel's 198 of 198.

## 18.520 mdnsd: what is on the network, by name (N11c)

`docs/sharing.md` N11c. `mdnsd` (`user/servers/mdnsd.c`), a server in C
started by init after the network stack, binds port 5353 and the group
224.0.0.251 (N11a) once the machine has an address - trying every second
until it does - and answers `/Discovery`, mounted for every program as
`/Network` is, in a declared shape (`mdnsproto.h`): `BROWSE` a service type,
answered at once with how many instances are known and asking the network
at once and after one, two and four seconds, then every minute, while it is
asked about in the last ten seconds; `INSTANCE` n of a type - its name, host,
port and address - an item a message; `RESOLVE` a `.local` name, the caller
parked until the address comes or its wait ends. Answers are read with
`dnsmsg.c`, twice over - names and services, then addresses - so an
address is taken whatever order a message lists its records in; an instance
whose SRV or address did not come is asked for after the message. Kept for
the time to live given, a goodbye (a time to live of 0) taken at once, and
**only what somebody here asked about**: a stranger's records are read and
forgotten. `mdns.lua` for programs and `mdns`, a program: `browse TYPE
[SECONDS]` and `resolve NAME`.

**`x86-mdns`** (new, 5 checks, three boots): the wire and the Python peer of
`x86-udp`, the peer now a file server called Studio answering as a Mac or a
NAS does - a PTR, SRV, TXT and A in one message, compressed. `mdns browse
_smb._tcp`: the question to the group at a time to live of 255, and "Studio
studio.local:445 10.9.0.1"; `mdns resolve studio.local`: 10.9.0.1; and
`stranger.local`, whose A the peer sent before anybody asked and then does
not answer for: "nobody answered for that name". **Controls**, in one run:
every A kept, and the SRV's port read two bytes early - "studio.local:?"
and "stranger.local is 10.9.0.66".
The whole gate, 63 of 65: `x86-film`'s carded flake, and **`x86-udp`, a
real one** - it ran `udp echo 5353 224.0.0.251`, and port 5353 is
`mdnsd`'s from boot now, so the program was refused, and said only "udp: 13"
since it printed the code and not the sentence. The suite has a port and a
group of its own (9000, 239.255.0.1), `udp` prints the sentence, and
`x86-udp` passes 6 of 6 again.

## 18.521 The TCP ring, measured: 64 KB each way

18.517 gave TCP a window and could not show its speed under QEMU; on the
M700 (Diego, 10 October: "You can restart the m700 whenever you like to
test") it did not change much: a whole 9.9 MB frame in 6.5 s, 1.5 MB a
second, at most 7 KB in flight. So the stack now says, once a connection has
sent 4 MB, why sending stopped as well as the most in flight: the ring empty
(the program behind) or the window full (the network behind), with the
segments, the acknowledgements and the time. On the M700: **663 stops with
the ring empty in 4 MB, and none with the window full** - the program
refilled the 16 KB ring about once a scheduler tick, so what went was a
ring a tick. `tcpring.h` had said its size was a guess that "a measurement
of throughput against window size" should decide.

The ring is 64 KB each way now - the most the far end can be offered
without window scaling, the window being sixteen bits - and a connection a
132 KB region. On the M700: **a whole frame in 1.53 s, from 6.6; 6.5 MB a
second, 4.3 times as fast.** The ring still runs empty (194 stops in 4 MB),
so what limits it next is how soon the writer is woken to refill it, and
after that window scaling.

The stack's line had grown past the 160 bytes a console line holds, so
`x86-tcploss` read "lost 1" off a line that said "lost 106": it is shorter
now - "net: 4 MB to ADDRESS, at most N in flight, T ms, S sent, A acked;
stops: R ring, W window; lost L" - and both suites read it.

**The gate found what the bigger ring broke**: `x86-tls` and all seven mail
suites - a 200 KB page over TLS "cut short: 15360 of the 204800 bytes", with
a TLS error. The TLS Kit read the connection into its 16 KB buffer by asking
for everything that had come and keeping the first 16 KB - "a ring holds no
more than this", its comment said, true of a 16 KB ring - and dropping the
rest. `conn:read(most)` now takes at most what the reader holds and leaves
the rest in the ring, and the TLS Kit says how much. The failing suite was
the control: `x86-tls` 9 and `x86-mail` 21 pass with the fix.

On the M700, `mdns browse _smb._tcp` and `_airplay._tcp` found the network's
own: a Mac's file sharing on port 445 with its address, and three AirPlay
receivers (N11c, on real hardware; their names are Diego's and not here).
The whole gate, 64 of 65: `x86-film`, which passes alone - and which has
failed in every whole gate of 10 October, so its card says so.

## 18.522 Servers seen, in Tracker, and reached by name (N11d)

`docs/sharing.md` N11d, which closes N11. Tracker, with the network pass it
already makes, asks `/Discovery` for `_smb._tcp` - answered at once from what
`mdnsd` keeps, and keeping it asking - and its Network group lists each
server heard of that `smbfs` does not already have, as seen and not signed
into: its page says what it calls itself, its address and port, and offers
Sign in, which opens Connect at its address. Connect takes a `.local` name:
asked of `/Discovery` with a wait of one tick, so the window never waits,
and again on its clock; `mdnsd` now keeps a question alive five seconds after
a short wait has been answered "not yet", so the answer is there for the
next look. `smbfs` is given the address.

`x86-mdns` 7, a fourth boot: the desktop on the wire, Tracker's Network group
"Studio seen", and Connect given `smb://studio.local` saying "studio.local
is 10.9.0.1". **Controls**, in one run: Tracker not passing what it heard -
"tracker: network none"; Connect handing the name to `smbfs` as typed -
"Asking studio.local". The same run failed the stranger check through a
race in the test, not the server: the peer's unasked record could arrive
after the program had asked for that name, when keeping it is right; `mdns
after 3 resolve` asks three seconds on, and the suite passed twice after.
The whole gate, 62 of 65: `x86-share-2` (the Mac's peer "not answering"
partway through a 64 MB read), `x86-mdns` (Tracker not yet listing in 60 s -
the desktop boot now has two minutes) and `x86-display-1`, all three passing
alone. `x86-share-2` under load is the one to watch after the TCP changes.

## 18.523 The app switcher, Super+Tab, and Alt+Tab

`docs/switcher.html`, agreed as drawn on 10 October ("All mockups are
perfect"). `user/lib/wm/switcher.lua`, a part of the window manager:
Super+Tab, held, shows the running applications - each its icon, the
windows of one process together, in the order last used, which is the
stack's - in a panel in the middle of the screen, the second lit and named.
Tab moves on and Shift+Tab or the left arrow back; the down arrow opens a
row of the lit application's windows, each a small picture of the buffer it
committed, and the up arrow closes it; Esc puts it away; Q asks the lit
application's windows to close, as their close box does; letting go of
Super brings the lit application forward, back to front so the window used
last has the keys, or the one window chosen. The pointer lights an icon and
a click chooses it. Its keys are the events', taken first by `capture_key`;
while it shows, every key and character is its own. The panel is a picture
in a region the scene blends over every window and under the pointer - the
scene grew a panel (`scene_core.c`, the wire, the window server), and
`test_draw` 18 holds it: by its own alpha, and nothing where it is clear.
Icons are stretched with an alpha of 255 - without it `stretch` copies, and
their clear corners came out black on the first look.

**Alt+Tab** steps the windows with nothing shown, which Super+Tab did
before; Alt+Shift+Tab steps back. The keyboard sends no Alt, so Alt+Tab
arrives as a Tab and Alt+Shift+Tab as `ESC [ Z`; both are kept from the
window while the left Alt is held - not the right, which is AltGr on a
Spanish keyboard and types @.

**`x86-switcher`** (new, 11 checks): Calculator and Preferences opened on a
desktop, keys as QEMU's events - Super held, Tab pressed and let go, Super
let go - "Preferences, [Calculator], Log, Processes, Tracker, Monitor", the
panel's dark on the screen; Tab on, Shift+Tab back, the windows row and out;
Super let go and Calculator has the keys; Esc changing nothing; a click on
the second icon choosing what is listed second; Q quitting Calculator, its
process ending; Alt+Tab stepping the windows with no panel. **Controls**, in
one run: Super+Tab opening nothing, and Alt+Tab stepping nothing - 10 of 11
fail.
The gate found two of its own on the way. **Super chords broken**: Alt+Tab's
holding back of `ESC [` (a possible Shift+Tab) also ran with Super held, and
every Super chord begins `ESC [ 1 ; 9` - `x86-dock` and `x86-display-3`
stopped at theirs; only the left Alt starts it now. **`x86-share-2` under
load**, the second time since 18.521: a 64 MB read from the Mac's Samba
stalled "not answering". This stack keeps nothing out of order, and the 64 KB
ring had become a 64 KB window offered - some forty-five segments a burst,
one lost and the rest dropped and sent again; the window offered is 16 KB
again (`TCP_RECEIVE_WINDOW`), as it was while it never failed, and sending
keeps the whole ring. The whole gate, 66 of 66 in 6:56.

## 18.524 Maps: a drag moves the map rather than drawing it again

The card "Maps: dragging the map feels sluggish". Measured first: a dragged
frame took 840 ms under QEMU, of which 840 were the map's tiles drawn from
their vectors - the names 3 to 6 ms, the window's chrome and commit nothing.
Two changes, each measured:

- **A tile kept as a picture** at a size of whole pixels, every whole zoom:
  a network tile's on the land's colour, copied; the region's clear,
  blended over - 840 to 565 ms, since the region's tiles past its deepest
  zoom are drawn 2048 pixels a side at zoom 16 and too big to keep (16 MB).
- **The map kept as a layer, which a drag shifts**: drawing one of those
  big tiles cost 120 ms whole and 1 ms into a one-pixel clip - the cost is
  pixels - so the tiles drawn last are kept in two map-sized pictures that
  take turns, a frame that only moved the centre shifts them by whole pixels
  and draws the strip that came into view, and anything else (a zoom, the
  look, the window's size, a tile arriving) draws all of it. **A dragged
  frame 840 ms to 56 ms, fifteen times**, and a frame drawn again in place
  9 to 15 ms. The names go on top each frame.

Maps says, when a drag ends, its frames and the mean and worst of the map
and of the whole. `x86-maps` 27: after the drag, the map zoomed in a step and
out again - the same place, drawn whole - and its pixels held to the dragged
ones, at least 97% the same. **Control**: the layer shifted the wrong way,
27.4% the same.

## 18.525 Shortcuts K1: a chord as words, drawn as keycaps

The first step of Shortcuts (`docs/shortcuts.md`). `keys.caps` takes a chord
written as words - `Super+Shift+3`, `Ctrl+W,Q` for a sequence - into the
caps drawn, each spelled one way however it was written ("control", "cmd"
and "win" are Ctrl and Super), and refuses a word that is not a key;
`keys.spelling` does the same for a word typed into a search. `g:keycaps`
in the UI kit draws one as raised keys with "then" between steps. The
window manager's edit keys are declared once, with their words, in
`wm.lua`'s `EDIT_BINDINGS`, which its dispatch is built from - the list
`wm/keys.lua` kept beside it is gone - and every key it lists is spelled as
a chord. The current Shortcuts window draws them as keycaps, and says how
many it drew and how many were not keys.

Smaller than the design first said: the text keys that work everywhere are
the window manager's four, so there is no `ui.TEXT_KEYS`.

`host` (`test_keys.lua`, 72): chords as caps, sequences, aliases, a
character key, function keys, refusals. **Control**: "control" dropped from
the spellings, 2 checks fail. `x86-dock` 54: the modal Shortcuts window
drew 20 keys in 3 groups as keycaps, none refused. **Control**: `Ctrl+W,Q`
spelled back as `Control-W Q`, "1 not keys: Control-W Q".

## 18.526 Shortcuts K2: a person's own keys, in the window manager

The window manager's half of making and changing shortcuts
(`docs/shortcuts.md`). Each Super binding has an `action` and a `group`;
Super alone and Super Tab are fixed. The dispatch table is built from the
defaults and the setting `/Home/Preferences/shortcuts` - only what differs,
each entry in full (`{ keys = "Super+T", action = "open", program = ... }`,
`{ keys = "Super+M", action = "hide" }`) - read when the window manager
starts and handed again by Shortcuts in `handlers.keys`, each entry checked
and anything else set aside and said. A window with the keyboard may
listen: the next Super chords are posted to it as `chord` events, not acted
on, the switcher included, and listening ends when it loses the keyboard;
a window without it is refused, and the refusal said. The answer to
`shortcuts` is paged, as the window list is (`wmproto.shortcuts`): with
groups and actions it no longer fit one message - "value does not fit in a
message", and the window drew nothing, found by `x86-dock`.

`x86-shortcuts` 9, new: the setting saved and applied; Super T a Terminal;
hiding moved from Super H to Super M, the old chord doing nothing; the
switcher's entry and a Control one set aside; Super Q and Super Tab heard
by the listening window and not acted on; a window without the keyboard
refused; listening over once another window had it; the setting read when
the desktop started again. **Controls**, together: the focus check taken
out of listening, and the setting not read at the start - 4 checks fail,
the two of each.

## 18.527 Shortcuts K3: the window, as drawn

Shortcuts redrawn as `docs/shortcuts.html` has it: the header with the
book, the title and the search; the sidebar's groups with their pictures
and counts, the chosen one filled, and Yours under Made here; each group's
title with its picture, its rows - what a key does on the left, its keycaps
on the right, every other row shaded, Change beside a key that can move,

`s:wash`, the paint command, `g:wash`), which dims the window behind the

Diego, on the M700: "printi screen saves a black image, not the actual

only the image's assets; a path, `/Home/Captures/...`, found nothing and

decoded from there, the last four kept - is now `pictures.lua`, one door,

`pictures.kept`); the window manager's copy and its stale comment are gone.

Nothing had looked inside Photo since the change. `x86-dock` 55: a capture
taken by the keys is opened in Photo and its frame sampled on a 12 by 12
grid - many colours, not one - then closed by its handle and waited for.

## 18.529 A window being resized keeps its picture's size

Diego, on the M700: "when resizing a window, for a couple of milliseconds
it looks that the app stretches to the new dimensions and then redraws in
the new size". The frame took its new size at once and the scene stretched
the old picture into it until the application drew again. Now a window
that makes a region at the new size is marked `stale` from the resize to
its first picture at the new size (`SC_STALE`, `scene_core.c`'s
`stale_into`): the old picture is shown as it is in the frame's top left,
its last column drawn on across the new room, its last row down, the
corner from its last pixel - the window's background, nearly always. A
window that cannot make a new region is still stretched, as before.

`host` (`test_draw`, 25): a 40 by 30 picture of all different pixels in a
60 by 50 frame - shown pixel for pixel, the room right its last column, the
room below its last row column for column, the corner its last pixel,
nothing past the frame; without the flag, stretched. **Control**: the stale
branch taken out, 3 checks fail. Gate 67 of 67.

## 18.530 Processes: Nebula, and what draws means now

Diego, on the M700: the kernel's row should be "nebula", of kind
"kernel"; "the draws column now is empty in most of the processes", "now
deskbar says direct in draws? why?". Blank was always a process with no
window - most of them, servers and drivers - and since every window paints
its own pixels there was no "commands" left, so every application said
"direct". The column now says what differs: `kit` for a window the UI kit
draws in its own process, `pixels` for one that draws every pixel itself,
`screen` for the window server, blank for no window - the window list
carries `kit` (a window's `draws_itself`). The row Nebula, kind kernel.

`x86-sysapps` 27: Processes says, beside its rows, each one's kind and how
it draws - Nebula a kernel; the window server the screen, Processes the
kit, `binfs` nothing. **Control**: the window server's `screen` taken out,
"windowserver ('server', '-')".

## 18.531 A new window shown only once it has drawn

Diego, on the M700, opening the launcher: "for some milliseconds it draws a
black rectangle and then on top it draws the actual app drawer", "its like
its drawing twice something". A window was shown the moment it was made,
and its region is empty - black - until the application's first frame; the
launcher's first paint is long enough to see. A window with a region of its
own is now held back until its first commit (`win.drawn`), then shown
frame, shadow and all ("wm: Quick drawn, shown after 214 ms") - **but at
most half a second**: one that has not drawn by then is shown anyway, so a
hung application keeps a window to move and close, and its buffers start in
the look's window colour rather than the black of fresh pages. The first
version held a window back for good, and `x86-display-4`'s hung application
had none; the harness then waits for a window to be *shown*, not opened,
and for the hung one's title rather than looking once - its spin now begins
before the pass that shows it.

`x86-shortcuts` 18: Quick, drawing at once, shown when it has drawn and not
before; Slow, three seconds from drawing, shown at half a second in the
window colour - not black - and its own picture once it draws. **Control**
(the first version, before the limit): shown at once again, "a window not
yet drawn was shown: 000000 where the desktop was f6f5f4".

## 18.532 The machine says when it is ready

Diego, 10 October 2026: "Why don't you do a small script that when kosmos
boots it send a small message to the mac over udp or tcp to let it know the
kosmos is booted and ready". The Mac restarting the M700 watched Telnet go
away and come back, and missed the going on a quick restart - "did not go
away" about a machine that had, twice that evening. Now `ready` (a program,
`user/bin/programs/ready.lua`) is started by init from the command line's
`opt/kosmos/ready=ADDRESS:PORT`, waits for the desktop on a boot to one,
and sends three datagrams a second apart: `kosmos ready 0.11.137 build ...
up 14.2 s desktop`. `make netboot` adds the word with this Mac's address and
port 47700, and `kosmos_telnet.py restart` listens there rather than guessing
when to look.

`x86-udp` 7: on its own wire, a machine told `ready=10.9.0.1:47700` says

## 18.533 The network measured: 50 MB/s each way on the M700

Diego, 11 October 2026: "can you measure how much it takes to send a 100 mb
to kosmos from the mac?". `netspeed` (`user/bin/programs/netspeed.lua`)
reads a connection to its end keeping nothing, or writes N MB; its peer on
the Mac (`tools/netspeed_peer.py`) serves bytes on 47701 and swallows them
on 47702, and times its own end. On the M700 (0.11.138, I219, gigabit to
the Mac through the house's switch):

    Mac to M700   100 MB in 1.92 s   52 MB/s   (both ends agree)
    M700 to Mac   100 MB in 2.06 s   49 MB/s

About half of what the wire carries (~112 MB/s). The 6 MB/s said that
evening was a figure from before the 64 KB ring; what was slow was Telnet's
`get`, base64 printed through the shell.

## 18.535 smbd signs in: the server side of sharing, N12a

`docs/sharing.md` N12a. The SMB Kit's socket gained a server's half -
`bind`, `listen`, `accept`, `poll` and `select`, each the Network Kit's C
door (`netclient.c` gained `net_client_listen`, `accept` and `poll` over the
stack's `NET_OP_LISTEN`, `ACCEPT` and `POLL`) - so libsmb2's own
`smb2_serve_port` runs on Kosmos with libsmb2 untouched. `smbd`
(`user/servers/smbd.c`), a role of `init.elf` started only when the boot
says `opt/kosmos/smbd=PORT ACCOUNT HASH`, answers NEGOTIATE and an NTLMv2
sign-in for one account against its NT hash, and refuses every share as
"bad network name" - by queuing that reply itself, since libsmb2's own for a
refusal is "not implemented". Shares are N12b.

`x86-smbd` 4, new: Samba's `smbclient` through a forwarded port signed in

## 18.536 smbd shares folders of /Home, read only: N12b

`docs/sharing.md` N12b. `smbd` is handed the disk's main door, which reaches
`/Home` and nothing else, and shares the folders the boot names
(`opt/kosmos/smbd_shares=Projects:/Home/Projects,Notes:/Home/Notes`): a
tree connect by name, any case; CREATE opening a file or folder that exists
and refusing write access, a delete on close and every disposition but open
as "access denied"; QUERY_DIRECTORY in pages that fit the client's room,
"." and ".." first, a pattern matched without case; QUERY_INFO's basic,
standard, all, network-open and attribute-tag facts, and the volume's;
READ from the disk into one region and out in the reply, up to 1 MB a read;
CLOSE; and an open file's id good only on its own connection and tree.

**libsmb2's directory encoder is wrong, and is left alone.** It writes each
entry's NextEntryOffset as the entry's place in the buffer, where MS-FSCC
2.4 counts from the entry itself, and pads to four where entries align to
eight. `smbclient` showed "." and "..", then `NT_STATUS_INFO_LENGTH_MISMATCH`.
`smbd` encodes FileIdBothDirectoryInformation and FileIdFullDirectoryInformation
itself and sends them through libsmb2's passthrough mode, on for the one
reply and off again.

`x86-smbd` 13, was 4: Samba's `smbclient` through a forwarded port, on a
disk made by the suite with made-up files: signed in over SMB 3.1.1;
`Projects` listed with its sizes and folder; `hello.txt`, a 1.5 MB file and
a file in a folder fetched byte for byte; the second share listed; a put
refused as read only; a climb never served; a share not offered "bad network
name"; a wrong password and another account refused; the server answering
after all of it; a machine not told to share answering nothing.

`host` gains `test_smbpath` 20: a name in a share as a path - backslashes
and slashes, the root, "." and ".." anywhere refused, a stream refused, a
long path refused, "..." and ".hidden" kept. `smbclient` cleans ".." before
it sends a name, so this is where the refusal is held.

**Controls**: every read at offset 0 - the 1.5 MB file did not arrive as it
is. That control first *passed*, and showed the test was what was wrong: the
file's "random" bytes were one byte repeated, a generator seeded afresh for
each, so a read from anywhere gave the right bytes. Made from one generator,
it bites. `smbpath.c` without its ".." refusal: 5 of 20 failed. The listing's
control is the first run, on libsmb2's encoder: "." and ".." and a mismatch.


## 18.537 A command line longer than 200 characters, over the network

On 11 October the M700, netbooted into 0.11.142 with smbd's two options on
its command line, came up at a bare `kosmos>` - no `/Home` from its stick,
no desktop, no Telnet, no smbd, no ready datagram - though it answered
ping. None of the line's words had arrived: the loader read
`kosmos.cmdline` into 200 bytes while `CMDLINE_MAX` was 384, and the line
was 278. From a stick a longer file is cut at the buffer, silently; over
the network the firmware's TFTP read fails when the buffer is too small,
and the kernel was told nothing. `mkusb_image.py` refused a stick's words
over 200, so sticks never met it; `netboot.py` checked nothing.

Now: the loader reads 384 characters of words (`CMDLINE_WORDS`) and keeps
room for its own after them (`CMDLINE_MAX` 640), and **refuses a longer
file in words** rather than boot with a line cut short - a cut line loses
its last words, and `/Home`'s GUID is among them. The kernel keeps 1,024
bytes of it (`hal/pc/memory.c`). `mkusb_image.py` and `netboot.py` both
refuse words over 384 when they write them.

`x86-netboot` 7, was 5: the line served padded to 362 characters with
`opt/kosmos/tail=reached` at its end, and the machine asked for it -
`tail: reached`; and a line over 384 refused by the loader with its
sentence, no prompt after it.

**Control**: the loader's buffer back at 200 bytes - over the network the
line did not arrive, `tail: nil`, "the disk: none": the M700's evening,
under OVMF.

## 18.538 smbd told through its own door: N12c-1

`docs/sharing.md` N12c-1. init starts `smbd` at every boot, idle; it holds
no port until its door (`user/include/smbdproto.h`) says START. The door is
lent as the keyring's doors are - by the shell and the desktop, to a
program the image serves that declares `kosmos: needs sharing` - and the
`sharing` program at the prompt is its first holder, the Servers window
the next (N12c-2). ACCOUNT carries a password once: `smbd` takes MD4 of its
UTF-16 and keeps that NT hash in the keyring, under KEY_KIND_SHARING
through the keyring's new `sharing` door, which sees that kind alone.
SHARES_CLEAR and SHARE set the folders one at a time, a folder of `/Home`
that exists. Serving, `smbd` reads its door from libsmb2's `extra_service`
hook, between passes at most 100 ms apart; STOP sets libsmb2's
`stop_requested`, and the loop's end lets every handle and share go. The
boot options `opt/kosmos/smbd` and `smbd_shares` are gone.

`x86-smbd` 18, was 13: a copy of `sharing` in `/Home` not handed the door;
a start before any password refused; the account in the keyring under its
own kind, the password nowhere in its listing; then the thirteen; then
stopped, nothing answering, and started again, serving.

**Controls**: the hash taken of the password's UTF-8 rather than UTF-16 -
every sign-in a logon failure, nine checks; STOP not setting
`stop_requested` - smbd never stopped. The door lent without
`keyring_grant`'s rule did **not** bite: a file in `/Home` carries no
`needs` words at all, since only the image's store reads them, so on that
path the rule is a second guard and the first is the store.

sends it once; Guests off; the name on the network; Start with the machine,

answers STATE from a door thread of its own at once and hands everything

## 18.540 Who is connected, and This network only: N12c-3

`docs/sharing.md` N12c-3. `smbd` keeps a visitor for each connection - its
address, which the Network Kit's accept now keeps (`net_conn.peer`), when it
came, the account it signed in as and the share it last opened - in slabs
that never move and are never freed, so the door's thread answers
CONNECTION at once while the serving thread fills them. DISCONNECT closes
the visitor's connection; the next pass lets it go. With This network only,
a sign-in from an address outside this machine's subnet - asked of the stack
(`net_client_address`) at each sign-in - is refused as a logon failure.
`sharing who` and `sharing disconnect ID` at the prompt; the page's Connected
now, each with Disconnect, and its This network only switch, on by default.

`x86-smbd` 31, was 23: an smbclient that stays, on a terminal of its own -
on a pipe it holds its output back - listed by `sharing who` as kosmos in
Projects, and told NT_STATUS_CONNECTION_DISCONNECTED at `sharing
disconnect`; the netmask set to one address, the Mac refused, and set back,
let in; in the window, the visitor under Connected now and its Disconnect.

Two things the first runs taught: `use` is not at the prompt, so the suite
writes an address with `string.char`; and a line waited for by a word the
typed command also contains is found in the command's echo.

**Controls**: sign-in not asking the network - the Mac outside it let in;
Disconnect closing nothing - both visitors not told.

## 18.541 The share list over IPC$: N12d's first step, and the dock's rocket

`docs/sharing.md` N12d. On the M700 the Mac's Finder signed in to `smbd` -
SMB 3.1.1, the password right - and then asked for `IPC$`, the pipe share
a client asks what is shared through; refused, it gave up, even given a
share by name (`smb://192.168.1.40/Music` opened Music and still asked).
`smbd` now offers `IPC$` and its `srvsvc` pipe: what is written into it, or
sent through FSCTL_PIPE_TRANSCEIVE, is answered by `smbrpc.c` - a BIND for
srvsvc in NDR accepted, MS-RPCE's bind time feature negotiation
acknowledged with no features, NetrShareEnum (levels 0 and 1, IPC$ among
the shares), NetrShareGetInfo, NetrServerGetInfo 101, and anything else
the fault "operation out of range". Over IPC$, no DFS: "not found".

**libsmb2's ioctl is passthrough or nothing**: without it the request's
input is dropped for every control code but VALIDATE_NEGOTIATE_INFO, and
the reply's output refused - smbclient's bind on the pipe ended
NT_STATUS_CONNECTION_DISCONNECTED. Every connection now runs in
passthrough; each other place it changes is a client's path or something
`smbd` refuses or encodes itself.

`host` gains `test_smbrpc` 18: a BIND of three contexts - srvsvc in NDR
accepted, the feature negotiation acknowledged, a stranger refused; the
share list at levels 1 and 0, every name read back out of the NDR;
NetrShareGetInfo by "music" finding Music, and "Private" WERR 0x906;
NetrServerGetInfo's name; an unknown operation a fault; half a PDU waited
for; a non-DCE one refused; an answer too big for its room refused.
`x86-smbd` 32, was 31: `smbclient -L` lists Projects and Notes as Disk and
IPC$ as IPC.

**Controls**: each entry's comment pointer left out at level 1 - four of
the eighteen failed, and `smbclient -L` listed nothing. The suite's has
both changes in one image; the evidence for passthrough is the run before
it, the bind's connection dropped.

**The dock's Kosmos button wears the rocket** - Haiku's Launchbox, as

icon for the kosmos button in the dock?". `x86-dock` 56, was 55: no blue
in the button's picture, which the three cubes have, and red, which the
rocket has. **Control**: the cubes back - 7 blue pixels, failed.

## 18.542 Finder mounts a share; Start with the machine; the keyring taken back

`docs/sharing.md` N12d. On the M700, Diego, 11 October: "it works!" - the
Mac's Finder connected to `smb://192.168.1.40` as diego and showed Music.
Found one refusal at a time, with `smbd` now saying every request it
refuses and what was asked (all but the normal ends - no more names, the
end of a file, an empty pipe):

- **`lsarpc`**, opened after the share list: LsarOpenPolicy(2) and
  LsarClose a handle; LsarGetUserName the account and this machine as its
  domain; LsarLookupNames (opnum 14, the one Finder asked, twice) the
  account's SID - S-1-5-21 and three fixed numbers, RID 1000 - and any
  other name not mapped. Any operation still not answered is a fault and
  said with its number.
- **A compound's related file id**: CREATE, QUERY_INFO and CLOSE in one,
  the last two naming the file as all ones. `smbd` keeps the last file each
  connection opened, and forgets it when a CREATE fails.

**Start with the machine did not**: at boot it asked the keyring for the
account before `/Home`, on the stick, was there. A start from the boot is now
patient - `smbd` waits and asks again each second, and serves when it
answers. And under that, worse: **the keyring set aside the M700's whole
file** - the reader in `keyfile.c` held an entry's kind to SMB..MAIL, and
the sharing account is kind 5. Fixed with `KEY_KIND_LAST` in `keyproto.h`;
and since `keyring.md` promises nothing is lost by trying again, a keyring
that opens empty now takes back the newest set-aside file that opens with
this machine's key - which on the M700 brought the file back.

`host`: `test_smbrpc` 24, was 18 - lsarpc's bind, OpenPolicy2,
GetUserName, LookupNames, an operation not answered; `test_keyfile`'s 200
entries now cycle through every kind up to `KEY_KIND_LAST`. `x86-smbd` 34,
was 32: a patient start waiting for the keyring and serving when the
password is kept; libsmb2's own stat (`smb2-stat-sync`), a related
compound, answered. `x86-keyring` new, 20: the ARM suite on x86, and a
fourth case - a set-aside keyring holding mail's entry taken back.

**Controls**: the reader's old limit - 2 of 5,500 failed; the related id
ignored - libsmb2's stat failed (found by accident first: a control's
image left unrebuilt); taking back never tried - 2 of 20.
`smbclient allinfo` turned out not to send a related compound, so it is
not the check.

should". A page taller than the window scrolled by the wheel alone, and a
TrackPoint has none. The page now carries the kit's pill along its right
edge below the header, drawn and dragged by `ui.scrollbar` and
`ui.scrollbar_mouse` - the same bar Processes and Log View have, so a drag
that drifts off it carries on, and the trough pages. `ui.scrollbar_thumb`

ground that is not opaque now takes `over`, with the coverage as the ink's
alpha; the lanes keep their speed on a window's opaque ground, 3.4x.

## 18.545 Quick Look, Q2: a PDF as its pages; a read into a region from memory

Space on a PDF in Tracker shows it as its pages, one under another, as the
PDF viewer draws them - through the PDF Kit (`pdf.open`, `pdf.render`) into
a surface a page at the panel's width, lent to the painter by name
(`ui.lend_picture`, `gc:lent`) so the window draws it without a copy. Pages
are drawn as they come into view and the four nearest kept; the wheel
scrolls, and a badge says which page is at the top.

**Found by the suite: `fs.read_into` did nothing on ramfs.** On a machine
with no disk `/Home` is served from memory, as `/Temporary` always is, and
ramfs answers a read with the bytes; it has no pages to lend. The
namespace's ramfs path took a read into a region as an ordinary read, and
`read_into` - which looks for a count, not a value - said nil with no
reason. So the PDF had "no %PDF header". `ram_request` now reads the pieces
and writes them into the caller's region itself, at its start, as the
disk's server does. On a disk this never happened, which is why the M700
and the T14 never showed it.

**And a test that drew nothing.** The suite's first PDF was coloured
squares with no font, so its pixels could be counted; the PDF Kit draws text
from an embedded face and no shapes yet - the PDF viewer the same - so it
was blank paper. The suite now makes its PDF with `tools/mkpdf.py`, which
embeds one: three pages of words, the paper and the darker pixels counted.

`x86-quicklook` 6 -> 9: the PDF shown as 3 pages; its first page's paper
and words on the screen; the wheel bringing the second into view. The
picture's wait is for the picture rather than for the first red pixel,
which four stray ones once satisfied.

**Control**: the ramfs path as it was - "no %PDF header; this is not a PDF",
the PDF shown as its facts.

## 18.548 Each processor says how fast it ran

Diego asked why the M700's older i7 renders faster than the T14's newer i5
(21.7 against 16.8 million rays a second, 1.29 to 1). Nothing in Kosmos sets
a processor's speed, so each runs where its firmware left it - most likely
its base clock, 3.4 GHz against 2.6, which is 1.31 - and that stayed an
inference until the cores could say.

**Now they can.** Each core reads its own IA32_APERF (0xE8), which counts at
the speed the core ran, and IA32_MPERF (0xE7), which counts at a fixed
reference rate, on its own tick - nowhere else can read them - into its
`percpu`; `sysinfo` carries both per core in `struct cpuload`, and
`sys.cpuload()` hands them on. Between two readings a core ran at
`counter_hz` times the ratio of the two differences (`pulse.speeds`). They
exist when CPUID.06H:ECX[0] says so, asked once rather than on every tick,
which under a hypervisor would be an exit a tick; the numbers checked
against Linux's `msr-index.h`. AArch64 has nothing like them on QEMU's
Cortex-A72 or the Pi's A76, and says so.

`clocks` prints each core's speed over a second, or that the processor
does not say - which is what QEMU's does.

`host` gains `test_pulse.lua`, 5: turbo (37 against 34 at 3.4 GHz is
3,700 MHz), a core at its reference, an idle core beside a busy one, and
no speeds at all where the processor keeps no counters. **Control**: the
ratio inverted - 2 of 5 fail.

What QEMU cannot show - the counters themselves - is read on the M700 and
the T14, and recorded here when it is.

## 18.550 Doom and Quake are heard

Diego, 11 October 2026: "doom and quake need sound support". Both now play
their sound effects through the audio server, written from C straight into
the stream's ring, as the Super Nintendo's sound always was - no Lua string
at either end, so a minute of gunfire allocates nothing.

**Doom** gets the sound module doomgeneric leaves to the platform
(`DG_sound_module`, with `FEATURE_SOUND` on and an empty `SDL_mixer.h`
standing in for the one `i_sound.c` includes, so id's file is not edited).
It claims the Sound Blaster Doom's settings choose; reads each effect's DMX
lump - three, the rate, the length, sixteen bytes skipped at either end,
8-bit unsigned samples - as Chocolate Doom does; steps sixteen channels
through them at their own rate against the device's in 16.16, with Doom's
volume and separation; and mixes six periods ahead of the speaker once a
tic, a tic and a little, about 35 ms. Music is a later step: it is MUS, a
score, and wants a synthesiser.

**Quake** mixes its own sound into a circular buffer it believes is a card's,
a tenth of a second ahead, and asks the card where it has got to; so each
time it asks, what it painted goes from the buffer into the ring, six
periods ahead and no more, and where that stopped is the card's position.
The engine reads its card through `shm`, which every backend sets itself -
the first run faulted at address 0x24 for want of it.

**One ring writer, not three.** The Super Nintendo's `feed` moved into
`audioring.h` as `audio_ring_feed`, with `audio_ring_room` beside it, and all
three use it. `test_audioring` 41 -> 53: frames in pieces that do not line up
with a period, a slot published only when full, in order, and what did not
fit said rather than written over the slot the server reads.

**Found by Quake's suite: the console's log was 4 KB.** Quake given a card
precaches its sounds when a map loads, a line each - eighty in one frame -
and the line saying which demo it played was overwritten before the Lua
side drained it. The spill ring in `stdio.c` is 64 KB.

**And the Super Nintendo had not been heard on x86.** Its suite set
`KOSMOS_AUDIO_WAV`, which adds a sound device to the ARM board alone, so on
x86-64 the console found none and paced by the clock. It, Doom's and Quake's
suites give the x86 machine an HDA card whose output QEMU writes to a file.

Out of the gate, each needing the game (`make doom-check`, `quake-check`,
`snes-check`): `run_doom.py` 3 -> 5, its sound opened and the demo heard,
loudest 20,526; `run_quake.py` 6 -> 8, its sound opened and its card found,
and heard; `run_snes.py` 7, sound out of the device, on x86 for the first
time. **Controls**: Doom not handed its ring - loudest sample 0; Quake not
handed it - "No sound: Quake was not given a stream".

waiting; and the tiles server's HTTPS suite.

## 18.555 Nebula's own memory, counted

Diego, 10 October: "why does the kernel does not show any memory
consumption in processes?". Its row was made up by Processes, at 0, and
the kernel reported only the machine's total and free pages.

**Counted where a page is taken.** `pmm` keeps what is in use when it
starts - the kernel's image and its own bitmap - and every page taken
since by the kernel for itself, through three calls beside the plain ones:
`pmm_alloc_kernel_page`, `pmm_alloc_kernel_contiguous` and
`pmm_free_kernel_page`. Page tables on both architectures, the pools'
slabs, the capability tables, kernel stacks and the profiler's ring go
through them; a page backing a process's memory does not, and is in no
count of the kernel's. Worked out from what processes hold instead, a
region two of them share would be counted twice. The count is kept under
the allocator's lock: an atomic add on AArch64 is a call into a library
the freestanding kernel does not link, which the first build found.

`sysinfo` carries `pages_kernel`; `/Devices/memory` says `pages_kernel` and
`kernel_mb`, `/Devices/kernel` `memory_kb`, and Processes' Nebula row shows
it. Under QEMU, 512 MB: about 62 MB, most of it the 38 MB image, which
carries the userland's too.

`x86-sysapps` 32 -> 33: the row holds more than a megabyte and less than
the machine.

**And `x86-dock`, which the gate failed after it.** Preferences opened at
y 734 of the M700-sized 1440 screen - a window opens where there is room,
and the windows around it had changed - so made 160 taller it ran off the
bottom, the window manager kept it on the screen, and the pixel the check
reads was outside the picture. The suite moves it up by its header first
when there is not room below, which is the check's assumption made true
rather than hoped for.

## 18.556 The processor chooses its own speed, when asked (step 2)

Diego, 11 October: "what about the need to change clock on cpus as
needed". Intel's HWP (Speed Shift), which both machines have - Skylake
brought it - lets the processor choose each core's speed by its load
within a millisecond; what software chooses is the range and the leaning.

`cpu_speed_set` on x86-64 turns it on for the calling core
(IA32_PM_ENABLE, 0x770), reads the core's lowest and highest performance
(IA32_HWP_CAPABILITIES, 0x771) and asks for the whole range, turbo
included, with the processor choosing within it and the leaning as its
energy-performance preference (IA32_HWP_REQUEST, 0x774) - when CPUID.06H
says HWP is there (EAX bit 7) and the preference is (bit 10). The fields
are checked against Linux's `msr-index.h`. AArch64 has nothing a core can
be asked from EL1, and says so.

**The registers are each core's own**, so a core applies the wanted
leaning on its own tick, once each time it changes (`thread_set_speed`, a
generation), exactly as each reads its own speed counters (18.548). It is
asked for at boot by `opt/kosmos/speed=performance`, `balanced` (0x80),
`battery` (0xC0) or a number; **without the word the speed is the
firmware's, as it always was**, so the M700 can be measured before and
after on one build by its command line alone. HWP, once on, stays on until
the machine restarts. Each core reports its leaning in `sys.cpuload()`, and
`clocks` says who chooses the speed.

`x86-sysapps` 33 -> 34, booted with `opt/kosmos/speed=battery`: the kernel
says it heard a leaning of 192, and a machine whose processor has no HWP -
QEMU's - comes up as before. What HWP does to a render is the M700's to
show.

Next: the leaning as a Power setting in Preferences, which needs a call a
privileged program makes to change it while the machine runs.

## 18.557 The M700's speed, measured: the base clock, never turbo

On the M700 (i7-6700, 0.11.155, the speed the firmware's), each core's own
counters over three seconds. **Idle**: between 1.3 and 3.4 GHz, never above
the 3.40 GHz base. **Under load**, eight `spin`s at once: **every core at
3,410 MHz exactly** - the base clock, while the i7-6700 runs all four cores
at about 3.7 GHz on turbo. So nothing asks it for more, and yesterday's
explanation of the M700 against the T14 (21.7 against 16.8 million rays a
second, 1.29 to 1, their base clocks 1.31 to 1) is now a measurement.

**Found by it: `pulse.speeds` overflowed.** `counter_hz * da` is past 2^63
after a few seconds of a busy core - 3.41 GHz times ten billion - and Lua's
integers wrap: every loaded core read -172 MHz. Idle cores were small
enough. The ratio is taken first, in floating point. `test_pulse` 10 -> 11,
with the M700's own numbers. **Control**: the old order - -196 MHz.

Next, the same machine booted with `opt/kosmos/speed=balanced`.

**And with it on** - the M700 booted with `opt/kosmos/speed=balanced`,
0.11.163: idle, **every core about 1.3 GHz** (against 1.3 to 3.4 before -
the processor letting an idle core down); under eight `spin`s, **every core
at 3,709 MHz**, the i7-6700's all-core turbo, against 3,410 - 8.8% more on
every core, with nothing else changed. `clocks` says "the processor chooses
its own speed, leaning 128 of 255". What it is worth in a render is
Cafesa3D's to say, against 21.7 million rays a second before.

**And over a render it does not last.** Diego, watching Monitor while
Cafesa3D rendered: "the processor went to 3.7ghz and then stabilized at 3.41
ghz", "it might be the cooling". The render read 21.0 million rays a second,
where it read 21.7 the day before at the firmware's speed. The M700 is a
Tiny: either the package reaches its temperature limit, or the firmware's
long-term power limit (PL1, with turbo allowed past it for a window of
typically 28 s) is set low for the case - the processor's thermal status
and power-limit registers would say which. Turbo is real and short; the
gain that lasts is the idle cores at 1.3 GHz.

## 18.559 The processor's heat and power, read

Diego, 12 October, after the M700's turbo lasted a burst and settled at its
base clock under a render ("it might be the cooling at work"): "yes read the
temperature and power limit".

**What is read** (`arch/x86_64/cpu.c`, the registers checked against
Linux's `msr-index.h`): each core's temperature from its own sensor
(IA32_THERM_STATUS, 0x19C), on its own tick - the register is the core's;
and on core 0's tick the package's - its temperature (0x1B1), the limit it
slows at (TjMax, 0x1A2), whether it is held now by heat (bit 0) or by a power
limit (bit 10), its sustained and burst limits and PL1's window (0x610, in
the units of 0x606), and the energy counter (0x611), which wraps in about a
minute and so is gathered into a 64-bit total of microjoules a tick at a
time. A power is two readings of that total over the time between them.

**Only where it is known to be there.** Reading a register the processor
does not have is a #GP in the kernel, so nothing is probed: GenuineIntel,
family 6, a digital sensor (CPUID.06H:EAX bit 0), a model on the list
Linux's RAPL driver keeps (Sandy Bridge to Arrow Lake, cores only), and not
under a hypervisor, which can name a model without giving its registers.
ARM says nothing: the Pi's sensor is the firmware's, a board's question.

**Where it shows.** `sys.cpuload()` gains each core's `temp_c`, `sys.info()`
the package's (`package_c`, `limit_c`, `held_hot`, `held_power`,
`power_limit_mw`, `power_burst_mw`, `power_window_ms`, `energy_uj`), all
only where known; `pulse.heat` turns two readings into a temperature, a
power, the limits and why it is held; `clocks` prints them before the
speeds, and Monitor's processor card shows "62 °C · 28 W" under the speed,
and "held: power limit" or "held: too hot" while it is.

**Tests.** `host`'s `test_pulse.lua` 11 -> 18: a power from two readings,
the limits, why it is held, the hottest core when the package has no sensor
of its own, no power from one reading, and nil on QEMU's processor
(**control**: the power not divided by the time - it fails, "30 J over 2 s
was not 15 W: 30.0"). `x86-sysapps` runs `clocks` first and reads that
QEMU's processor says nothing of its heat or its power - every core's tick
has asked and been answered no, without a fault (34 -> 35). The gate: 70 of 71, `x86-film` its known flake under load, alone 13 of 13. The numbers
themselves can only be seen on the M700 and the T14.

## 18.560 Network Monitor N1: the network server counts, and says over what

`docs/netmonitor.md` step N1. The network server (`net.c`) counts every
frame in and out with its bytes, where it enters and leaves the process,
and what the stack itself had no room for - a datagram with no room in its
ring, a frame the card's ring would not take. Each connection keeps its
payload in and out and the process that opened it, asked of the kernel with
`SYS_SENDER` on `NET_OP_CONNECT`, `NET_OP_LISTEN` and `NET_OP_UDP_BIND`; a
connection a listener made is its listener's.

**`NET_OP_STATS`** answers into a region the caller sends, as `NET_OP_POLL`'s
list is: a `struct net_stats` and a `struct net_stats_conn` a connection,
`ready` written of `length` there are. The kit keeps one region and grows it
when there were more (`net.stats`); the namespace has `fs.net_stats`; and
`netstat` prints the totals and every connection with its program's name.

**A byte sent again is not counted again.** The first run read 38 bytes out
for a 19-byte request: TCP had sent it twice, and the count followed every
send. A connection's `bytes_out` is now the advance of the highest sequence
sent, so it says what its program sent; what the network cost - resends
included - is in the frame totals.

**What is not counted yet: the card's own drops.** The driver protocol
(`ethproto.h`) carries no counter, so "dropped" is the stack's; a card's is a
field in the driver's reply, for N3 or later.

**Tests.** `x86-network` 34 -> 36: a program names itself, fetches over one
connection from a server on the Mac and asks the stack, finding its
connection by its own process - 491 bytes in of 491 read, 19 out of 19
written; and `netstat` prints the totals. **Control**: `SYS_SENDER`'s
answer thrown away - the program finds no connection of its own, and the
suite fails.
The gate: 70 of 71, `x86-film` its silence under load (`roadmap.md` 6zw),
alone 13 of 13 - its sixth failure in seventeen gates this session.

## 18.564 A worker a core: the 3D Kit's render threads where it says

Diego, 12 October, Monitor beside a Cafesa3D render on the M700: "why core
3 is not being used". The 3D Kit starts a worker per processor in one loop,
and each was placed where the fewest threads wanted to run at the instant
it was made; something on core 3 then put two workers on another core, and
a thread never moves, so core 3 sat idle for the whole render. Asked why
threads do not move, the answer is `docs/smp.md`'s: a fixed home is what
lets IPC release its lock before the switch, and what keeps lazily saved
floating-point registers on the core that owns them - correctness, more than
speed. Moving threads stays with the Scheduler's work (`roadmap.md`); this
is the narrow answer Diego chose meanwhile ("Yes").

- **`THREAD_START_ON`**, a flag of `SYS_THREAD_CREATE` with the core in
  bits 15:8: the new thread's home set between creating and waking it, the
  one moment `thread_create_on` says a home can be set. A core past the
  last given threads is `SYS_ERR_NO_DEVICE`; core bits without the flag are
  refused as a word left over. `kosmos_thread_start_on` is its door.
- **The 3D Kit** starts worker i on core i, round the cores; a core refused
  falls back to placement.

**Tests.** `x86-kernel` 198 -> 199, "thread: on the core its process asked
for": a C role in init asks for a thread on the last core, which the test
has first loaded with three parked fillers - placement's worst choice - and
reads the thread's home while it sleeps; the role's code says a core past
the last and bits without the flag were both refused. **Control**: the home
not set - it fails. The first version of the test asked for the last core
of an idle machine, and its control *passed*: placement's rotation had put
the unasked thread there too. Loading the core is what made it bite.

**`smp: a new thread avoids a loaded core` failed 3 of 13 runs alone**
today, and 0 of 3 on the tree before this - too few to say this caused it,
and its own comment records the same failure on 4 and 6 October under load.
Its question needs every other core free of ready threads at the instant
it places one; a diagnostic printing what was ready made it pass four times
in four. On the roadmap.
The gate: 71 of 72 - `x86-mdns` at 143 s, its fourth gate running at that
figure since 0.11.168 moved the meters into the kit; it passes alone. Four
in a row is a pattern rather than load, and it is on the roadmap.

**On the M700, 0.11.171 netbooted with `opt/kosmos/speed=performance`**, the
same F12 render of `still-life.scene` (640 x 360, 256 samples, 7.7 s), its
busiest two seconds read by a program over Telnet: **every core 67-68% busy
and at 3.60 GHz**, the package at 68 C and 38.9 W - core 3 working with the
rest, and the speed held where `balanced` had settled at 3.41 GHz at 81 C
and 45 W. So the settling was the speed leaning, not heat and not the power
limit: 65 W sustained and 100 C were never near.

## 18.565 The dated picture: every application in it, arranged, on x86

`make shot` had been writing a picture of a desktop nobody arranged: on 11
and 12 October Groove lay maximised over the rest. Four causes, each found
by making the picture say what it saw:

- **It did not wait for the arrangement**: forty seconds, while `tile`
  waits up to two minutes for every window. `run_gallery.py` now waits for
  `tile` to say it arranged them, and fails if it did not.
- **`tile` gave up on one unanswered question**: with twenty applications
  starting, the desktop did not answer one `windows` in time and the whole
  wait ended - "the desktop did not answer" with every window open. No
  answer is now "ask again next second"; and it waits four minutes for a
  count it was given.
- **The picture's machine was too small**: the ARM board assumes 512 MB
  whatever `-m` says (`hal/qemu-virt/memory.c`), and Groove's window was
  refused and Maps ended. The picture is taken on x86-64 now - where the
  suites run since 8 October and the memory is read from the firmware -
  with a gigabyte and four processors.
- **Cafesa3D laid itself out at the size it asked for**, and when the window
  manager granted another its 3D view did not fit the surface - "a view of
  1534 by 1004 does not fit the surface at 46, 46" - and it ended. It takes
  the granted size before making the view now, as `FULL.fit` does on a
  change of window. `x86-cafesa3d-1` and `-2` 72 and 55, as before.

And **an application that ends on the way fails the picture**, with the
lines it said before it went: `tile` counts windows, and it had counted
twenty while Cafesa3D and Groove had opened and gone.

## 18.566 Disk Monitor D1: every drive says what it read and wrote

`docs/diskmonitor.md` step D1. `.device` under a drive's path answered for
`/Home` (`diskfs`) and a share (`smbfs`), for Disk Benchmark; now a stick's
volumes (`drives`) and `/Temporary` (`ramfs`) answer it too, so every drive
Disk Monitor shows can say what it did.

- **One shape**: `struct disk_device` moved out of `diskproto.h` into
  `deviceproto.h`, which the disk, drive and memory protocols include - so
  the four servers answer in the same struct, and the protocol stamp covers
  it (a header outside `*proto.h` would have escaped it).
- **The drive server** counts each volume's reads, bytes and the time each
  took, in a table kept by the volume's name rather than in the volumes
  themselves, which a rescan rebuilds; `DRIVES_OP_DEVICE` answers it. A
  stick is never written here, so its writes stay zero.
- **`ramfs`** counts requests and bytes in the store (`ram_counts`), which
  is also built on the Mac, and the server adds the time each read and write
  took around it; `RAM_OP_DEVICE` answers it.
- **The namespace** reads every one of them through one function,
  `device_counts`, where the disk side had its own unpacking.

**Tests.** `x86-usb-2`'s `usb_drives` part 83 -> 85: a program reads the
stick's and `/Temporary`'s `.device` before and after known work, and the
differences are exact - "device 3000 in 3 timed true", the 3000-byte file in
three 1024-byte requests with time counted, and 5000 bytes written to
`/Temporary` and read back. **Control**: `/Temporary`'s writes not counted -
"temporary wrote 0 read 5000 of 5000", and it fails.
The gate: 71 of 72 - `x86-mdns` at 143 s, its fifth gate running.

## 18.567 The desktop's backdrop refused as "already starting"

`x86-mdns` failed in every gate from 0.11.168 - five running, each at about
143 s, where it takes 30 alone: "Tracker's Network group did not list Studio
as seen", and no line from that Tracker at all. Reproduced beside five heavy
suites, with the suite now printing the desktop's last words when it fails:
`desktop` ended at once, before Connect had even started, and no Tracker was
ever started.

**The cause was the window manager's rule against a second click** (29
September, `docs/launching.html`): a program still starting is not started
again. It compared the program's file and not its words - so the Deskbar's
login set opening Tracker as a window made the desktop's request for
`tracker desktop`, the backdrop, "already starting" whenever that Tracker
had not reached its window yet. `desktop` asks for an answer when what it
launched has started; an answer that fast is that refusal, and it ended
having started nothing. Alone, the login set's Tracker was up first; under
the gate's load, never. Nothing in 0.11.168 touched it - that build only made
the gate slow enough. Now **the same program with the same words** is what
is already starting.

Under the same load with the fix, `x86-mdns` passed twice in two; the gate
below is the evidence that matters, since the race also passed once without
it.
The gate: 70 of 72 - **`x86-mdns` passed, in 32 s**, after five failures
running; `x86-network` typed a command that arrived as `host` alone (its
words lost under load; alone it passes), and `x86-film` (6zw), which failed
again beside one other suite and passed twice alone.

## 18.568 Disk Monitor D2: which programs read and wrote each drive

`docs/diskmonitor.md` step D2. Every drive's server keeps a row for each
program that read or wrote it - its requests and bytes each way and the
last path it touched - and answers `.programs` under the drive's path, a
page at a time.

- **One table, `progcount.c`**, used by the four servers rather than four
  copies: a row a process, grown as processes arrive (no fixed number), a
  long path cut keeping its end. Held on the Mac by `test_progcount` (8
  checks; **control**: paging that says no more follow - twenty-one rows page
  as eight, and it fails).
- **Who asked is `SYS_SENDER`'s**, asked as a read or write is answered -
  except through `diskfs`'s doors, whose thread forwards the request and so
  is what the main thread hears; the door thread asks who sent it and leaves
  the answer beside the door. `smbfs` holds a read until the network
  answers, so it notes the program as the request arrives and puts each
  piece's bytes to it as they come.
- **One shape, `struct disk_program`** in `deviceproto.h`, and one function
  in the namespace that pages it into a list; `diskstat` prints every
  drive's totals and its programs, as `netstat` does the network's.

**Tests.** `x86-usb-2` 85 -> 88: a program names itself, reads the stick's
3000-byte file and writes and reads back 3000 bytes on `/Temporary`, and
finds its own row on each by its process id - the stick's 3000 bytes with
the file's name, `/Temporary`'s 3000 written and 3677 read, which is the
3000 and the program's own 677-byte source, read from `/Temporary` to run
it - and `diskstat` prints the stick. **Control**: the drive server crediting
every read to nobody - "programs nil nil", and it fails. `x86-disk` 33 ->
34: the shell's row on `/Home` grown by exactly the 2000 bytes it wrote and
read back, its last path `/Home/counted.bin`.
