## 18.570 `install`: packages from the Mac, on demand - and the shell after `sys.exit`

Diego, 12 October: "perhaps add a program in kosmos that requests those from
the mac as needed?", "where we show all available packages", "and we can
install them on demand", "from the server (which is the mac now)" - in place
of pushing Doom, Quake, the SNES and the developer files over Telnet after
every netboot, ten minutes when the developer files went too.

- **The Mac's side**: `make packages` (`tools/packages.py`) zips each of
  them from this tree, its folder inside, with an index - name, title, where
  it installs, size, build, a sentence; `make packages-serve`
  (`tools/packages_serve.py`) serves that folder on port 47701, reading only.
  `make netboot` names it on the command line, `opt/kosmos/packages`.
- **Kosmos's side**: `install` lists the server's packages and which are
  installed from which build (`/Home/Packages`), and installs by name or
  `all` - downloaded to /Temporary, unpacked beside the installed folder on
  the same disk, the old renamed away, the new renamed in, the old removed,
  so a failure leaves what was there.
- **On the M700**: Doom, 10 MB, installed in 1.2 s, Quake in 1.8 and the
  SNES in 0.9, against about a minute pushed; Doom then ran at 62 to 70
  frames a second from its package.

**And the shell after `sys.exit`.** `install` refusing a broken package
ended with `sys.exit(1)`, and the machine's own shell never prompted again:
a program runs in a process of its own that answers the shell when it
finishes, `sys.exit` ended that process on the spot, and the shell waited
for the answer on an endpoint that outlives it. Reproduced with a one-line
program that prints and exits 1. Telnet's shell copes, so the M700 never
showed it. Now, while a program runs in the shell's foreground, `sys.exit`
ends the program as an error does, the shell hears its code, and the
process ends with it; and the shell says "run: ..." only for an error, not
an exit with a code the program has explained itself.

**Tests.** `x86-install`, new, 5 checks: a server on this Mac offers two
packages and the guest, its server named on the command line, lists them,
installs one with its file, says it installed, installs it again over
itself with nothing left behind, and is refused a zip that will not open
with what was there kept - the check after that refusal is the one the
shell's fix is held to: it was never reached before, the prompt never coming
back.
The gate: 71 of 73 - `x86-display-1`, whose keyboard echo "2+2" had the
network driver's first line printed into its middle (alone, 74 of 74), and
`x86-dock`, whose slider check read the settings file in the instant after
the Deskbar was told and before Preferences had written it - 3 runs in 5
today. It waits for the value now, as the checks here wait for the thing,
and passes.

`wm diskmon` (`user/bin/apps/diskmon.lua`), as `docs/diskmonitor.html` draws
it: every drive down the left - `/Home`, each stick's volumes, each share
connected (never connecting one by looking), and memory - drawn as what it
is, with its rates and a small graph of the minute; the chosen one on the
right, its card, the minute mirrored (reading above, writing below), how
long a read and a write take, how often the cache answered, what it has read
and written, and the programs using it, busiest first, with the last file
each touched; the pace and bytes or bits from the dots. It reads `.device`
and `.programs` under each drive's path once a pace (D1, D2) and takes
differences; the graphs and the card are the kit's.

**`x86-diskmon`**, new, 7 checks: the guest boots with a FAT stick and a
program named `reader` reads its 3000-byte file again and again in the
background; Disk Monitor is opened, the stick chosen by a click on its row,
and the window says the stick is read at about 100 KB/s with `reader` the
busiest program at the same rate, by its name; its graph is blue above its

own logic was wrong - it took the line where the drive's rate was highest,
which was the first reading after the stick was chosen, with no earlier
reading of `reader`'s to subtract from; it takes `reader`'s own highest now.
And two things seen in that picture, fixed: the list's small graphs drawn on
the big graph's dark ground, which read as black bars, and a total's words

## 18.572 Packages P1: manifests, sums and the protocols they are for

`docs/packages.md` step P1. A package is now a zip of its folder with
`package.txt` inside - what it is, its version and build, **the protocols
it was made for** (`sys.protostamp`'s value for the tree, computed by
`tools/packages.py` as `tools/protostamp.py` computes it), where it goes, its
icon, needs and dependencies, and every file with its size and SHA-256 - and
the index is the manifests without their files, a package a paragraph.
Written from the application's header: Doom, Quake and the SNES gained
`-- kosmos: kind` and `-- kosmos: about`, so `packages.py` keeps no facts of
theirs. A line a fact, a file's path last because a path may have spaces.

`/Kosmos/Libraries/packages.lua` begins as the design has it - the one copy
`pkg`, `install` and the window will share: the index and manifests read,
and a package put in place only after its manifest says this build's
protocols and every file has its size and sum; the manifest kept in
`/Home/Packages` as the record of what is installed. `install` is a thin
program over it.

**Tests.** `x86-install` 5 -> 8: the server now offers manifests in the new
shape, and a package whose file's bytes are not what its sum says and one
made for other protocols are each refused with why, leaving no folder.
**Control**: the sum not checked - the tampered package is installed, and the
suite fails. `x86-game` and `x86-nogame` unchanged with the new header
words.

## 18.573 Packages P2: `pkg` - dependencies, removal, update

`docs/packages.md` step P2, in `packages.lua`: `plan` - what was asked and
what it depends on, the dependencies first, each once, a missing one or a
circle refused with why; `remove` - exactly the files the kept manifest
lists and its `package.txt`, then each folder they leave empty, deepest
first, and the record, so a file a person put beside them stays;
`needed_by`; and `command`, the text at the prompt - `pkg`, `pkg install`,
`pkg remove`, `pkg update` - which `pkg` and `install`, now its short form,
both are. A removal is refused while an installed package depends on what
goes, unless both go in one command; `pkg update` installs every installed
package whose version or build on the server differs, saying 1.0 -> 2.0.

**Tests.** `x86-install` 8 -> 12: `addon`, which depends on `hello`,
installed with `hello` brought first; `pkg remove hello` refused while
`addon` needs it, naming the command that removes both; both removed
together, a file a person put in Hello's folder kept; and a newer `hello` on
the server installed by `pkg update`. **Control**: nothing ever said to need
`hello` - the removal goes through, and the suite fails.

## 18.574 Packages P3: the window

`docs/packages.md` step P3, `user/bin/apps/packages.lua`, as
`docs/packages.html` draws it: kinds and states in the sidebar with their
counts, a row a package with its state's button - Install, Update, or
Installed - and the chosen one's facts in the details, with Install, Update
and Remove. **It shows and asks; it installs nothing itself.** The index is
read with `http.get` in a coroutine stepped on the window's clock (`pause`),
and an action is `pkg` in a process of its own, started through the window
manager without waiting, whose `--report` file the window reads each tick
until its last line says `done ok` or `done failed` - then it reads the
index again. Install asks first when it brings dependencies ("Install 2",
with each and the total), and Remove when an installed package needs what
goes ("Remove 2"), as the drawing has them.

## 18.576 Sandboxes V1: a guest runs ten instructions and stops

`docs/virtualization.md` step V1, on AArch64 under QEMU with the processor's
virtualization on - Diego's choice that morning, because QEMU emulates EL2
and not VT-x. Nebula stays at EL1; a core that arrives at EL2 leaves a stub
there (`arch/aarch64/hyp.S`, installed by `boot/start.S` on core zero and on
any secondary started at EL2), and the kernel enters a guest with an `hvc`
carrying a `hyp_vcpu` (`hyp.h`): the host's EL1 registers and callee-saved
registers put aside, the guest's loaded, stage 2 on (`vcpu.c`: 39 bits from
level 1, 4 KB pages), and whatever EL2 traps returned as the `hvc`'s answer.

**Tests.** `vcpu: a guest runs ten instructions and stops`, in the kernel's
suite: a page of guest code at guest address 0x40000000 counts x0 to 9 and
stops on `hvc #0x4b` (EC 0x16, the immediate, x0 9, PC past it); a load from
0x80000000, mapped by nothing, stops with EC 0x24 and HPFAR naming the page;
three hundred `hvc` exits give the round trip - 1,286 counter ticks at
62.5 MHz under TCG, kept as a regression number only; and the host's
SCTLR_EL1 and TPIDR_EL1 are what they were. On a machine started at EL1 it
says there is no EL2 and passes. **`arm-sandbox`**, new, boots the whole
kernel suite at EL2 (`run_tests.py --virt`, `virtualization=on`) and refuses
a run where the guest test stood aside: 202/202 in 8 s, beside `arm-kernel`'s
202/202 at EL1. It runs in every gate, the one ARM suite that does while the
rest stay paused. **Control**: the guest's x0 and x1 not kept at its exit -
x0 reads 0, and the test fails.

## 18.577 Sandboxes V2: a guest and a vCPU, by capability

`docs/virtualization.md` step V2. A guest and a vCPU are Nebula objects
(`kernel/vm.c`, `vm.h`): two capability kinds, `CAP_GUEST` and `CAP_VCPU`,
owned by the process that made them - as an interrupt line is - and ended
with it, before its capabilities; each from a pool that grows. Four
syscalls: `SYS_GUEST_CREATE`; `SYS_GUEST_MAP`, a region at a guest physical
address, held by the guest until it ends; `SYS_VCPU_CREATE`; and
`SYS_VCPU_RUN`, once into the guest with a `struct vcpu_regs` and back with
why - every exit, the host's own tick included, so the interrupt is taken
on the way back to user level and a kill works as for any syscall. The
architecture's half is `arch_vm_*`: the stage-2 tables, VMIDs and
`hyp_vcpu` on ARM, and `SYS_ERR_NO_DEVICE` on x86-64 until VT-x.

**Tests.** `vm: a monitor runs a guest, by capability`, in the kernel's
suite on both machines: a user process (`guest_role`, `user/init/main.c`)
makes a guest, refuses a region capability that names nothing, maps a
two-page region it also maps itself at 0x40000000 and writes the guest's
code into it; the guest reads the monitor's 0x1234, writes 0x1235 beside
it and loads from 0x50000000 - it stops there with EC 0x24 and that address,
and the monitor reads 0x1235 in its own memory; stepped on, it stops on
`hvc #7`. After the process ends, no guest, no vCPU and no region of it
are left. Code 0 at EL2, 50 ("cannot enter a guest") at EL1 and on x86-64.
`arm-sandbox` refuses a run without the monitor's line. 203/203 at EL2 and
EL1, 200/200 on x86-64. **Control**: the release at process exit taken out
- a guest and its region outlive the monitor ("guests left 1, regions 1 of
0"), and the test fails.

## 18.578 Sandboxes V3: Alpine Linux runs in a sandbox

`docs/virtualization.md` V3, toward Diego's "the initial goal for sandboxes
is to run a linux distro like alpine". `sandbox run alpine` (a program)
reads `/Home/Sandboxes/alpine` - `Image` and `initramfs` - into a region
through a 256 KB window, so the 36 MB kernel is never a Lua string, writes a
setup page (`vmmproto.h`) and asks the namespace to start `vmm`
(`fs.vm_start`), which spawns the role with the program's console and the
two regions. **Spawn hands a child a region now**, not only an endpoint
(`ipc_cap_grant`): the first thing that needed one at birth.

`vmm` (`user/servers/vmm.c`) writes the guest's device tree (`fdt.c`),
makes the guest and its vCPU (V2's syscalls) and runs it on core zero,
answering: the PL011 and GICv3 distributor and redistributor by their
stage-2 faults (ESR's ISV: register, size, direction); PSCI by `hvc`; `wfi`
(trapped, HCR.TWI) by sleeping until the guest's timer is due; interrupts
by the list registers, which EL2 loads and saves with ICH_VMCR around each
entry, beside the guest's virtual timer. The guest's FP registers are lent
to it around each entry (`fp_lend`, `fp_take_back`), with interrupts masked.

`tools/alpine.py` fetches Alpine 3.24.2's netboot tarball and minirootfs
once into `build/downloads/alpine` (436 MB the first time), holds each to
the SHA-256 Alpine publishes, unwraps the kernel from its EFI zboot, and
writes the minirootfs as a newc archive with our `/init` and the
`/dev/console` an initramfs has to carry itself.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux`, new, in every gate: the ordinary ARM image
started at EL2 with 1 GB and a `/Home` disk holding Alpine, `sandbox run
alpine` typed - Linux's banner with Alpine's build, `ttyAMA0` claimed
through the emulated GIC, Alpine's `/init` saying "Alpine Linux 3.24.2,
Linux 6.18.52-0-virt, in a Kosmos sandbox" and one processor, and the guest
switching itself off with the sandbox ending 0; 5 checks in 10 s. The screen
is kept beside the log. **Control**: the timer's interrupt never offered -
Linux stops before its userland and the suite fails. **A check that did not
bite, found by that control and removed**: "the guest's clock moved" passed
without the timer, because a timestamp is read from the counter.

## 18.579 Sandboxes V3c: an Alpine prompt that answers

What is typed at Kosmos's console reaches the sandbox: `vmm` takes the
console's bytes (`CON_OP_KEYS`) into the PL011's receiver, whose data
register, flag register and receive interrupt now say so, Enter as a
carriage return and Backspace as DEL; when the guest idles, the monitor
waits on the console itself (`CON_OP_WAIT`) for a key or until the guest's
timer is due. A prompt has no newline, so what the guest said is written out
before it is waited on. **A terminal's escape sequences are dropped** on
the way out - busybox asks where the cursor is and `ls` colours its names,
and Kosmos's console carries colour as a field, not as bytes in the text.
`tools/alpine.py --shell` makes an initramfs whose `/init` names the host
`alpine` and ends in `setsid sh -l` on `ttyAMA0`, with job control.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux` 5 -> 11: a second sandbox, `alpine-shell`,
reaches `alpine:~# `; `cat /etc/alpine-release`, `echo $((6*7))` and `uname
-m` typed at Kosmos's console answer `3.24.2`, `42` and `aarch64`; no escape
byte reaches the console; `poweroff -f` ends the sandbox with code 0. 19 s.
**Control**: the console's keys never taken - the prompt comes and nothing
typed is answered, four checks fail. **Found on the way, in the suite**: its
waits compared the raw serial text, whose lines end `\r\n`, with patterns
the checks matched after stripping `\r` - so each wait ran its whole 30 s
and the check passed after it, 107 s for 19.

## 18.580 Sandboxes S1: the monitor as a server, and `sandbox`

`docs/sandboxes.md` S1. **Each running sandbox is its monitor, registered
in `/Running`**: `vmm` makes its own endpoint, registers it as
`sandbox-<name>` (`appproto.h`) and answers `vmmproto.h` - its state, its
console from an offset, keys in, stop - on one thread while its vCPU runs on
another. The guest's console is a 64 KB ring kept by the monitor, so a
service outlives whoever started it and anyone may attach later; keys come
by message into a single-producer, single-consumer ring the PL011 empties.
Once its guest ends it waits ten seconds for its last lines and exit code
to be read, and goes at once when asked to stop. Its exit codes before the
guest runs are numbers `sandboxes.lua` turns into sentences.

**One library, `sandboxes.lua`**, for the window to come and `sandbox`:
definitions in `/Home/Sandboxes/<name>/sandbox.txt` (a line a fact), images
in `Images/`, start (the image read into the RAM region through a window),
stop, state, the console by offset, keys, a task run and thrown away.
**`sandbox`**: `run IMAGE -- COMMAND`, `run IMAGE` (a shell), `list`, `new`,
`start`, `stop`, `console` (Control-W then D leaves it running), `delete`,
`images`. **Alpine's `/init`** names the machine after the sandbox and, given
a command (`kosmos.run=`, hexadecimal), runs it and says its exit code on a
line beginning with the starter's token (`kosmos.end=`), which the monitor
reads and keeps off the console; given none, it is a shell with job control
whose end switches the machine off. **Alpine is a package** (`tools/
packages.py`, into `/Home/Sandboxes/Images/alpine`).

**Found on the way**: a Lua program has no `io` - `sandbox` and `telnet`
both called `io.write`; `telnet` would have died at its first answer. Both
write to `/Devices/console` now. And `fs.raw` now forgets a name `/Running`
gave once its process has ended, as `request` already did.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux` 11 -> 13, rewritten around `sandbox`: the
image listed; `sandbox run alpine -- echo $((6*7)); uname -m; exit 3` -
`42`, `aarch64`, "echo exited 3", the program's own code 3, and the end line
nowhere on the console; `sandbox run alpine` - a prompt named `shell-N`,
`cat /etc/alpine-release` answered, `exit` ending it; a service made,
started, listed running, its console attached and printing, Control-W D
leaving it running, stopped and listed stopped; no escape on the console.
18 s. **Control**: the end line never read - it reaches the console and the
task "exited without saying"; two checks fail.

## 18.581 Sandboxes S2: the window, and the ARM board's memory asked for

`docs/sandboxes.md` S2, `user/bin/apps/sandboxes.lua`, as `docs/sandboxes.html`
draws it: the sidebar's groups with their counts (All, Running, Stopped,
Tasks), the images, and the machine - its processors, the memory given of
what it has, and whether it can run a guest at all (`sysinfo.guests`, new,
`arch_vm_available`); every sandbox a card with its state's pill, its
processor share and memory, what it was given and its buttons; a double
click opens one - its processor graph, what it was given, the last lines of
its console - and its tabs: the whole console, typed into when clicked
into; folders and ports (said to be S3 and S4); its log (the monitor's and
the kernel's lines); its settings (its `sandbox.txt`). New sandbox is a
sheet: a name, an image, a task, a service or a shell, the command, memory,
and whether to open its console. **Nothing on the desktop waits on a
start**: Start and Restart run `sandbox start NAME --report FILE` in a
process of their own, and the window reads the report on its clock and
says why a start failed; Stop is one message to the monitor.

**Found by the window's suite, and fixed where it was**: the ARM board's
memory was 512 MB compiled in (`hal/qemu-virt/memory.c`), whatever `-m`
said - a second guest "could not spawn (-105)" on a machine given 1 and
then 2 GB. QEMU's `FW_CFG_RAM_SIZE` reads zero on this board and it leaves
no device tree at RAM's base for an ELF kernel - both tried - so the size
is the SMBIOS tables' type 19 regions, read over fw_cfg into a buffer of
its own before the page allocator asks. And `sys.spawn` now says its error
number rather than only "could not spawn".

**Tests.** `arm-sandboxwin`, new, in every gate: two sandboxes made at the
prompt and one started; the window shows web running and shell1 stopped;
Start on shell1's card is heard and shell1 arrives running; a double click
opens it, its Console tab is clicked into and `echo $((6*7))` typed there
answers 42; New sandbox's sheet is filled - 128 MB, a name - and Create and
start makes it and it arrives running. 8 checks, 20 s. **Control**: the
card's Start doing nothing - four checks fail. `arm-sandbox-linux` 13 -> 14:
a 1 GB machine is seen as 1024 MB.

## 18.582 Sandboxes S3: a folder of /Home in a sandbox, by virtio-fs

`docs/sandboxes.md` S3, Diego's virtio choice of 12 October. `sandbox run
IMAGE --share /Home/x[:/at][:ro]`, a definition's `folder` lines and the
window's sheet give a sandbox up to four folders of `/Home`; each is
`share<i>` on the guest's command line (`kosmos.share<i>=`) and in its setup
page (`vmmproto.h`), and `fs.vm_start` hands the monitor `/Home` - only
then. In the monitor (`user/servers/vmmfs.c`) each folder is a virtio-fs
device on virtio-mmio at 0x0a000000 + 0x200 i, SPI 16 + i, in the device
tree: registers emulated, the split queues served in the guest's RAM on a
notify, FUSE 7.31 answered over `diskproto.h` - init, lookup, getattr,
access, statfs, opendir, readdir, releasedir, open, read, write, flush,
fsync, release, create, mkdir, unlink, rmdir, rename, setattr (a size).
Every path is the folder's with one name appended, a name with `/`, `.` or
`..` refused; a read-only folder refuses every change. A file opened for
writing is kept whole and written back on flush or close. Alpine's `/init`
loads `virtio_mmio`, `fuse` and `virtiofs` - carried into the initramfs
from Alpine's own, in `/kosmos/modules`, since its `/lib` is a link the
unpacker does not follow - and mounts each folder where it was asked to.

**Found on the way**: the handle table counted from 0 where 0 means none,
so the first `opendir` wrote 56 bytes past a NULL table - the monitor died
at address 0x38, which `addr2line` put in `memset`.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux` 14 -> 18: a project folder on the disk,
shared read only - `ls -R` lists it, `cat` reads Kosmos's file, a write is
refused "Read-only file system" - and read and write - a file and a folder
made in it, and the file read back at Kosmos's prompt, "made in alpine".
24 s. **Control**: reads answered with nothing - the folder lists but its
file does not read, and the suite fails.

## 18.583 Sandboxes S5, its first half: started with Kosmos

A sandbox whose `sandbox.txt` says `starts with Kosmos` - the New sandbox
sheet's "with Kosmos", or `sandbox new --at-start` - is started at boot by
`init`, which runs `sandbox start NAME` in the background beside the servers
the Servers window marked, so the boot does not wait for its image to be
read. VT-x, S5's other half, needs the M700.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux` 18 -> 19: `boot1` on the disk, marked to
start with Kosmos, is running when `sandbox list` first asks, nobody having
started it. **Control**: the definition never taken as starting with
Kosmos - `boot1` is stopped, and the suite fails.

## 18.584 Sandboxes S4, outgoing: a sandbox's network through Kosmos's

`docs/sandboxes.md` S4. A sandbox given the network - `sandbox run
--network`, `sandbox new --network`, a definition's `network outgoing`, the
New sandbox sheet's "Outgoing only" - has a virtio-net device at
0x0a000800, SPI 20, on the virtio-mmio transport its folders use
(`user/servers/vdev.c`, moved out of `vmmfs.c` when the second device
arrived), and `kosmos.net=1` on its command line. Alpine's `/init` loads
`virtio_net` and the two modules it needs (`failover`, `net_failover`),
takes 10.0.3.15/24 with a route through 10.0.3.2, and asks 10.0.3.3 for
names. Behind the device, in the monitor, is a gateway
(`user/servers/vmmnet.c`): ARP and ping answered for its two addresses,
DNS answered by Kosmos's resolver (`net_client_resolve`), and each TCP
connection the guest opens carried over one Kosmos opens to the same
address and port. A segment goes to the guest only into a buffer it has
posted, and bytes are taken from Kosmos's side only then, so the gateway
never sends a byte twice and keeps no copy. The monitor is handed
`/Network` by the namespace only when its sandbox has the network, and
waits a tick at a time, rather than for the guest, while a connection has
something to carry.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux` 19 -> 22, with a network card and an HTTP
server on this Mac: from `sandbox run alpine --network`, the gateway
pinged; a page on this Mac fetched by `wget` through Kosmos's own TCP,
"hello from this Mac, through Kosmos"; and `nothing.invalid` answered
NXDOMAIN by the name server. `arm-sandboxwin` 8 -> 9: the sheet's
"Outgoing only" clicked, and `made1` read back from the disk with `network
outgoing`. **Controls**: frames never delivered to the guest - the ping is
lost, the host unreachable and no name server reached, three checks failing;
the sheet's choice ignored - `made1` written with `network none`, and the
window's suite fails.

## 18.585 Sandboxes S4, ports: Kosmos's port carried into a sandbox

`docs/sandboxes.md` S4. `sandbox run|new --port N:M`, a definition's
`port N:M`, and the New sandbox sheet's Ports with its field: the setup page
carries four (`vmm_setup.ports`), the guest has the network device whenever
it has a port, and the monitor listens on each N (`net_client_listen`). A
thread of the monitor's own (`waiter` in `vmmnet.c`) polls the listeners
with `NET_WANT_ACCEPT` a second at a time, accepts who arrived, and leaves
the connection in an eight-slot ring whose head only it writes; the guest's
thread takes it on its next pump, sends the guest a SYN to port M from
10.0.3.2 and an unused port of the gateway's, and carries bytes once the
SYN-ACK comes. The guest's FIN now closes Kosmos's side as well, after
every byte written - so a server that ends its answer by closing ends the
connection, both ways. A sandbox with ports and without `network
outgoing` has its own SYNs refused with a reset and its DNS unanswered.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux` 22 -> 24, with QEMU forwarding a port of
this Mac to Kosmos's 8081: a sandbox given only `--port 8081:80` and a
shared folder holding a one-answer script runs `nc -l -p 80 -e` under
`timeout`; the suite fetches it from this Mac and gets exactly `HTTP/1.0
200 OK`, a blank line and "served by alpine", the connection ended by the
guest; and the same sandbox's `wget` to this Mac is refused. Busybox in
Alpine's minimal root has no `httpd`, which is why `nc`. `arm-sandboxwin`'s
last check now picks Ports and types `8082:80`, and `made1` is read back
with `network outgoing` and `port 8082:80`. **Controls**: arrivals never
handed to the guest's thread - the fetch times out; the guest's FIN not
closing Kosmos's side - the fetch times out with the page unfinished; the
sheet's port field ignored - `made1` written with no port. Each fails its
suite.

## 18.586 Sandboxes S4: what a sandbox's network carried

The gateway counts the bytes it carries each way (`vmmnet_counted`, relaxed
atomics: written on the guest's thread, read on the one answering
`/Running`), and the monitor's state reply carries them (`vmm_reply.net_in`,
`net_out`). The Sandboxes window samples them with the processor's time and
draws the Overview's Network panel as a mirrored history - `ui.history`'s,
Network Monitor's colours - titled with the last second's rate each way;
`sandbox run` with `--network` or `--port` ends saying what was carried.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux` 24 -> 25: the network task ends saying it
carried at least the 36-byte page in and its request out. **Control**: the
count in never read - "it carried 0 B in and 99 B out", and the suite
fails.

## 18.592 SATA (AHCI), A1: a disk behind the controller found and read

`drivers.md`, *SATA (AHCI)*. The board finds an AHCI controller by its
class and gives the ABAR (`HAL_DEV_AHCI`); `ahci.c` runs at every boot, takes
the controller from the firmware where it offers, enables AHCI, brings up
each implemented port with a device present (DET 3, IPM 1), checks its
signature is a disk's once FIS receive is on, asks IDENTIFY DEVICE and reads
LBA 0-1 into contiguous memory whose bus address it knows. Polled, with a
deadline: a probe before it serves anything.

**Tests.** `test_ahcidecode` (host), 16 checks against the standards'
bytes: READ and WRITE DMA EXT's FIS, a 65536-sector count as 0, the command
header's word and the PRDT's count, a disk's model, serial and size by LBA
48 and by LBA 28, a 4K logical sector, an invalid word 106 not believed, an
ATAPI page refused, GPT's signature. `x86-ahci`, new, 5 checks: q35's ICH9
(8086:2922) found in AHCI 1.0 with six ports and 32 slots; a 64 MB disk on
its first port - a protective MBR, a GPT and a Microsoft basic data
partition beginning with an NTFS boot sector - answering IDENTIFY as QEMU
HARDDISK, 131072 sectors of 512; its MBR and GPT read; one disk said; and
the image's SHA-256 the same afterwards. **Control**: the disk never looked
at - no IDENTIFY line, and the suite fails.

**Found by the first whole gate, and worth keeping**: the driver *returned*
when it had said its piece, and a role that returns falls through
`main.c` into init's own chunk - a second init, which took the screen from
the shell; thirty suites failed at once, and the gate ran 25 minutes. It ends
with `kosmos_exit` now, as the power button's does, and `main.c` exits after
it whatever it does. `x86-ahci` 5 -> 6: the driver ends with 0. **Control**:
both exits taken out - the driver never ends, and the suite fails. Whole
gate then: 81 of 82 in 8:27, x86-film the known flake, passing alone.

## 18.593 kfs version 2: when a file was made

`diskfs.md`, *Version 2*. The inode's word at offset 4 - a link count,
never read - is when the node was made, in seconds since 1970, from its
stamp; below the first second of 2000 it is not known, which is what
version 1's 1 and 2 read as. `kfs_upgrade` makes a version 1 disk version 2
by its superblock's version word; `diskfs` calls it at mount, after the
journal. `disk_node.created` carries it, `getattr` says it as `created`,
`setattr` refuses it, a query may ask for it.

**Tests.** `test_kfs.lua` 101 -> 111, run twice, the second through the
block cache: a new disk version 2; a file stored at a dated stamp keeping
that second; one stored without a date keeping none; a folder the same; a
file written over keeping its Created and taking a new Modified; a version 1
disk - superblock word 1, an inode's word 1 - mounting as version 1,
upgraded by its superblock (the word on the disk 2), its inode and its bytes
as they were, a second upgrade doing nothing, and a version 3 disk refused.
`x86-trackerlist` 9 -> 11: its `/Home` booted as version 1 is said to be
made version 2 and is version 2 on the image afterwards; and a file made in
Kosmos shows a Created of its own, not "its modified". **Controls**:
Created never kept - three of the format's checks fail; `diskfs` never
upgrading - the two new checks of Tracker's suite fail. Whole gate: 81 of
82 - arm-sandbox's "ipc: a receive with a deadline gives up", a timing test
nothing here touches, late once under the gate's load and 203 of 203 alone;
watched for a second time.

## 18.594 The virtualization probe, before VT-x

`docs/sandboxes.md`, S5. Before VT-x is written, the kernel says at boot
what the processor and its firmware allow (`arch_vm_probe`): on x86-64 CPUID
leaf 1 ECX bit 5 for VMX, and only then `IA32_FEATURE_CONTROL` (MSR 0x3A) -
bit 0 locked, bit 2 VMX outside SMX - as "vm: VT-x, locked on by the
firmware", "... locked off ... turn on Intel Virtualization Technology in
its setup", "... not locked", or "nothing to run a guest with"; on ARM, EL2
or nothing. `sysinfo.virt` carries it (`VIRT_*`, in what was
`guests_reserved`), and the Sandboxes window's Machine panel says it - so
the M700's first netboot says whether its setup needs changing.

**Tests.** `x86-virtprobe`, new, 2 checks: QEMU's x86, which has no VMX,
says "nothing to run a guest with" at boot and goes on to its prompt - the
probe neither faults nor stays silent. The other answers are the M700's to
give.

**On the M700, netbooted, 13 October**: "vm: VT-x, locked on by the
firmware" - an i7-6700 whose setup has Intel Virtualization Technology on,
so nothing there needs changing - and the Sandboxes window says "VT-x is on;
Kosmos does not drive it yet". The same boot made its stick's `/Home` kfs
version 2 ("the disk is kfs version 2 now"), and the SATA driver's first
real disk: 8086:a102, AHCI 1.3, port 0 a Samsung MZ7LN256HCHP (PM871b,
256 GB SATA in M.2), 500118192 sectors of 512, a protective MBR and a GPT -
read, not written.


## 18.595 VT-x in the kernel (X1), proved on the M700

`docs/sandboxes.md`, X1. The kernel enters a guest on x86-64 behind the
same four syscalls as on ARM (`arch/x86_64/vcpu.c`, `vmx.S`). The probe
reads what the processor offers once at boot - a VMCS of a page,
write-back; EPT walked in four levels, write-back, with an all-context
INVEPT; and the TRUE control MSRs, which let CR3 loads and stores go
unexited - and a machine short of any of them cannot run a guest. A core
enters VMX operation (CR0 and CR4 into the fixed bits, CR4.VMXE, `vmxon`)
the first time a vCPU runs there. A vCPU is three pages - its VMCS, an MSR
bitmap, and its FP registers and the five `syscall` MSRs the VMCS does not
swap - and its VMCS is cleared after every run, so every entry is a
`vmlaunch` and the next run may be on any core. Host state is read as it
is at each entry, and what an exit leaves wrong is put back by hand: the
GDT's and IDT's limits, DS and ES. The guest's FP registers are swapped
eagerly, as the context switch does; external interrupts exit without
being acknowledged, so the host takes its own as soon as the flags are
restored. `struct vcpu_regs` on x86-64 is 33 words: the sixteen registers
in the instruction set's order, RIP, RFLAGS, CR0, CR3, CR4, EFER, the
GDT, and the exit's reason, qualification, guest physical address,
length, whether the guest can take an interrupt, and the VM instruction
error. The monitor's ARM machine is guarded to ARM; its x86-64 half is X2.

**Tests.** The miniature monitor moved from `main.c` to `vmtest.c` and grew
an x86-64 half: five pages at 0x10000 - code, data, and the guest's own
PML4, PDPT and directory of 2 MB pages - entered in long mode; it reads
0x1234, writes 0x1235 beside it, stops on an EPT violation reading 0x200000
(qualification: a read; RIP at the load), is stepped past it and stops on
`hlt`. `CTEST_GUEST` runs it in the kernel suites (ARM: the guest runs;
x86 under TCG: 50, "cannot enter a guest"), and `ROLE_VMTEST` in the image
a machine boots, when the boot line says `opt/kosmos/vmtest`. Suites:
arm-kernel 203/203, x86-kernel 200/200, arm-sandbox, arm-sandbox-linux,
arm-sandboxwin, x86-virtprobe.

**On the M700, netbooted, 13 October (0.11.201)**: "vmtest: a guest ran
and stopped as it should", the first try, and the desktop came up after it.
**Control**: a kernel whose EPT leaves the data page out -
"vmtest: failed at 5, reason 00000030, error 0, address
0000000000011000, at 0000000000010000": an EPT violation, on the guest's
first instruction, at the page it was not given. The real kernel booted
again afterwards and passed.

## 18.596 Magnet from the keyboard, and Super inside a key's sequence

`docs/magnet.html`, `ui.md` 16.31. Diego agreed the encoding on 13 October
("Yes on the super + arrow proposal"). `hal/keys.c` puts every modifier in a
sequence's modifier number - Shift 1, Alt 2, Control 4, Super 8, so `m` is
two digits up to 16 - and a character with Super is xterm's
`ESC [ 27 ; m ; c ~`; Super tapped alone stays `ESC [ 1 ; 9 ~`. The PS/2,
virtio and pushed (USB) keyboards track the left Alt - the right is AltGr -
and a sequence typed with Super now marks Super used, so letting it go
after Super+→ opens no menu. VNC sends the same shapes. The applications'
decoder (`keys.lua`) reads both; the window manager reads each sequence
whole before deciding whether it is a chord, and hands on whole what is not
- which also took Alt+Shift+Tab's `ESC [ Z` out of a watcher that, with
Alt held, had handed the first two bytes of any sequence straight to the
window. Bindings: Super+arrows, Super+Alt+arrows, Super+Shift+↑/↓,
Super+Alt+1 to 5, Super+C (`OUT.magnet_key`); a Keys group on the Magnet
page.

**Tests.** `x86-magnet` 8 -> 14: through QEMU's PS/2 keyboard, Super+Right
the right half to the pixel, Super+Alt+Up the upper quarter on that side,
Super+Up the whole room, Super+Down back where it was, Super+Alt+1 the
left third to the pixel, Super+C the middle at its size. The kernel's
sequence test grew six Super and Alt cases and the three Super shapes;
`tools/test_keys.lua` 77 checks, the decoder reading them back - Super+Right,
Super+Shift+C and Super+C three keys. `x86-switcher` (Alt+Tab, Alt+Shift+Tab)
and `x86-shortcuts` pass. **Control**: Super left out of a sequence's

## 18.597 Sandboxes on x86-64: Alpine on the M700 (X2, X3)

`docs/sandboxes.md` X2 and X3. **The monitor split in three**: `vmm.c`
what both machines share (the console ring, keys, `/Running`, the setup,
its folders and network), `vmm_arm.c` the ARM machine moved as it was, and
`vmm_x86.c`, through `vmm.h`. **The PC's devices**, `x86dev.c`, pure: two
8259As as Linux's `i8259.c` programs and probes them, levels held and the
cascade; an 8254, channel 0 periodic or one-shot, channel 2 behind port
0x61; a 16550A that passes `8250_port.c`'s autoconfig and THRE test, its
line gated by OUT2; CPUID without APIC, x2APIC, XSAVE, AVX, VMX, PCID,
RDTSCP or the speculation MSRs, one processor, the TSC's frequency kept;
Linux's 64-bit boot - the zero page with the setup header copied, e820 in
three, the command line, a GDT with `__BOOT_CS` and `__BOOT_DS`, the first
4 GB identity in 2 MB pages, entered at 16 MB + 0x200; the guest's page
tables walked; and the `mov` forms of `readl`/`writel` decoded for MMIO.
**The run**: ports, CPUID, MSRs (EFER, PAT; the rest 0), CR0/CR4, MMIO by
EPT violation and decoding, `hlt` - waiting with interrupts on, ended with
them off - and the 8259's vector injected when the guest can take it, an
interrupt window asked for when it cannot. The command line adds `noapic
nolapic acpi=off pci=off nokaslr tsc=reliable 8250.nr_uarts=1` and each
virtio device as `virtio_mmio.device=0x200@0xd0000000:5` and on.
`sandboxes.lua` loads an x86 bzImage so its protected-mode kernel is at
16 MB, and says it when an image is for the other machine; `alpine.py
--arch x86_64` makes the PC's image, which the `alpine` package now is.
The end line found anywhere in a line (a `wget -qO-` page without a
newline lost its exit code), and Linux's "Power off not available" kept
off the console. `sandbox run` refused (a folder outside `/Home`) now
says why instead of a Lua error - found by the M700 suite's new checks.

**Tests.** `tools/test_x86dev.c`, host, 91 checks; control: CPUID leaving
the APIC showing fails "the APIC was not hidden". ARM's arm-sandbox,
arm-sandbox-linux and arm-sandboxwin pass over the split. **On the M700**
(0.11.203), `tools/run_m700.py`'s new sandbox checks, 6: VT-x found; a
task's 42, `x86_64` and exit code 3; a folder read only; a page fetched
through the network; a page served on port 8081 fetched from the Mac. And
by hand, a shell in the Sandboxes window answering `uname -a`. Linux asked
seven MSRs nobody answers (0x8b, 0x3a, 0x140, 0xce, 0x64e, 0x34,
0xc0011029) and booted on the zeros.

## 18.598 A sandbox's console, answering as it is typed

Diego, 13 October, typing into an x86 sandbox's console on the M700: "it
take several miliseconds to show the characteres", "shouldnt be instant?".
A key went to the monitor at once; the guest's echo then waited for the
Sandboxes window, which read a sandbox's console only on its half-second
clock - up to 500 ms - and before that for the monitor, which looked for
keys every two scheduler ticks while the guest idled - up to 8 ms. Now the
window reads the open sandbox's console on every pass of its loop while it
runs (`win.on_frame`), a pass every scheduler tick, painting only when
something arrived; and the monitor looks every tick on both machines. A
key's round trip is a few milliseconds of waiting at most, two ticks.
arm-sandboxwin and arm-sandbox-linux pass; on the M700 (0.11.204) for
Diego to feel.

## 18.599 A backspace in a sandbox's console; TCP through a narrow router; a guest's date

Three things Diego found using an x86 sandbox on the M700, 13 October.

**"backspace is not working, is printing some weird characters".** The
guest's shell erased correctly; Linux echoes an erase as `\b \b`, which
Kosmos's console has always obeyed and the Sandboxes window drew as a
glyph each. The window now steps back over a character, a whole UTF-8 one,
never past a line's start (`added`). `arm-sandboxwin` 9 -> 11: `echo abcd`,
two Backspaces, the shown line `echo ab`, and the shell running `echo ab`.
Control: the window adding bytes as they come - "shell1:~# echo abcd\x08\x08".

**"does the linux client has internet access? to download packages?"**
Plain HTTP did (Alpine's 528 KB index); HTTPS to anywhere past the house
did not - `apk` said "TLS: unspecified error" and nothing came back. Not
the sandbox: **Kosmos's TCP sent 1460-byte segments with don't-fragment
set whatever the far end said, and ignored ICMP "fragmentation needed".**
Diego's line is PPPoE - `ping -D -s 1472` from the Mac: "frag needed and
DF set (MTU 1492)" from 192.168.1.1 - so every full segment Kosmos sent to
the internet was dropped, and a request over one segment never arrived. A
GET fits in one, and so does Kosmos's own TLS hello, which is why nothing
had shown it; a guest's OpenSSL hello, with a server name and a
post-quantum key share, does not. `net.c`: a connection's segments are
the MSS the far end's SYN or SYN-ACK announced (`mss_of`, 536 when it said
nothing, never over 1460), and "fragmentation needed" (`too_big`, RFC
1191) makes them fit the router and sends again what was in flight.
**`x86-tcpmtu`, new**: `opt/kosmos/net_mtu=1400` puts a router on the
path that passes nothing over 1400 bytes and says so; three whole screens
by VNC must cross it, the segments made 1360. Control: the stack hearing
the router and changing nothing - "only 0 of 3 whole frames arrived".

**The guest's date**: it read 1 January 2026 on a PC (a fixed RTC) and
1970 on ARM (none), and a certificate is checked against it. The setup
page carries the time (`vmm_setup.epoch`, from `/Devices/clock`, in what
was 8 reserved bytes), and the x86 monitor's RTC answers it, counted on by
its own counter, in BCD (`x86_rtc`; `test_x86dev` 91 -> 97: 13 October 2026
15:04:05, a Tuesday, 29 February 2028, the epoch). ARM's guest has no RTC
yet - roadmap.

**On the M700 (0.11.205)**: `sandbox run alpine --network -- date; apk add
htop` - "Tue Oct 13 15:10:48 UTC 2026", htop 3.5.3 installed from Alpine's
HTTPS mirror, 3.3 MB in 5 s.

Whole gate: 81 of 84 - x86-maps, x86-mail-5 and x86-smbd. Maps and Mail's
attachments pass alone. **x86-smbd failed three runs in a row with the
new `net.c` and passed with the old**, so it was not waved through: its
visitor (an `smbclient` on a pseudo-terminal) signed in and its connection
ended during its first `ls`. Every incoming connection's MSS was 1460, the
same segments as before; one line of logging at accept made it pass; then
two more runs of the new `net.c` passed (90 s each), and it had failed once
in 0.11.203's gate before `net.c` changed. A race in that step, not the
MSS - watched, with the serial capture to take next time it fails.

## 18.603 The Sandboxes window: the machine's whole memory

On the M700 the sidebar said "0.3 of 3 GB given" and the title "of 2894 MB"
on a machine with 8 GB. The window read `ram_size` from `sys.info()`, which
is `hal_ram_range` - the first range of RAM, and on a PC that range ends at
the hole below 4 GB. It now reads the pages the kernel hands out,
`pages_total` times `page_size`, which is what Machine calls Installed and
`/Devices/memory` calls `total_mb`.

**Tests.** None that bites: QEMU's ARM board has one range, so `ram_size`
and the pages agree there, and `arm-sandboxwin` (16) cannot tell them apart.

## 18.604 A process's own memory, given on first touch

Roadmap 6j, found 24 September: every process held its image's writable
half (3.4 MB, most of it FFmpeg's tables), a 2 MB heap and a 256 KB stack
from the moment it was made - `process_create` allocated, copied and zeroed
them all. Now they are address space at spawn and a page each the first
time it is touched (`process_fill`): a copy of the image's page there, or
zeroes in the heap and the stack. A translation fault from EL0 on AArch64,
or a not-present fault from ring 3 on x86-64, in one of those three ranges
is given the page and retried; a pointer a syscall is handed is filled by
`range_ok` before the kernel touches it. The page above the heap and the
one below the stack get nothing, so an overflow is still a fault.

**The kernel was half of it.** The first M700 boot with only that freed
the heap and the stack and nothing else: every process still held 3.4 MB,
the whole writable image - because `_start` zeroed `.bss` again, on both
architectures, "so the image stops depending on how it was built", and that
loop touched every page. The image carries `.bss` as zeroes and the fill
copies them, so the loop went.

**x86's page fault runs on `tss.ist[0]`**, the stack that makes a kernel
stack overflow survivable, and one stack per core is not somewhere a thread
can be switched away from. A ring-3 page fault used to end its process;
now it returns all the time. So `vectors.S` does not act on a pending
preemption after #PF or #DF: the flag stands and the next interrupt acts
on it, the timer's at the latest.

**Measured on the M700**, the same windows open (Files, Sandboxes,
Monitor, Processes, VNC) and shell86 running with its 256 MB:

| | in use |
|---|---|
| 0.11.209, as it was | 682 MB |
| heap and stack on first touch | 652 MB |
| and `_start` not zeroing `.bss` | 524 MB |

After boot alone, before any window: 332 MB with the kernel change only,
224 MB with both. A C server - `devices`, `binfs`, `libfs` - holds 16 to
24 KB where it held 5816; `init` 612 KB, `diskfs` 3.2 MB.

**Tests.** `x86-kernel` and `arm-sandbox` (the AArch64 kernel suite at EL2)
gain `el0: memory is given on first touch`: the system image made into a
process that never runs holds nothing of its writable half, heap or stack;
the first page of the writable half with a non-zero byte, touched, is the
image's bytes; a heap page is zeroes; the page past the heap, the one below
the stack and the one above it are refused; a pointer handed to
`process_may_write` is filled by the check; and the pages come back when
the process is abandoned, on top of the ten an untouched one keeps in its
thread's slot. `el0: code shared, writable not` now asserts the heap and
the stack are unmapped until touched, and different pages after.
**Controls**: a fill that copied nothing failed the new test, and with it
`mail: a message read through the kit` - the first version of the check
looked at the first page, all `.bss`, and passed; not freeing the heap at
exit failed it by exactly the four heap pages it touches. The gate: 84
suites, `x86-network` failing once under load on a lookup and passing three
times alone.

## 18.605 A sandbox's memory, given on touch

The second half of 18.604, for a sandbox. Its RAM was a region of 256 MB
(or whatever it was given) allocated and zeroed when it started, so a shell
sandbox doing nothing cost the machine all 256 MB. A region can now be made
**given on touch** (`MEM_ON_TOUCH`, `sys.memory(pages, "on touch")`): its
index starts empty and a zeroed page goes into a slot the first time
anything touches it (`memobj_fill`), one page to everybody - which is what
lets two sides share it:

- **the monitor**, which maps the region to load the kernel and to read
  and write virtio's rings: a fault in a mapped region given on touch is
  answered by `sharemap_fill`, under the lock that taking a mapping down
  holds, so a page never lands in a range on its way out;
- **the guest**: an EPT violation on an entry that is not there at all
  (basic reason 48, qualification bits 3-5 clear) or a stage-2 translation
  fault (EC 0x20 or 0x24, fault status 4-7) is `arch_vcpu_missed`; if the
  address is in a region given on touch, `vm_vcpu_run` fills it, puts it in
  the second stage and goes straight back into the guest, without the
  monitor hearing. The same page missed twice running goes to the monitor.

`SYS_MEM_SIZE` with a second argument of 1 answers the pages behind a
region, and the monitor's reply carries it as `ram_used`: the card says
"84 of 256 MB", the Overview's Memory panel graphs it as the drawing has it
("Memory · 38 of 256 MB", green), and `sandbox list` prints it. It is a
high-water mark: memory Linux frees stays given.

**Measured on the M700**: shell86 started with 84 of 256 MB in use and the
machine's free memory fell by 87 MB, not 256; `dd` of 60 MB into its
`/tmp` took it to 131, and the graph stepped with it. Alpine's `free -m`
agrees with what it was doing throughout.

**Tests.** `mem: a region given on touch` in both kernel suites: nothing
behind a region of a thousand pages but its index; a page given zeroed, the
same page on every later fill, two counted, nothing past the end, no region
of nothing and no run given on touch, and every page back when it goes. A
fill that never kept its page failed it. `arm-sandbox-linux` 26 -> 27:
`sandbox list` shows web, running, with fewer than 128 of its 256 MB in
use; made whole at the start it read "256 of 256 MB in use" and failed.
The x86 path, EPT, is not in any suite - QEMU's TCG has no VT-x - and was
seen on the M700.

## 18.607 Restart in the Sandboxes window, seen

Diego, 13 October: "does restarting a sandbox work? i dont see linux
restarting at all". It did restart, and the window could not show it, for
two reasons. The window reads a console from the offset it last reached,
and a restarted sandbox is a new monitor whose console begins at nothing -
so the new boot showed nothing until it had said as much as the old one,
and then from the middle. And Restart waited for the old monitor to go,
which stays ten seconds after its guest ends so its last lines can be read.

Now a console that has said less than the window has read is a new one,
read from its start under "--- started again ---"; and a restarting
sandbox whose guest has ended is told to go at once.

**Tests.** `arm-sandboxwin` 16 -> 18: Restart in the watched sandbox's
header, then the first console line shown, past the old monitor's "vmm:
stopped, as asked", is the first line the first boot showed; and shell1
running again. **Control**: without the new-console check it showed
nothing within two minutes and failed.

## 18.609 The scheduler's policy, changed on every core

`docs/scheduler.md` G1. Diego, 11 October: "I cant change the scheduler
policy any more". `sched_switch_to` refused once more than one core
scheduled - every machine since 0.10.22 - because swapping drained every
core's queue at once. The design said: keep the choice as a setting and
apply it when Kosmos starts, "before a second core takes work". That could
not work either: the setting is in `/Home`, read through servers that are
already running on every core.

**Each core changes over by itself.** The kernel keeps the policy asked for
and the policy each core runs (`core_policy[]`); a core's entry changes only
under its own queue lock, where everything that touches its queue already
holds it. `change_over` drains that core's queue out of the policy it runs,
empties the new policy's queues for that core (`reset`, new beside `init`),
and enqueues what it drained. The core that asks changes at once; every
other at its next tick, before its policy judges the thread running there.
A thread woken onto a core in between is queued in whatever that core runs,
under its lock, and moves over with the rest - none is stranded.

The choice is kept by name in `/Home/Preferences/scheduler`
(`scheduling.lua`), and the window manager puts it back as the desktop
starts, saying so in the log. The Scheduler window keeps every choice made
in it and says when one is refused, with the policy's name.

**Tests.** Kernel, both architectures: `sched: the policy changes on every
core` - two threads on every other core that only yield, so each has one
queued while the other runs; round-robin asked for from core zero; every
core seen running it within a second; every thread still moving after; and
back. **Controls**: a changeover that dropped what it drained failed it, and
`sched: the higher priority runs first` and `a wake preempts a lower band`
with it; the old refusal put back did *not* fail it, because the suite
narrows placement to one core (`thread_cpu_count` is 1 there) and the
refusal asked that, which is how the suite never saw the bug - the new test
puts its threads on other cores itself. `tools/test_scheduling.lua` (host),
7: a choice kept by name, made the kernel's number at the start, nothing
set that is already so, an unknown policy said; control: `index_of` finding
nothing failed 3.

## 18.610 The Scheduler window, as drawn

`docs/scheduler.md` G2, `docs/scheduler.html` agreed on 11 October
("Perfect"). The window was two cards of facts and two dropdowns; it is now
the drawing: **the modes as cards** - Balanced (priority) and Fair
(round-robin), each saying what it is for, what it buys and what it costs,
the one in force marked, a click putting it in force on every core and
keeping it; Game mode drawn and marked *next*, which says so when pressed.
**Who ran**: a lane a processor over its last 512 ticks - two seconds - a
colour a band, idle empty. **The bands** as a ladder with what lives in
each; under Fair, said to be unasked. **A turn**: 4, 12, 20, 40 and 100 ms,
the one in force lit, and a bar from snappier to more work done. **The
numbers**: switches a second, the keys' longest wait, and a game's slowest
frame, which waits for game mode. Sizes are measured from the faces in
force rather than copied from the drawing's pixels, so a larger look fits.

**What the kernel had to say for it** (`SYS_SCHED_LANE`, `struct
sched_lane`): each core writes, at every tick, the band of what it is
running into a ring of 512; counts its switches; and keeps, for each band,
the longest a thread waited from its wake to running over this second and
the one before - in counter ticks, named so (`wait_counter_max`). A thread
is stamped when woken (`woken_at`) and the wait taken when it is switched
in. Each core writes only its own; a reader's snapshot may be a tick old.

**Tests.** Kernel, both architectures: `sched: a core says what it ran` - a
thread on core one working two milliseconds and sleeping a tick: its lane
shows the normal band at recent ticks, its switches climb, its wakes leave
a wait in the normal band's slot, and a core that is not there answers no.
**Control**: a wake that does not stamp the thread failed it. New suite
`x86-scheduler` (8), on four processors: the window opens on priority, says
where its cards and turns are, reads every lane and counts switches; Fair
pressed is round-robin in the kernel; a turn of 20 ms; Game mode says it is
next; Balanced puts priority back. **Control**: the refusal of 0.11.213
put back - Fair failed with "this process does not hold that device", the
words Diego saw on the M700.

## 18.611 Game mode, for one application

`docs/scheduler.md` G3. Diego, 11 October: "Let's do per app game mode
yes"; Super+G as Windows has it; a notification as it starts and ends; and
any application chosen in the Scheduler.

**The band** (`SCHED_PRIO_GAME`) sits between normal and display, so DISPLAY,
AUDIO and INPUT moved up one: 4, 5 and 6. A thread's `game` flag puts its
normal work there, read as it is next queued - waking, yielding, preempted
- since a priority queue files a thread under its band and a band cannot
change under a queued thread. **The budget**: a game thread that runs a
second without sleeping is held at normal until it sleeps. **The bands'
names** are now the kernel's (`schedinfo.band`, `sys.scheduler().band_names`):
`init.lua`, `htop`, Processes and the Scheduler each kept a list, and a new
band would have left all four wrong.

**Who gives it**: only a process's parent (`process_set_game`,
`SCHED_SET_GAME`), the authority `kill` has - nothing promotes itself. The
window manager opens applications, so it is their parent: `wm/gamemode.lua`
holds one application at a time with game mode, gives its process the band
while one of its windows is in front and takes it back when another is, and
ends it when the last window goes. An application has it when its window
opens if its header's `kosmos: kind` is `game` or `emulator` (Doom, Quake
and the Super Nintendo already said so; the design's new word would have
been a second one); Super+G gives it to the application in front or takes
it away; the Scheduler's Game mode card lists the applications with a
window and gives it to the one chosen. A program started by a shell has the
shell for a parent and cannot be given it - written down, not hidden.

**Tests.** Kernel, both architectures: `sched: game mode, given by a
parent` - the system image made into a process: refused to anyone not its
parent, given and taken by "no parent", every thread marked; a game thread
on core one that works and sleeps runs in the game band, above normal and
below display; one that spins a second and a half is held at normal.
**Controls**: a budget never spent, and the flag ignored, each failed it.
`x86-scheduler` 8 -> 11: Super+G over the Scheduler gives it game mode and
the band while it is in front; its card's menu offers the applications;
Super+G again ends it. **Control**: the band never asked of the kernel
failed it. `arm-synth-load` still holds Groove's sound under four display
spinners after the renumbering.

## 18.612 A core of the game's own, and the first thread that moves

`docs/scheduler.md` G4. Diego, 11 October, to "allow Nebula to move a
sleeping thread to another home, once, when game mode starts": yes.

**Placement and the give.** While a process has the game band, the least
busy core other than zero - zero wakes the sleepers and reads the input - is
reserved (`reserved_core`): `place_new_thread` skips it, the game's first
thread is asked to move there, and every other movable thread living there
is asked to move to the least busy of the rest (`thread_give_core`). Taken
back with the band, and the core is open again. The window manager says
which core in the log, and the Scheduler on its Game rung.

**The move.** Nebula has never moved a thread, and three things in it
assumed so:

- a thread's floating point is saved lazily on AArch64 - in its core's
  registers until another thread there wants them - so a thread that ran on
  another core would load stale values: **a move is taken up only by the
  thread itself as it blocks, on its own core** (`take_up_move`), which
  first hands its registers back into its context (`fp_hand_back`);
- a thread that has just blocked is still running on its core's stack until
  the switch away is over, and its home core is the only one that could pick
  it up, which was always busy finishing that switch: **a thread is
  `on_cpu` from being switched in until the next thread on that core has
  arrived**, and the waker of a thread waits for that before handing it to
  its (new) core;
- `switch_into` read its core once, since what resumes is always on the
  same core: it reads it again after the switch.

**And a home read before its lock may be stale**: `thread_wake` asks for the
thread's home again under the lock, and follows it if it moved. Threads
made for a core (`thread_create_on`, `THREAD_START_ON`) are `pinned`, and
idle threads are never moved.

**The first version deadlocked, and the suite found it.** It put the wait
in the switch - the core about to run a moved thread waited for its old
core to be off it. Two cores each switching to the thread the other was
leaving waited for each other with interrupts masked, for ever; on the
third of eight runs `x86-kernel` panicked "tlb: processor 1 never answered
a shootdown". The wait is the waker's now, which is never in the middle of
a switch - as in Linux - and ten runs of both kernel suites in a row passed.

**Tests.** Kernel, both architectures: `sched: a thread moves cores` -
three threads working and sleeping; one asked to core two is homed there
and seen running there within a second; core three given to it as a game's,
everybody else off it, and twelve threads placed across every core none of
them there; all still running after. **Controls**: moves never taken up
failed it; placement ignoring the reservation failed it once the placed
threads were held until all twelve were placed (before that the control
passed, which is how the first version of the check was found vacuous).
Not held here: a moved thread's floating point, since the kernel suite has
none; a game on the M700 is where that shows. `x86-scheduler` 11 -> 12: on
four processors the game is given a core, and not core one.

**Seen twice in the gate since G3, and not explained**: a suite that waits
for `telnetd` at boot ("the guest never telnetd listening within 120s") -
`x86-drawself` in the gate at 0.11.216, `x86-tracker` at 0.11.217. Each
passed three times alone, and the ten suites that wait for `telnetd`, run
together twice, all passed. `telnetd` waits for DHCP from QEMU's network;
before G3 it was never recorded. Watched: a third time is investigated
before anything else lands.

## 18.613 Every control published, by what a person sees

`docs/automations.md` A1: the kit names its controls, and a window answers
for them at `/Running/<name>/controls`, so any application can be driven by
name without its author writing anything.

**What it is.** `window:controls()` walks the window's views, skipping
hidden ones, and each of the kit's controls describes itself - a button by
its words or the name it was given, a checkbox or switch read and set
`on`/`off`, a dropdown chosen by an item's words, a field typed into,
segments and tabs one control an item, a slider a number, a menubar's items
`menu/<menu>/<item>`. An icon button that says what it opens (`menu`, a list
or a function as a menubar's) publishes that as `menu/<icon>/<item>`, which
is how the Text Editor's dots became `menu/more/Find and replace`. A view an
application drew itself says `control`, a `label` and `read` or `press`:
Calculator's keys are `button/7` and `button/×`, its display
`display/Result`. A press runs **the handler a click runs**, and a disabled
control refuses with "disabled".

**A folder at any depth** lists the next part of every address under it -
`controls` its kinds, `controls/button` its labels, `controls/menu/more` the
dots' items. The first version knew only one level, and the suite's own
`menu/more` listing was what failed.

**And a key it would have missed.** The kit's button description read only
`text` and `on_click`; Calculator's keys give `label` and a `press` method,
so they would have been left out silently. It takes either now.

**Test.** `x86-controls` (`tools/run_controls.py`), one boot over Telnet,
names only: Calculator's kinds and its eighteen keys listed by their faces,
its display read 0, C 7 × 6 = pressed by name and the display read 42, a
key that is not there and a press on the display refused; the Text Editor's
dots' menu listed, its Replace button not a control while the find bar is
hidden, and `menu/more/Find and replace` chosen by name bringing it. 11
checks, 25 s. **Control**: with an icon button's `menu` not published, 3
of the 11 fail - the listing, the choice, and the Replace button.

## 18.614 A new thread starts masked: the hang G4 brought

**Found by the gate for A1**: `x86-share` stopped answering at a different
step each time, the guest silent, no panic. It had passed at 0.11.217's
gate. Attributed before explained: with the kernel files of 0.11.216 - before
threads could move - it passed twice; with 0.11.217's it hung three runs of
three. Nothing in SMB had changed.

**What a probe said.** A spinlock here panics after a bounded wait, so a
silent hang is an unbounded spin, and G4 added exactly one: `thread_wake`
waiting for a thread's `on_cpu` to clear. Bounded and made to name names, it
fired: `smbfs` on core 0 waking `init`, whose mark was never cleared; the
core's last switch was from `init` *to* `smbfs`, and the switch count one
ahead of the arrivals. So `smbfs` was running without ever having passed
`arrived()`. The per-CPU pointer was the same after the switch (probed), and
no thread had switched from outside its own stacks (probed).

**The cause.** `context_switch` ends with `popfq` (`msr daif` on AArch64),
the incoming thread's flags, and says "nothing that matters happens after
it". A resumed thread's flags are masked, since `switch_into` runs masked.
**A new thread's were planted unmasked** - `rflags = 0x202`, `daif = 0` - so
`thread_entry` ran with interrupts on until `thread_switch_finished`. Before
G4 that call stored `leaving`, and an interrupt in the window only made the
same store first. With `on_cpu` it matters twice over: an interrupt there
can wake the thread just left - still marked on this core - and wait for the
mark with the core masked under it, for ever; or preempt, overwriting
`switching_from` and leaving a thread marked on a core it is not on.

**The fix.** A new thread is planted masked (`0x002`; `daif` I and F), and
`thread_entry` lifts the mask (`sti`; `msr daifclr, #3`) right after
`thread_switch_finished`. The thread's own function still starts with
interrupts on. Both architectures; AArch64 had the same window.

**Test.** `thread_switch_finished` panics if it runs unmasked - "a new thread
started with interrupts enabled" - so the invariant is checked on the first
new thread of every boot rather than by a race one run in three.
**Control**: either architecture's thread planted unmasked again, and its
kernel suite panics at once with that line (`x86-kernel`, `arm-kernel`).
`x86-share` then passed nine runs of nine; the kernel suites, both, and
`x86-scheduler` pass.

**The `telnetd` flake of 18.612 is probably this.** A core stuck in that
spin is lost for good while the others go on, and a suite whose `telnetd`
was homed there waits two minutes for it - seen only since G3/G4, under the
gate's load. Watched still: if it is seen again, this was not all of it.

## 18.615 The verbs of an automation, and two ways a window did not answer

`docs/automations.md` A2. **`automate.lua`** is the verbs: an application
opened by the name it declares and found when it is open, and on it
`press`, `menu`, `read`, `type`, `set`, `choose`, `wait` by what a person
sees - a label alone when one control has it, refused with every address
when two do - and `mail`, `check`, `copy`, `move`, `notify`, `wait`, `run`.
**`mailout.lua`** is the Outbox's writing, taken out of the composer
rather than copied: the composer builds and posts through it, and so does
`auto.mail`. **`automate`** runs one verb at the prompt.

**Two hangs, both older than A2, found by its suite.**

- *A reply too big for a message.* The first `addresses` answer was a
  table per control; the Text Editor with its find bar open was more than
  2048 bytes, `sys.reply` raised, and the window's `pcall` swallowed it - so
  the caller waited for good. Now every window request is answered, with
  "the answer does not fit in one message" when the real one does not; and
  `addresses` comes a page at a time, four letters and an address an entry.
- *A window in a loop of its own.* Mail draws itself and loops around
  `wmproto.poll`; only `win:run` served the window's endpoint, so any
  request to `/Running/Mail` - its controls, its title - waited for ever.
  `ui.window` now registers every window with `wmproto`, and `poll` answers
  its requests on every pass; a change it answers is kept for `run`, which
  polls the same way and would otherwise not repaint.

**Mail publishes nothing yet**: its buttons are pixels. Roadmap A1b.

**Tests.** Host: `tools/test_automate.lua`, 19 checks - an address said
exactly, a label alone, two of one label refused with both named, `#2`,
the kind deciding a field from a button beside it, a missing label said;
an application's windows by name, by number (`Mail2`) and by title (`notes.md
- Text Editor`), and never `Mailbox` for Mail. **Control**: `resolve` taking
the first of two - 2 fail. Guest: `x86-automate` (`tools/run_automate.py`),
29 checks over Telnet, `automate` lines only: Calculator opened by its name
and found again, C 7 × 6 = pressed and Result read 42, a missing label
said; the Text Editor opened with a file, Find and replace chosen, its Find
field typed into by its hint and read back; a window of 120 buttons listed
whole and Key 117 pressed by name, its own handler running; Mail answering;
a mail written to the Outbox with its envelope; a page this Mac serves
checked by its title and one refused in words; a copy into a folder, a
banner, a wait, a program run. 67 s. **Controls**, together: paging off and
`poll` answering nothing - the 120 refused in words ("does not fit in one
message") rather than hanging, and Mail never answering.

**Whole gate**: 86 of 87. `x86-packages` read "the others still installed"
after a removal - its second time (18.589 watched for it). Found: the
install step waited for the window's `listed` line and moved on, and the
`states` line that follows it reached the serial line after the removal's
mark, so the removal's check read the install's states. The check now reads

## 18.617 The composer by name: a mail written and sent from a script

## 18.618 Automations on their triggers: `autod`

`docs/automations.md` A3. **`automations.lua`** is the model: an
automation is a table in `/Home/Automations/<name>.automation` - its
trigger (`at` a time on chosen days, `every` so many minutes, `start`, a
`folder`'s new file, a `drive` arriving, by `hand`) and its steps, each a
verb of `automate.lua` with its words - checked in words before it is run
or kept. What a step finds is named for the next (`{page title}`,
`{answer}`, `{file}`); a `check` whose page does not say what was asked,
and `stop_unless`, stop the run as a success. Each run is kept with every
step's sentence, outcome and time, the last fifty.

**`autod`** is started by the Deskbar at login when there is one, as
`maild` is. It sleeps until the nearest time, looks at the folders and
drives it watches every five seconds, and answers `run`, `status` and
`reload` at `/Running/autod` - a run is queued and answered at once, and
between a run's steps it answers whoever asked meanwhile. A failure is a
banner the first time, none while it goes on failing.

**Tests.** Host: `tools/test_automations.lua`, 21 checks - 8:00 asked at
7:59:30 is this morning, 7:00 is tomorrow, Mondays' 7:00 next Monday, a
weekend time Saturday; every 30 minutes from its last run; `{page title}`
filled and `{nothing}` left as written; seven ways a file is not an
automation, each in words. **Control**: the days ignored - 2 fail. Guest:
`x86-autod`, 16 checks, 56 s - five files written (one with a verb nobody
knows, said so and not run); `automate automation Answer` opens
Calculator, presses 7 × 6 =, reads Result as `{answer}` and posts "The
answer is 42", its history 8 of 8 steps; a file put in `/Temporary/inbox`
copied to `/Temporary/out`; Broken fails with "no control called Launch"
and a banner, and again with none; `automate automations` saying which
failed and which is bad; Stops kept as stopped, not failed. **Controls**:
a banner for every failure, and folders never looked at - 3 fail.


**Whole gate**: 88 of 88.
