## 18.621 Mail as a trigger, through a file

An automation can start on a mail arriving - from someone, about
something, or any. **`maild` writes, `autod` reads**: `say_arrived`
adds each message to `/Temporary/maild/arrived` through
`mailarrived.lua` - numbered, the last fifty - and `autod`'s five-second
look takes what came after the newest number it has seen, starting from
the newest when it starts, so old mail is not news. `{sender}`,
`{subject}` and `{message}` are what it finds. The window knows the
trigger: its words, its card, From and Subject in the When sheet. **Why a
file, not a call**: Nebula's IPC is call and reply, so `maild` calling
would wait while `autod` is in a step, and `autod` holding a call could not
answer anything else. Pulses - one-way messages - are to be designed
(`roadmap.md`); the file is behind one library, which is all that changes.

**And a failure 0.11.225 carried**: the new `.automation` type had no
group on Preferences' File types page, which grew an "Other" the drawing
does not have - `host`'s `test_filetypes` said so, and 0.11.225 ran only
the window's own suite. The type is in the Kosmos group now, with its
sentence. A file type is `filetypes.lua`'s, a shared piece: the whole gate.

**Tests.** Host: `test_automations.lua`, 25 checks - a mail trigger is an
automation; what arrived numbered in order, what came after a number, and
the newest fifty kept. **Control**: the cap at five hundred - the fifty
check fails. Guest: `x86-autod`, 21 checks - a mail written down before
`autod` started runs nothing; one from ana@ runs "Mail in", whose banner
says "Mail from ana@example.test: Lunch"; the automation for zed@ does not
run.


**Whole gate**: 89 of 89.

## 18.622 Pulses in Nebula: news sent without waiting

`docs/pulses.md` P1, and the runtime half of P2. **The kernel**: each
endpoint keeps a ring of 32 `struct pulse` - a code, a count, a value -
beside its queues (`ipc.h`, about 600 bytes an endpoint now). `ipc_pulse`
hands a pulse straight to a receiver already waiting, or merges it into a
waiting pulse of the same code (counted, the newest value), or takes a free
slot, or refuses a new code into a full ring with `IPC_ERR_FULL` (-8) - and
never blocks. `ipc_receive` takes a waiting caller first, then a pulse, as
a message tagged `MSG_TAG_PULSE` with no sender, so a reply to it is
refused (`ipc_reply_token(0)`). `wait_for_caller` and `has_caller` count
pulses, so a server sleeping until somebody calls wakes for one too. A new
endpoint starts with an empty ring; a destroyed one takes its pulses.
`SYS_PULSE` is 72. **The runtime**: `kosmos_pulse` and `struct
kosmos_pulse` in `kosmos.h` (the layout checked against the kernel's in
`sys_user.c`), `sys.pulse(cap, code, value)`, and `sys.receive` returning
`{ pulse = true, code, count, value }` and no sender.

**Test.** Kernel, both architectures: "ipc: a pulse is sent without
waiting" - two of code 7 and one of 9 with nobody receiving read back as
code 7 counted twice with the newest value, then 9, then nothing; 32 codes
fill the ring, a 33rd is refused at once and one already there still
merges, and the 32 drain in order; a thread blocked in receive gets a pulse
directly, with no sender; a destroyed endpoint refuses a pulse. **Control**:
merging off - the test fails on both, naming merged, second, empty,
merged-when-full and drained.

**Whole gate**: 88 of 89. `x86-dock` read Preferences, made 160 taller,
not yet laid out at its new height - a new signature for this suite under
load; it passed alone twice (3:47, 3:41). Nothing sends a pulse yet, so
nothing P1 changed runs in that path. Watched.

## 18.623 maild tells autod by pulse; the file goes

`docs/pulses.md` P3. `mailarrived.lua` is still the one door, with both
halves now: in `maild` it keeps the last fifty arrivals, numbered, each
with the counter when it came, and pulses every subscriber once a batch
(`sys.pulse`, code 1, the newest number); a subscriber whose endpoint is
gone is let go. It answers `subscribe` - the subscriber's endpoint passed
beside it, which `maild`'s loop now keeps from `sys.receive` - and
`arrived`. In `autod` a pulse is taken in its receive loop with no reply
(nobody waits) and sets mail due; `autod` then asks what came after the
newest it saw. `/Temporary/maild/arrived` is gone.

**A race the suite found at once**: Bob's message arrives during `maild`'s
first IDLE, seconds after it starts - before `autod`'s next look had
subscribed - and subscribing then took "newest" as seen, so Bob was never
news. In use the Deskbar starts `maild` and `autod` together, in either
order. Now a first subscription to a `maild` looks at everything it kept
and takes what came since *`autod`* started, by each arrival's counter.

**Tests.** Host: `test_automations.lua`, 30 checks - a subscription needs
an endpoint passed with it; a request it does not know is left for
`maild`; each batch pulses a subscriber once with the newest number; a
gone subscriber is released; what came after a number, in order; fifty
kept. Guest: `x86-mail-2`, against the Mac's IMAP server - `autod` with
three mail automations started before `maild`; Bob's message, delivered
during IDLE, runs "Bob wrote" and its banner carries `{sender}` and
`{subject}`, and "Zed wrote" does not run; the long letter delivered much
later runs "Digest arrived". **Control**: `maild` keeping arrivals but
pulsing nobody - the digest's automation never runs, since nothing in
`autod` looks for mail on a clock (2 of 15 fail).

**Whole gate**, first run: 86 of 89. `x86-autod`'s "no second banner"
matched the *first* banner's "notifications: banners at ..." reaching the
serial line after the mark - the suite's check, not `autod`; it looks for
a second post of the failure now. `x86-film`, the known flake. And
`x86-mail-3`: telnetd never listening, the network never given an address
- 18.612's flake, back after the fix it was thought to be part of. With
only the suite's last 3000 characters there was nothing before the silence
to read, so **every suite's guest now keeps its whole serial line** in
`build/gate/serial/<suite>-<n>.log` (`Guest.close`, `KOSMOS_SUITE` from the
gate). Watched, with the whole log next time. Second run: 89 of 89.

## 18.624 Folders that tell: Tracker sees a change at once

`docs/pulses.md` P4; Diego, 14 October: "Will this allow then tracker so
see filesystem changes in real time? Right now you need to refresh the app
to see new files". **The servers**: `folderwatch.c`, one door both
filesystem servers use - a watch is a folder, the capability passed with
it, a code and who asked; a change of a name in that folder pulses every
watcher of it; the same asker and code moves a watch, its old capability
let go; a watcher whose endpoint is gone is let go at the next change; the
list grows. `diskfs` answers `DISK_OP_WATCH`/`UNWATCH` (14, 15) and tells
watchers wherever it already noted "anything that may have changed the
disk", for a change that happened - a rename's destination too. `ramfs`
answers `RAM_OP_FOLDER_WATCH`/`UNWATCH` (14, 15), told by the store whether
its last answer was the one asked for (`ram_answered_ok`). **The
namespace**: `fs.watch_folder(path, code, pass)` and `fs.unwatch_folder`,
in each server's own protocol; and `fs.send` now returns a capability that
came back with an answer, as `reply.passed`, where it was dropped unread.
**The window manager**: `watch_code` hands a window a code and passes a
capability to its own endpoint; a pulse there with a code it handed out
becomes a `changed` event in that window's poll, and any other is dropped.
**The kit**: `win:watch_folder(path, fn)`, one folder a window, taken back
when it watches another or closes. **Tracker** watches the folder it shows
and lists it again when told, the chosen file still chosen.

**Test.** Host: `tools/test_folderwatch.c`, 15 checks - the folder a change
is in told and no other, whatever the slashes; moved by its owner and code,
the old door let go; taken back by its owner only; a gone subscriber let
go; a hundred kept. **Control**: the parent computed wrong - 5 fail. Guest:
`x86-folders` (`tools/run_livefolders.py`), 14 checks, 22 s - Tracker on
`/Home/Live` and `/Temporary/Live`, each saying it tells; a file written,
renamed and deleted by another program over Telnet listed again by itself
each time, in 0.13-0.16 s including the Telnet round trip; a change in
another folder telling it nothing. **Control**: the servers never pulsing -
6 of 14 fail, every change unseen.


**Whole gate**: 90 of 90.

## 18.626 The PDF Kit reads a page's text, its outline and its pictures

The PDF reader's step 1 (`docs/pdfview.md`), in the kit rather than the
application, so Quick Look, Write and anything after can have them through
the same door: `pdf.text(doc, page)` gives the page's characters in reading
order and, for each run, where it is - which Find and Copy will draw over;
`pdf.outline(doc)` gives the document's contents, titled, with their pages;
and `pdf.render` now draws a JPEG picture (`DCTDecode`) where the page's
matrix puts it, before the text, decoded by `gfx.jpeg` straight from a
region and stretched in C. The text comes through the font's `/ToUnicode`
map - bfchar and bfrange, deflated when it is - because an Identity-H font's
codes are glyph ids, and a glyph id is not a character.

`tools/mkpdf.py` learned to write the three, as real producers do
(`--tounicode`, `--outline`, `--jpeg`), so the fixture is made in the test
rather than kept. **Test**: `x86-pdfkit`, 16 checks - two sentences on page
1 in order and nothing of page 2, the first run at the top left, the
outline's two chapters on pages 1 and 2, and each of
`test-quads.jpg`'s four colours where the page puts it. **Controls**: the
same text made without each addition - no map is no text at all rather
than wrong text, no outline is no entries, no picture is the paper's own
grey where the quadrants were.

The suite found two faults in the picture path on its first run, neither
of which reading would have shown: an image's dictionary is the stream's
`.dict`, not the object, so every picture was "not an image"; and a
region was handed to `read_into` where it takes the region's capability.
And `stretch`'s alpha is 0 to 255 - there is no "opaque" of -1.

## 18.627 The PDF Viewer's window

Step 2 of the PDF reader made again (`docs/pdfview.md`): `pdfview.lua`
rewritten as the window the mockup draws. The kit's band carries the
document's name and its menus - File, Edit, View, Go - and under it the
header has back and forward a page, the page and its count, and the zoom
as a chooser; under that the whole document as one column of pages on a
grey desk, a scroll bar, and a foot saying the zoom and where the file is.
Zoom by Fit width (the default, following the window), Fit page, Actual
size (96 to the inch), and steps from 50% to 400% - Control-plus, -minus,
-0, -1. One page at a time from the View menu. The window resizes and lays
its pages out again at the page being read.

**Scrolling is a blit**: each page is rendered once at the zoom into a
surface of its own, the pages in view and one either side, one a pass while
nothing else waits - and a page at another zoom is drawn stretched until
it is rendered again, so a zoom answers at once. The menus are the kit's,
so published by name, and the header's buttons and the page are published
beside them (`menu/View/One page at a time`, `field/Page`) - Automations
can drive it, and the suite does. `window:retitle` now redraws a direct
window's band, which said "PDF Viewer" over every document before.

**Test**: `x86-pdfview`, 19 checks, on six pages made by `mkpdf.py` with a
picture on the first: open at Fit width with page 1 and page 2 rendered
and the picture's red on the screen (3 red points before, 14,455 after);
End and Home, the page arriving in view rendered; Control-plus a step in
from Fit width and page 1 rendered again at it, Control-0 back; View, One
page at a time, Go, Next page, and the Page field written 4 and read back,
by name; back to the whole document at page 4; the window made 620 by 520
by the window manager, laid out again smaller at Fit width, at page 4, and
rendered again at the new size.

## 18.629 The PDF Viewer finds, copies, goes to a page and back

Step 4 (`docs/pdfview.md`). **Find**: a field at the header's right end,
Control-F; each page's text read once through `pdf.text` and kept, the
pages read a pass at a time from the page being read round to it again,
so a key typed is answered at once and the matches arrive after. Every
match marked on its page, the current one stronger; Return and
Shift-Return between them (Shift read from the keys' own `rawkey` events,
since the board sends Shift-Return as Return); a Found tab in the sidebar
listing them by page with the words round each; a document with no text
says so rather than finding nothing. **Copy**: a selection dragged across
a page - the runs the rectangle touches - or Select all on this page, and
Control-C, which the window manager sends as a `copy` event, to its
clipboard. **Go to page**: Control-G or a click on the number, a number
typed, Return. **Back**: a jump - a chapter, a thumbnail, a page by number,
the first match of a search, Home and End - remembers where it came from,
and Go > Back (Alt Left) returns there.

**Where words are is the kit's**: `pdf.text`'s runs now carry each
character's edge from the glyphs' own widths, and `pdf.boxes(text, from,
to)` is the door to where a stretch of text is. The viewer's first try
shared a run's width out by bytes, and its mark sat a letter to the left.

**Tests**: `x86-pdfkit`, 17 checks - `pdf.boxes` gives an m (9.60 points)
wider than an i (2.75), which a share of the run could not, and a whole
sentence its run's box. `x86-pdfview`, 37: "page" typed into Find, found 12
times on 6 pages, the first on the page being read, Return the next and
Shift-Return back; "numbered 2" by name, once, on page 2; Back to page 4,
where the searching began; Control-G 5; page 5 selected and copied, and
the clipboard read back; a selection dragged with the pointer across page
1 and copied; **control**: the document without its text map, where Find
says the document has no text.

## 18.631 Kosmos announced on the network (N13)

`docs/sharing.md` N13, moved up on 14 October (Diego: "i dont see kosmos on
the mac network", "do N13 and N14 next"). `mdnsd`, which only listened,
answers for this machine: what a server here publishes through the new
`MDNS_OP_PUBLISH` (`mdnsproto.h`; the request gains the instance's name)
is answered when the network asks - `_services._dns-sd._udp`, the type's
PTR, the instance's SRV and TXT, `_device-info._tcp` (`model=Kosmos`) and
the host's own A, `kosmos.local` from the name on the network - announced
twice a second apart on publishing and when the address changes, and said
gone with a time to live of 0 on `MDNS_OP_UNPUBLISH`. `smbd` publishes
`_smb._tcp` while it serves, under the name on the network, and takes it
back when it stops - the server that offers a thing says so, with the
declared shape both compile, rather than a second packing in Lua. A record
of this machine's heard back is never listed as seen. `dnsmsg.c` gains
`dns_put_record`. Not done: probing for a name another machine holds (RFC
6762 8.1).

**Tests**: `tools/test_dnsmsg.c`, 22 - a record written reads back the same,
one that does not fit and one whose name is not one refused. `x86-mdns`, 14
- a fifth boot, on a disk, sharing started at the prompt as Studio2:
announced unasked; asked for `_smb._tcp.local` as Finder asks, answered with
an SRV on 445 at `studio2.local` and its A, 10.9.0.2; asked what it is,
`model=Kosmos`; `sharing stop`, a goodbye at 0. **Controls**: asked before
sharing started, silent; asked about a name it does not hold, silent.

## 18.632 Writing to Kosmos over SMB (N14), and the filesystem writing in pieces

`docs/sharing.md` N14, and the way Diego chose for it ("go with B"): the
filesystem writes a file in pieces rather than `smbd` collecting a copy in
memory. **`kfs_write_range`** writes bytes at an offset: every block the
range touches is written anew to blocks nothing points at, the file's
extents rebuilt - its runs before, the new ones, its runs after, joined
where they meet - and the replaced blocks and the old chain given back,
all in the transaction it runs in. With `cut`, the file ends where the
range does: shorter or longer, a size set, zeroes - never the old bytes -
past a cut when it grows again. `kfs_write_file`'s tail is shared as
`store_runs` rather than copied. `diskfs` answers **`DISK_OP_WRITE_AT`**
(`DISK_CREATE`, `DISK_CUT`), counted as a write, a change watchers are told
of, and one transaction a piece.

**`smbd` writes**, in shares marked so: CREATE with every disposition -
made, opened, emptied by overwrite or supersede, a folder made - and
delete-on-close; WRITE through its region into `DISK_OP_WRITE_AT`;
SET_INFO's rename (replace-if-exists), disposition (a folder with
something in it refused at once) and end of file (a cut); its dates and
allocation taken as hints. A writable share answers full access at tree
connect. The Servers window's folders read only or read and write, as
`docs/sharing.html` drew them; `sharing folders NAME:/Home/FOLDER:write`.

**Tests**: `tools/test_kfs.lua`, 134 checks, plain and through the block
cache - six pieces off any block's edge read back as the whole with no
block more than it needs and the bitmap agreeing; a piece past the end, the
gap zeroes, filled in out of order; the middle written over; a power cut
before a piece's commit, the file as it was and its blocks still free; two
files written in turn past twelve extents and a range across the chain;
cut shorter, longer, on a block's edge and to nothing; refused outside a
transaction and for a file not there. `x86-smbd`, 38: into Notes, shared
read and write, a 5 MB file put a megabyte a write and fetched back byte for
byte, a folder made with a file put in it, a rename, a shorter file put
over a longer one and fetched as the shorter, a delete, and a folder with
something in it kept. **Control**: the same put into Projects, read only,
refused.

## 18.633 Tracker's Network view: the computers, as cards

`docs/network.html`, agreed the same day - Diego: "Mockup is great",
"Every machine", "Cards", "All". All of the network shows every machine
offering files (`_smb._tcp`) or its screen (`_rfb._tcp`) as a card - its
name, what kind of machine, what it offers, signed in or not - those the
network announces under "On this network" and those reached by an address
under "Connected by address"; a double-click opens its shares, or its
sign-in card, and a machine offering only its screen says Remote Screen
will open it. The foot counts the computers. The sidebar keeps every one.

What kind of machine is `mdnsd`'s to find out: each instance it keeps has
its `<name>._device-info._tcp` TXT asked once, and its `model=` kept and
returned (`mdns_reply.model`). `netshares.servers` makes one machine of
what announces files and its screen, and joins what the network announces
to a server already signed into; `netshares.card` says what a card shows
and `netshares.kind` turns a model into Mac, Kosmos, Server or Computer.
Each computer is published as `computer/<name>`.

**Tests**: `tools/test_netshares.lua`, 41 - five announcements as three
machines, the Mac signed into and announced as one card "Mac · files,
screen · Signed in · 2 shares", a server seen with files alone, a machine
with only its screen, an address-only server under Connected by address,
kinds from models. `x86-mdns`, 15 - Tracker opened on /Network on a wire
where Studio (`Macmini9,1`, files and screen) and Pixel (only its screen)
answer: two cards, Studio "Mac · files, screen; Not signed in" and Pixel
"Computer · screen; Screen sharing".

## 18.635 The tail of a compressed band: ZRLE that TigerVNC hung up on

Diego, from his iMac the evening of 0.11.238: "tigervnc closed and now ...
it loads for a second the screen and it quits" - every connection after a
first one that had worked. `vncd` logged each viewer as leaving, with no
error; TigerVNC run on the home Mac said "End of stream" after 36 ZRLE
rectangles. `kosmos_vnc.py` asking as TigerVNC does, an update after an
update, stopped on the third: a band of 1080x64 whose tiles wanted 60
bytes more than it carried. That band fetched alone - raw, and as ZRLE -
and encoded on the Mac by `zrle.c` was 76,401 bytes, the same as the M700's
for its first 76,194 and then nothing: **the encoder was right and the
stream lost its tail.** `compress.zstream`'s deflate stopped at the first
call that gave less than a 16 KB buffer, while miniz still held 207 bytes
in its lookahead - exactly the missing ones. It happens only when a piece
deflates to more than a buffer and the deflater's buffers fill just before
its end: a photograph's band on the M700, never QEMU's plain desktop.

**The fix**: `user/kits/compress/zsync.c`, a piece deflated and flushed
until the input is taken, the output given and the lookahead empty -
`zstream:deflate` through it. **Test**: `tools/test_zsync.c` in `host`,
400 pieces on streams of their own, all over a buffer, and 40 on one,
each inflated back byte for byte. **Control**: the old stopping rule on the
same pieces leaves 4 of the 400 short. On the M700, 0.11.240: the band
whole, 172 continuous updates in 20 s decoded, and TigerVNC connected and
staying - and Diego: "tigervnc works now again". `test_zrle` also gained
400 bands of runs of 17 to 127 colours, which passed before the fix: the
encoder was never the fault.

## 18.636 `/Sandboxes`: guests' disks on a drive of their own (Linux L1a)

Diego, 14 October 2026, on where Linux's disk lives: "what if instead /home
we crate a new /Sandboxes drive with virtual machibes disks?", "and not
just 1 big drive", "that pollutes the home?" (`docs/linux.md`). So a guest's
disk is a file on a partition of its own, served by a second disk server,
and a guest that fills its disk fills its own drive and never `/Home`.

**What it is.** `diskfs.c` serves either drive: `/Home`, or - as the role
`sandboxfs` - `/Sandboxes`, on the stick partition `opt/kosmos/sandboxes`
names by its GUID and nothing else (never `usb`, which is the first Kosmos
partition and so `/Home`'s, and never the kernel's disk). A blank one is
formatted with `/Sandboxes` at its root. init starts it only on a machine
started with the word, and the shell mounts `/Sandboxes` on the same word,
so the two cannot disagree; every program gets it as it gets `/Home`. The
USB driver guarded one partition a stick - `/Home`'s, keyring K7 - and now
keeps a list, as many as a disk server reads of a GPT, so both drives are
refused to `/Devices/blocks`. The Drives list calls it Sandboxes, opening
at `/Sandboxes`.

**Putting it on a stick in use**: `tools/sandboxes_drive.py`. A stick's
GPT ends where its image did - about 2 GB into a 128 GB Kingston - and a
new image would take `/Home` with it; the tool moves the table to the
stick's real end, adds `KOSMOS SANDBOXES` after the last partition with its
first megabyte zeroed, and puts the word on the stick's command line. A
second run changes nothing.

**Tests.** `usb_sandboxes` in `x86-usb-2`, 6 checks over three boots of a
stick given `/Sandboxes` by that tool: both partitions formatted, each by
its own server; a file written to `/Sandboxes`, its partition's blocks
refused to a program, the Drives list naming it; the file there on a second
boot and, read off the stick on the Mac with `kfs.lua`, in the second
partition and not `/Home`'s; and named a partition no stick has, `/Sandboxes`
saying so with nothing formatted. `tools/test_sandboxes_drive.py` in
`host`, 9 checks: the table moved whole with both copies agreeing, one
aligned partition of the size asked, `/Home`'s entry and every byte of it
unchanged, the word added with the others kept, a second run identical.
**Controls**: the driver made to look at its first guard only - the
`/Sandboxes` block read is answered and the check fails (1 of 6); and the
tool refuses, writing nothing, a drive past the room there is and a table
whose header does not hold to its CRC.

## 18.637 A sandbox's disk: virtio-blk, written in place (Linux L1b)

`docs/linux.md` L1, the second half: a guest given a disk that keeps.

**What it is.** `vmmblk.c`, virtio-blk on virtio-mmio in the sandbox's
monitor (VIRTIO 1.2 §5.2): read, write, flush and its id; a request's bytes
cross between the guest's RAM and the file through one 1 MB region, a piece
at a time, never as a message. The file is named in the sandbox's setup
(`vmm_setup.disk`, version 2), and the monitor is handed the drive it is
on - `/Sandboxes`, or wherever the path is served. On ARM it is
`virtio_mmio@a000a00` at SPI 21; on x86 the next 0x200 after the network,
line 12, said on the command line. Alpine loads `virtio_blk.ko` when
`kosmos.disk` is on its line. Written **in place** (`DISK_IN_PLACE`,
`diskfs.md`), so the file keeps the blocks it was made with; `sandbox disk
new FILE MB` makes one, zeroes grown 256 MB a piece (`fs.size`), and
`--disk FILE[:ro]` gives it to `run`, `new` and a shell.

**One door for the disk protocol from C**, `diskask.c`: `smbd`, the
keyring, the map's tiles and `vmmfs` each had a `disk_ask` of their own,
the same request built and reply read four times over (`CLAUDE.md`'s
premise); the disk would have been the fifth. All five use it now; it wipes
what it sent after every call, as the keyring's did.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux`, five checks more, Alpine at EL2 under QEMU:
an 8 MB disk made; a sandbox seeing 16384 sectors and writing its first
sector and the 12345th; a second sandbox reading both back; the file's size
and extents (2) as they were with the guest's bytes at its start, read by
Kosmos; and the disk given read only - "Operation not permitted", and the
bytes still read. `tools/test_kfs.lua` (142, eight new). **Controls**: the
disk server made to ignore `DISK_IN_PLACE` - every write still lands, and
the file goes from 2 extents to 4, which the check refuses; `kfs`'s in-place
write made to lay down one byte short, and its gap writer kept to a block a
call (517 against 517) - each failing its check.

**Found on the way**: `fs.send` refuses a disk path - the namespace speaks
each disk operation by a function of its own - so `fs.size` is one, and
`sandbox disk new` had made nothing; the suite then waited 240 s at every
step after, which read as a hang.

## 18.638 Linux's screen in a Kosmos window: virtio-gpu 2D (Linux L2)

`docs/linux.md` L2: the guest draws, and a Kosmos window shows it.

**What it is.** `vmmgpu.c`, virtio-gpu 2D in the sandbox's monitor (VIRTIO
1.2 §5.7): one display, the size its screen region says; resources made,
given backing pages of the guest's RAM, transferred and flushed; a flush of
the scanout's resource laid into the **screen region** (`vmmscreen.h`) as
Kosmos's own pixels - opaque, blue-green-red-alpha in memory, a surface's
pitch - and counted in its header's `frames`. Whoever starts the sandbox
makes the region and hands it over (`screen WxH`, setup version 3), as
Camera hands its ring to the camera server. The **Linux** window
(`user/bin/apps/linux.lua`) wraps the region as a surface (`gfx.wrap`) and
blits it when `frames` moved, on its own clock; no pixel passes through Lua.
Alpine loads `virtio-gpu` and the DRM it stands on for `kosmos.screen`, all
from its own initramfs. The window starts Alpine with a shell on `tty1`, so
what is seen until L3 is Linux's console.

**Found on the way**: the first boot's driver said "Could not reserve host
visible region" and gave up. virtio-mmio's shared-memory registers read 0
here, which a driver takes for a region of no bytes; "none" is a length of
all ones (VIRTIO 4.2.2), and `vdev.c` says so now for every device. Then the
pixel written at `/dev/fb0`'s corner read black: the console's cursor blinks
there, so the check writes and reads the middle.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux`, two more: a 640x480 `/dev/fb0` in the guest,
and a pixel written at its middle - blue 0x30, green 0x20, red 0x10 - read
from the region as `#102030` after 9 flushes. `arm-sandbox-linuxwin`, new,
3 checks: the window says where its picture is when the first frame came,
QEMU's screen there is Linux's console - light text on black - and the
window's header is above it. **Controls**: the monitor converting with red
and blue swapped reads `#302010`, refused; the window not blitting the
picture leaves no light pixel, refused.

## 18.639 Typed into and pointed at: virtio-input (Linux L3)

`docs/linux.md` L3: the Linux window's keys and pointer, to the guest.

**What it is.** `vmminput.c`: two virtio-input devices in the sandbox's
monitor (VIRTIO 1.2 §5.8), a keyboard and an absolute tablet, each telling
the guest what it is through its configuration space - its name, ids, the
events it sends, the tablet's axes from 0 to 32767 - which needed `vdev.c`
to let a driver write a device's configuration (`config_write`; nothing
had). Events come from the window through a ring in the screen region's
first page (`vmmscreen.h`), Linux's own `input_event`s in the guest's codes
- Kosmos's raw key numbers are Linux's - and go into the buffers the guest
has given, in order, as many as there are; the monitor looks every time it
wakes, which is a scheduler tick at most when the guest is idle. The window
writes the ring through **`sys.ring_push`**, a generic single-producer push
in C with the barrier Lua cannot say. It forwards every raw key, and every
move, press and wheel over the picture (`wmproto.track` for moves with no
button held); the header stays the window's. And it notices when Linux has
stopped, once a second, and says so.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linuxwin`, now 5: four clicks over the picture
raising the guest's tablet interrupts - the guest says its virtio
interrupts on its serial line a second at a time, which the window passes
on with `--tell` - and `poweroff -f` typed on QEMU's keyboard, run by
Linux's shell on its screen, the sandbox ending and the window saying so.
**Control**: the window pushing nothing - the tablet at 0 interrupts before
and after, and Linux not ending - both checks failing. Found on the way: a
plain `poweroff` is typed and run, and does nothing, since the sandbox's
`/init` is a script that does not answer it.

## 18.640 Linux from its own disk: set up once, then booted into `cage` (Linux L4, the path)

`docs/linux.md` L4, everything but the browser's own weight: the Linux
window makes Linux's disk, Linux sets it up, and boots from it into `cage`.

**What it is.** The image gains `modloop`, every module its kernel has (the
netboot's own, since the repository's kernel has moved on), which the guest
mounts through a read-only share of the image's folder - `squashfs` and
`loop` added to its initramfs. The guest's `/init` gains two paths:
**setup** - `ext4`, `e2fsprogs` into the initramfs's userland, the disk made
ext4, `apk --root` installing what it is told from the repository it is
told, said as a percentage through `apk --progress-fd`; and **root** - the
disk mounted, the modules carried in, a session written and `switch_root`
into it: its network, `udevd`, `seatd`, and `cage` with one application.
The window runs the stages a step a pass so it keeps drawing: the disk
grown 256 MB a pass (`fs.size`), the setup's progress in its header, a
`.ready` beside the disk when it is done, and Linux started again from it.
A sandbox can carry words of its own for the guest's line (`s.words`).
`tools/alpine_repo.py` fetches Alpine's packages once, with what they need,
held to the signed index's sizes, laid out as a mirror.

**Found on the way**: the window's `--disk-mb` was never read - a `-` in a
Lua pattern is a repetition; Alpine 3.24's `apk` draws a bar into a pipe
and names no package, hence `--progress-fd`; and the script's backslashes
were Python's before they were the shell's.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linuxsetup`, new, 5 checks: the disk made, 512 MB;
the install's percentage said; Linux set up from this Mac's copy of Alpine
through Kosmos's network; started from its disk into `cage`; and the
picture's middle foot's own background, #242424. The whole serial line is
kept in `build/gate/arm-sandbox-linuxsetup.serial`. **Control**: the window not
asking Linux to start from its disk - it boots its console instead, and the
session and the picture checks fail. The first try of that control passed,
and was right to: it renamed the word to `kosmos.rootless`, and `/init` asked
`grep -q kosmos.root`, which that matches - so `/init` reads the word's
value exactly now, and the control leaves the word out.

## 18.641 More than a gigabyte on ARM: processes moved to 256 GB

Found trying Epiphany in a 2 GB ARM machine: `init` - the first process -
died at its first push, a permission fault on a 2 MB block, and then
`pmm_free_page: double free`. Every ARM machine with more than 1 GB **and**
a disk did it; 1 GB, or no disk, booted.

**The cause.** AArch64 put processes at 0x80000000, level 1 slot 2, and
every space shares the kernel's top-level slots below. The kernel identity
maps RAM, and QEMU's `virt` puts RAM at 1 GB: with one gigabyte it ended at
exactly 0x80000000; with more, the kernel's own blocks were in the slot
processes start in. `mmu.h` said the split was "enforced rather than
documented"; past a gigabyte it was neither. x86-64's `mmu_init` has always
refused RAM that reaches its processes' region; ARM's never had the check.
A Raspberry Pi 5 - RAM from 0 to 8 GB - would have failed on its first boot.

**The fix.** Processes from 256 GB (0x4000000000), level 1 slot 256, the
top half of the 39-bit space; `mmu_init` panics if RAM would reach it. And
`CLAUDE.md`'s "processes use addresses above the 4 GB line", which was
never true on either architecture, is now true on ARM: any address kept in
32 bits fails here at once.

**Tests.** A 2 GB machine with a disk reaches the prompt (it did not), and
a 1 GB one still does; then every suite, ARM's included (`make test
ARM=1`), since every ARM process moved.

**And Downloads shared** (the same day): Kosmos's `/Home/Downloads` is
Linux's `~/Downloads`, read and write - a share mounted in the initramfs and
moved into Linux's root at `switch_root` (`mount --move`), which the image's
folder is not. `arm-sandbox-linuxsetup` gains its sixth check: a file the
application line writes to `/root/Downloads` read from the `/Home` disk on
this Mac once the machine has stopped (the desktop has the serial line's
keys while it runs, so `fs.read` typed there never ran). **Control**: no
Downloads share - the file is not there.

`run_linuxsetup.py --browser`: the same path with Epiphany (decision 4) -

## 18.643 Two found at the push: a test reading the wrong device, and the stick's command line

**`arm-sandbox-linuxwin` under load** read the tablet's interrupts as the
highest-numbered virtio device seen so far - and a read that had not yet

failed the same gate under load and passed alone, 38 of 38.

**`tools/sandboxes_drive.py` on Diego's stick** made the partition and

## 18.644 Linux on the M700: its screen and keys under VT-x

0.11.248 netbooted on the M700 with `opt/kosmos/sandboxes=4F8760C3-...` -
the stick's new partition, made by `tools/sandboxes_drive.py` - and the x86
Alpine package with its modloop installed from the Mac. `/Sandboxes` was

## 18.645 A region past a gigabyte: a third level in its index

Diego, on the M700, opening Linux with its 2 GB: "the linux window says no
room for 2048 mb ram". A region's index was a directory page of 512 index
pages of 512 pages - a gigabyte, the shape of the structure rather than a
decision - and a sandbox's RAM is one region. Now a top page holds up to 512
directory pages, each taken only when a region reaches it: 512 GB, so the
ceiling is `memobj_pages_max`'s other half - half the machine's memory -
and the index never refuses. Every reach into it goes through
`index_slot` and `page_slot`, in `memobj.c`, once.

Diego asked why there are limits at all. The pools' ceilings - threads,
processes, endpoints, regions - are derived from the machine's memory on
purpose, so no program can make the kernel spend all of it; a number that
falls out of how a thing was built, as this one did, is a defect.

**Test.** `mem: a region past a gigabyte`, in the guest suite: a region
given on touch, 1 GB and 1 MB long, a page past the old end filled, written
and read back, its last page there, everything given back. It asks the
machine's memory whether it can be asked - the first version asked
`memobj_pages_max`, which was the cap itself, and passed by skipping. The
suites' 512 MB machine skips it; run at 4 GB: **control**, the old index -
`not ok`; the new - `ok`, 211 of 211.

## 18.646 Linux's size following its window; its setup shown; Disk Monitor's sticks (L5, L4)

**Its size, following the window's** (`docs/linux.md` L5). The Linux window
is resizable: its region is made for the desktop's size (`most_width`,
`most_height` in `vmmscreen.h`), and a new size is written into its header
and counted in `sized`; the monitor sees the count move, tells the guest by
virtio-gpu's display event and a configuration-change interrupt (`vdev.c`
learned to raise one, and `config_gen`), and answers its next display query
with the new size. `cage` keeps the mode it began with, so the session runs
a loop beside it that sets each new preferred mode through `wlr-randr`. A
`udev` rule did that first and was useless: under udev, `wlr-randr` printed
nothing and did nothing.

**Its setup, shown** (Diego, at the M700: "a progress bar showing the disk
creation process", "a modal window", "from the linux app", "to show the
progress of the filesystem being created"): a panel over the picture, three
steps each with a bar - Linux's disk, its filesystem, Alpine and the browser.
The disk is made by `sandbox disk new ... --report FILE` in a process of its
own, a 64 MB step at a time; the window reads the report four times a
second. It had made the disk itself, and a drive writing zeroes answers
nobody else, so the window dropped the pointer for a quarter of a minute a
step on the M700's stick (about 8 MB/s - the stick is the bound).

**Disk Monitor's sticks**: a stick's volume was read at `/Drives/<name>`,
whose server counts nothing, so `/Sandboxes` - its server had written 2.2
GB - showed no activity (Diego: "i dont see activity in the usb drive").
It asks `drivelist.path` where each is served now.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linuxsetup`, 8 checks now: the window's corner
dragged, its picture 832x630, and foot's background at two points only a
resized Linux reaches - right of the old width, below the old height. The
first try sampled near the corner and landed in a 26-pixel strip along the
picture's foot that is there at any size (on the roadmap). **Control**: the
session without the follower - the picture stays 640x480 and the check fails.

## 18.647 Linux on the M700: a quiet window, one of it, and its RAM given back

**What the M700 showed** (15 October 2026, a photograph of Processes and
Monitor): the desktop very slow and the machine off the network, with the
Linux window's process at 100% of a core in the display band, `vmm` at
100% of another, 2.9 GB in use and three Linux windows open. Three causes,
each its own fix:

- **The window drew everything, as often as it was told.** Every flush the
  guest made - up to 250 a second while Epiphany drew - was a whole 3 MB
  picture blitted and committed, in the display band, with nothing between
  passes. It now draws at most sixty times a second, and only what changed:
  the monitor keeps, in the screen's header, the union of every rectangle
  flushed since the window last took a frame (`cleared`, the header's last
  word, which was reserved), and the window draws that and the rectangle it
  drew before - a commit flips two surfaces, and each has to catch up. The
  header and the panel are drawn whole twice, once a surface, when they
  change. A stopped window polls a quarter of a second at a time.
- **Each start kept the last guest's RAM.** `sandboxes.start` handed the
  monitor its RAM region and kept its own capability to it for as long as
  the window ran, so a window that started Linux again - the setup, then
  the run - held the gigabytes of the one before. It lets go of the RAM,
  the window and the setup once the monitor has them, and the window lets
  go of the last screen before it makes a new one.
- **Linux opened again opened another Linux.** It brings the window already
  open forward and goes (`wmproto.windows`, `raise`).

And two from the same evening: **Epiphany ended at once** without a D-Bus
session ("Cannot autolaunch D-Bus"), so the default application is
`dbus-run-session epiphany` and `dbus` is among the default packages; and
**virtio-blk wrote at 1.3 MB/s** with the guest's kernel reporting soft
lockups - Linux split every write into single segments, since the device
offered no `SEG_MAX`. It offers `SEG_MAX` (62, what a chain holds less
the header and the status) and `BLK_SIZE` (4096), and Alpine's install
wrote at 9.6 MB/s on the same stick. The setup's steps say what each is
doing: the package being installed, *N of M*, and apk's own error when it
fails.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linuxwin`, 6 checks: a program the desktop starts
beside Linux waits for its window and asks for Linux again; the second says
it brought the first forward and ends, and one picture arrives, not two -
typed at the prompt, the second never started, since the desktop has the
serial line's keys. **Control**: the check for an open window looking for
another title - the second Linux starts, and the check fails. The whole
transcript is kept in `build/gate/arm-sandbox-linuxwin.serial`.

`arm-sandbox-linuxsetup` failed once on the way, and rightly: the filter
reading apk's progress was rewritten to want `done/total` alone on a line,
and apk's progress arrives otherwise, so the setup said its packages and
never a percentage. It takes the last `done/total` anywhere in what is
left of a line once a package's line is taken out of it.

## 18.648 The screen is the desktop's while it runs

**What the M700 showed** (15 October 2026, a photograph): a line of green
text along the foot of the screen, under the Deskbar - `x8 cpu [.........]
0% 49/32208 thr 34/8064` - which VNC's pictures did not have. It was
`monitor`, run at a prompt this session reached by Telnet: it is handed the
screen and draws into the two rows the kernel's console keeps for itself,
with no window server between. VNC shows the desktop's picture, not the
screen, so it never saw it, and the desktop never paints those rows, so the
bar's last line stayed after `monitor` ended - its thread count, 49, was
the machine's of an hour before.

**Every program had the screen**, which `init.lua` said beside both places a
process is started ("the screen to everything, which is wrong and is
staying for now") - granting it only on `kosmos: needs screen` had once
starved programs that yield at NORMAL, and that is not this change. This
one is narrower: **while the window server composes, a console program -
what the store calls a `program` - is not handed the screen**, at the
shell's prompt (`run_program`) and where a Telnet session or a Terminal
starts one (`launch`). Anything else still is: an application asks it for
its size, and a file of somebody's own in `/Home` or `/Temporary` says
nothing of what it is - an installed application among them. `monitor` and `edit` say the desktop has the screen, and what
does the same in a window.

**Tests.** `x86-servers`, 35 checks: `monitor 1` at the Telnet prompt,
while the desktop runs, says `monitor: the desktop has the screen`.
**Control**: the first build held only the prompt's path, and the check
failed - `monitor` drew, saying nothing - since a Telnet session starts
programs through `launch`; with both, it passes.

**And one the gate found**: the first version refused the screen to all but
the store's applications, and `x86-scene` failed every time - its window,
a file in `/Temporary` started through the desktop, closed and left one
picture held (20 before it, 22 open, 21 after). Refusing only `program`s
mended the suite. It was taken for a leak of its own, and was not - the
check read its count at the wrong moment (18.652).

## 18.649 Keys in Linux's applications: `/dev/shm` for cage's keymap

**What the M700 showed** (15 October 2026): Epiphany up in the Linux
window, and Linux gone the moment an address was typed into it - Diego,
"it crashes when i type in the url". Its menu, a popup, opened and closed
without harm; one letter typed into the page, not the address bar, ended
it too. The console said only `Lost connection to Wayland compositor` and
`Segmentation fault`: `cage` had died, and Epiphany with it.

**Found by keeping cage's account.** The session writes `cage -d`'s output
to Linux's Downloads, which are Kosmos's, so it is read from `/Home` after
the guest has stopped - and it said, at the start, `Failed to allocate shm
file for keymap`. wlroots hands each client the keyboard's keymap in
shared memory; Linux's root from its disk had no `/dev/shm`, so there was
no keymap to hand, and the first key fell over. The session mounts a
`tmpfs` there. With it, `example.com` typed into Epiphany on the M700
loaded, the page drawn in the window.

The session also runs `cage` under `gdb` when the disk has
`/root/.kosmos-gdb` and gdb installed, its backtrace into the same file -
for the next one of these. It was not needed for this.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linuxsetup`, 9 checks: `foot` clicked into and a
line typed through the virtio keyboard - `echo typed >/root/Downloads/
typed.txt` - and the file read off the `/Home` disk afterwards.
**Control**: the session without the `tmpfs` - nothing written, the
session ended, and the check fails.

## 18.650 Why a monitor ended before its guest ran, in its own words

**What the M700 showed** (14 October 2026): Linux, set up, failed to start
the first time with "its monitor ended: the guest's machine could not be
laid out - its device tree, or its boot", and started the second time.
The monitor knew why - `x86_boot` has five reasons and says one through
`vmm_note` - but a note goes into the monitor's own ring, which the window
reads while the guest runs, and a monitor that ends before its guest runs
takes the ring with it.

**So the last note before the guest runs is left in the setup page**, the
page whoever started it made and still holds: its last half kilobyte,
`VMM_SETUP_WHY_AT` in `vmmproto.h`, after the setup itself.
`sandboxes.start` keeps its capability to the page until it has found the
sandbox in `/Running` or seen its monitor end, and on an end reads the
reason and says it after the exit code's sentence. The drive's refusals
say which: no file, not a file, smaller than a sector, no region to read
it through. The M700's failure has not been seen since; when it is, it
will say which of `x86_boot`'s five it was.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux`, 35 checks: a ten-byte file as a sandbox's
disk - the library passes it, the monitor refuses it - and the error says
`its disk: smaller than a sector: /Home/tiny-disk.img`. **Control**:
`sandboxes.start` not reading the page - the exit code's sentence alone,
and the check fails.

## 18.651 Two kernel checks that judged the host

**"Game mode, given by a parent"** failed at the end of 0.11.253's gate
and passed alone at once. Its spinner spun a second and a half by the
counter and the test waited one second for the band and three for the
budget to run out - and under the gate's load, with the Mac giving this
machine a share of a core, the counter ran on while the thread had not
yet run its budget. The spinner now spins until its budget is spent, and
the test waits for each thing to happen; ten and fifteen seconds are caps
a passing run never reaches.

**"A new thread avoids a loaded core"** failed under load the same way,
and here the test was wrong rather than slow. The policy takes the core
with the fewest *runnable* threads and counts blocked ones only to break
a tie; the test parks three blocked threads on a core and wanted the next
thread elsewhere - which is right only while some other core has nothing
runnable. With twelve busy processes on the Mac it reproduced, "placed on
the loaded core, 2", and the choice was correct: every other core had a
thread waiting. The test now looks first (`runnable_on`, counted as
`place_new_thread` counts) and fails a landing on the loaded core only
when a core with nothing runnable was there to take instead; otherwise it
says the round was not counted.

**Tests.** `x86-kernel` and `arm-sandbox` pass quiet, and three times
each with eight busy processes on the Mac (both failed under twelve before:
game mode did not, placement did). **Control**: placement as plain round
robin - "a new thread avoids a loaded core" fails on a quiet machine, twice
in two, with "a thread moves cores" beside it.

The third, "a processor held off is counted" (ARM, 0.11.250's gate),
already measures five times over and is left as it is; it is the host
stopping QEMU inside its window, which the count exists to show.

## 18.652 Not a leak: when `x86-scene` read the pictures held

18.648 recorded that a window from a process without the screen "keeps a
picture after it closes". **It does not.** Run again with that version and
the check given twelve seconds rather than two: 20 pictures before the
window, 22 while open, **20** as the window manager closed it - and 21
after, which was Tracker's: its sidebar gains a row for a machine it has
just seen on the network ("diego's Mac mini" - the Mac's own mDNS reaches
the guest through QEMU's user network) and drops it again, a picture each
time. Two things in the check made that a failure:

- it took the *last* count after the close, where another window's
  picture can arrive - now the **fewest**;
- it started counting at the program's "CLOSER closed", and the window
  manager says its count as it closes the window, before or after that
  line as the scheduler has it. Out of the display band the program spoke
  second, and the count of 20 fell before the point read from. It counts
  from the manager's own "closed Closer" now.

With both, the version that failed three times in three passes twice in
two. **Control**: the closer opening a second window it keeps - 20
before, 24 open, 22 at fewest after, and the check fails.

**Noticed**: the gate's guests see this Mac's network services by mDNS
(Tracker's sidebar row comes and goes). The suites are not as sealed as
they look; on the roadmap.

## 18.653 Linux's meter (L6a)

The Linux window counts, each second, the frames Linux hands it, the
longest wait between two while it draws, and each key's time from being
handed to Linux to Linux's next frame - in its header, and said with
`--tell` (`linux: meter fps=N gap=MS keys=MS,MS`). A frame after a key is
not proof it was the key's - a cursor blinks - so a key's time is an
upper bound only while nothing else draws. `tools/linuxbench.py` drives
Epiphany on a Kosmos machine from this Mac by Telnet and VNC - three pages
loaded, each scrolled for five seconds, twenty letters typed - and writes
what the meter said, with each process's share and each core's while it
ran; results in the next entry.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linuxwin`, 7 checks: after `poweroff -f` typed
into Linux's console, the meter has timed keys (5 to 12 ms there, under
QEMU) and counted frames. **Control**: no key's time taken - the meter's
lines say `keys=` and nothing, and the check fails.

## 18.654 Linux's desktop apps on the M700, measured (L6a)

Epiphany in the Linux window on the M700 (Core i7-6700, Linux with one
processor and 2 GB), `tools/linuxbench.py` and the window's meter:

| | |
|---|---|
| a key to the screen | median **14 ms**, slowest 27 (20 keys) |
| scrolling (wheel, ten notches a second) | 26-29 frames a second, longest gap under 55 ms |
| the processors while scrolling | ~20% of one core; the other seven idle |
| frames while a page draws | up to 51 and 63 in a second |
| YouTube, Big Buck Bunny (60 fps upload), its 640x360 player | **13-14 frames a second**, gaps 80-130 ms |
| the processors while it plays | **Linux's core at 99%** (`vmm` 88% of a core); the other seven idle |

**What it says.** Pages and typing are fine, and scrolling is held by how
the test scrolls rather than by the machine. **Video is held by Linux's one
processor**: decoding and drawing in software on one core while seven
watch - which is L6b, Linux given more than one. The first suspect for
scrolling, the monitor sleeping a whole 4 ms tick for a guest timer due
sooner, was tried (yielding until due) and changed nothing; undone.

**Found on the way**, each on the roadmap:

- **Keys dropped when typed quickly**: an address typed by VNC at full
  speed arrived as one letter, and a key's release lost left Shift held in
  Linux - the next address came out `eWWW>YOUTUB>COM`. Typed a key every
  120 ms, every key arrived.
- **cage fell over once more while an address was typed**, on the second
  page of a run; under `gdb` it did not, three times in three.
- **A file Linux rewrites in a shared folder keeps its old tail** - the
  session's log read as this run's start and an older run's end.
- **"Page Unresponsive"** on YouTube once, with the machine idle - the
  player clicked twice, played and paused; a reload and one click played.

## 18.655 Keys typed fast into Linux: held, not lost

**What the M700 showed**: an address typed into Epiphany at a VNC viewer's
full speed arrived as one letter, and a Shift released in the lost part
stayed held in Linux - the next address came out `eWWW>YOUTUB>COM`.

**Followed key by key.** The Linux window says each key it is given with
`--keys`, and how many it has had to hold. Two things were in the way:

- **The window's ring to Linux was written without looking.** It holds
  128 events and a key is four - its press, its release and a sync after
  each - and `sys.ring_push` answers false when it is full; nothing read
  the answer, so a burst while Linux was slow to take them lost the rest.
  What does not fit now waits in the window, in order, and goes as the
  ring empties. On the M700, three fast addresses made it **hold 70
  events** - each one a key or a release that was being lost - and every
  key arrived, Shift pressed and released five times each.
- **Not lost at all, the rest of the way**: `vncd`, the window manager's
  queue and its replies all carry every event - 86 of 86, 82 of 82 on the
  M700 - which the first counts seemed to deny because `log FILTER` shows
  the last forty lines only; the whole log, saved, has them.

**`keys`**, a program: text typed into the window keys go to, through the
window manager's remote door as `vncd` types a viewer's, every key at
once - `keys [--to TITLE] [--after MS] TEXT`. The desktop lends its door
only to a program it launches (`open keys ...`), not to its start-up list.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linuxwin`, 8 checks: `keys`, launched beside Linux,
types `echo` and 52 letters to Linux's serial line, and all of them come
back. **Its control does not bite in QEMU** - Linux there takes events as
fast as they come and the ring never fills, with the queue or without it;
the M700's 70 held events are the evidence the queue is what fixed it.

## 18.656 A file rewritten shorter in a shared folder

**What it was**: Linux opens a file for `>` without `O_TRUNC` - it keeps
that back - and then sets its size to 0 with no handle named (`valid`
0x208: the size and the lock owner). `vmmfs` set the size through a
handle of its own, written back at once, while the handle Linux was
writing through kept the file's old bytes - and wrote them all back on
release, the new line over their start. Followed with a note at each
step: open (15 bytes loaded), set size 0 (no handle), write 6 at 0,
release 15. A size set now reaches every handle open on the file.

**Tests.** `arm-sandbox-linux`, 36 checks: a file made `made in alpine`,
written again `short` by `>`, and Kosmos reading `short` and nothing
after. **Control**: before the change, Kosmos read `short` and then
`n alpine`.

## 18.657 The M700's desktop measured, before its GPU (`m700-2d.md` step 1)

`frames 20` on the M700 (Core i7-6700, 1720x1440, 0.11.259) while a
window's header was dragged in circles by VNC for sixteen seconds:

    3723 passes, 1444 of which composed something
    busy 11006 ms total, 2956 us mean, 18.4 ms WORST
    composing 98.6% of busy; keys, requests, pointer, polls, reaping <1% each
    composed 2127 rects, 2.23 Mpx a frame; drew 4.51 Mpx a frame (2.02x)
    3.4 ns a pixel, 7.52 ms a composing pass
    passes by busy ms: <1 2994, <8 46, <16.7 650, <33.3 11
    the worst pass a collection (16.95 ms)

**The time is pixels, and the processor is at its limit**: a full-screen
drag composes at 7.5 ms a pass on four vector lanes, and twice the damage
is drawn - composed into memory, then copied to the screen. At 3440x1440,
twice the pixels, the same drag would want about 15 ms a pass. Page flips
take the copy away; the render engine takes the composing.

Also from this machine, kept for the key loss that is still open: the
console server and the USB driver now say when a key event is dropped -
`console: N key events dropped, nobody waiting for them` and `a key
refused, the kernel's queue full` - so typing into Linux on the M700 can
say where its keys go (`roadmap.md`, Linux).

## 18.658 The M700's GPU found and read (`m700-2d.md` step 2)

A driver of the display engine, its first half: `intelgpu`, started by init
with device authority, finds the GPU (`DEV_INTEL_GPU`, a new kind -
GTTMMADR, BAR0 of 0/2/0, 16 MB, `hal/pc/devices.c` sharing its checks with
the backlight's), maps its first 2 MB, reads three pipes, three planes each
and a cursor each, and the global GTT's entry behind each surface - and
writes nothing. `SYS_DEV_MAP`'s bound rose from 4 MB to 16 for it, as
agreed. Every offset and field is Linux's i915, fetched into
`build/downloads/i915/` and cited in `intelgpu_decode.h`.

**The M700 said**, at its first boot with it (0.11.259 and this):

    intelgpu: Intel GPU 1912 at 00:02.0, GTTMMADR 00de000000, 16 MB
    intelgpu: pipe A on, 3440x1440, transcoder c0000000
    intelgpu: pipe A plane 1: 3440x1440 at 0,0, XRGB8888, linear,
              13760 bytes a row, surface at GTT 00000000 = memory 00bc000000
    intelgpu: pipe A cursor plane off
    intelgpu: pipe B off, 1x1; pipe C off, 1x1
    intelgpu: 1 pipe running; nothing written

**What it means for the next steps**: one pipe, one plane, linear 32-bit
XRGB with no padding, scanning from GTT page 0 - the firmware's screen in
stolen memory at `0xBC000000` - and the cursor plane free. The cursor plane
(step 3) and page flips (step 4) both start from here.

**Tests.** `host`: `test_intelgpu_decode`, 18 checks - a plane's format,
tiling, size, position and stride in each of its units (64 bytes linear,
512 X, 128 Y), a surface's bits 31:12, `PIPESRC`, a cursor's mode with the
bits beside it ignored, `CURPOS`'s signs, and a GTT entry's present bit and
address with the bits above 45 dropped. The first run failed on the test's
own stride - 1720 x 4 is not a multiple of 64, which no firmware sets.
Under QEMU, which has no Intel GPU, the driver says so and ends.

## 18.659 The cursor plane, tried: the first picture Kosmos showed with the M700's display engine (`m700-2d.md` step 3a)

`intelgpu` is a server now, `/Devices/gpu` (`gpuproto.h`), threaded through
init as `/Sandboxes` was - before it in the shell's list, since a list
with a gap ends there. Its first verb is a test, and `gpu cursor 20` asks
it: a 64 by 64 picture in four contiguous pages, out of the caches
(`clflush`), entered in four GTT slots a megabyte past the framebuffer's
(the GTT flushed through `GFX_FLSH_CNTL`), the cursor's share of the
display buffer just past plane 1's - blocks 446 to 477, which nothing
used: the firmware gave plane 1 0-445 of 896 - one watermark, its
position, its mode, and its base last, which arms the rest. Read back,
shown for the seconds asked, then off and every register and GTT entry as
the firmware left it.

**The M700, 17 October, Diego at the monitor** - the square in the middle
of the screen, white frame, orange inside, the wallpaper through the clear
square at its centre (his photograph); and:

    picture at memory 0009be5000, GTT 01300000 (its entries were 00000000bd300001 ...)
    on at 1688,688; read back control 00000027, base 01300000,
        buffer 01dd01be, watermark 80004008
    off again; underrun before no, after no

**Nothing VNC sees**: the plane is added by the display, after what the
window manager composed - which is the point of it.

**Tests.** `host`: `test_intelgpu_decode`, 21 checks, a share of the
display buffer and a watermark among them. The writes have no test but the
machine; under QEMU there is no Intel GPU, the driver says so and answers
`GPU_ERR_NO_DEVICE`.

## 18.660 The window manager's arrow on the M700's cursor plane (`m700-2d.md` step 3b)

The cursor of 18.659, set up once and kept: its four pages, its GTT slots,
its share of the display buffer and its watermark are taken at the first
`GPU_OP_CURSOR_SET` and never given back, so a later `set` is a copy and
three registers, a `MOVE` one position and the base that arms it, and a
`HIDE` the plane off. `gpuproto.h` grew three verbs and a request of eight
words - where, the hot spot, and the picture's place in the region that
comes with the message, which the driver checks against the region's size
before mapping it, copies, and unmaps. `gpu.lua` is the one door, and the
`gpu` program its first user.

**The window manager** tries `gfx.cursor` first - the kernel's virtio-gpu
cursor, under QEMU - and, when that says no, `gpu.cursor`; the move and
the hide are whichever said yes (`OUT.cursor_move`, `OUT.cursor_hide`).
Under QEMU nothing changes: virtio says yes where it is, and where it is
not the GPU's driver answers "no Intel GPU" and the arrow is composited as
before.

**The M700, 17 October** (0.11.261 and this, netbooted):

    intelgpu: the cursor plane ready: picture at memory 0008b7a000,
              GTT 01300000, display buffer 446-477
    wm: the pointer on the GPU's cursor plane
    wm: the pointer drawn by the display

**Diego, at the monitor: "Mouse works perfect", "And dragging windows work great".**

The test picture is refused while an arrow is on the plane
(`GPU_ERR_IN_USE`), which on the M700 is always once the desktop is up.

**Each move is a call to the driver** - a round trip through
`fs.raw` - where virtio's was a system call. The driver answers a move
with two register writes and never waits, so it cannot hold the pointer
up; a pulse (`pulses.md`) is what would take the reply away.

**Tests.** `host`: `test_intelgpu_decode`, 21 checks, unchanged; the
gate's pointer phases hold the QEMU path. The plane itself has no test
but the M700's monitor.

## 18.661 The copy to the screen, timed apart (`m700-2d.md` step 4a)

The window server's reply grew two words, `compose_us` and `copy_us` - its
composing into the back buffer and its copy from there to the screen,
apart, in microseconds because a counter tick means nothing in another
process - and `frames` prints them. The reply is six words now
(`windowproto.h`), `wm/windowserver.lua` reads them, and the profile adds
them up.

**The M700, 17 October, Diego dragging a window in circles for 30
seconds** (0.11.262 and this):

    15426 passes, 15426 of which composed something
    busy 1916 us mean, 4.655 ms WORST; composing 97.5% of busy
    composed 1197392 px a frame; drew 2490613 (2.08x the damage)
    window server: composing 1.37 ms a frame, the copy to the screen
                   0.45 ms (25%), 0.93 ms at worst

**Two things it says.**

- **The copy is a quarter of the window server's time**, not half. 18.657
  read "drew 2.02x the damage" as the frame composed and then copied; it is
  not - `drawn` is what `scene_compose` drew, and the 2x is overdraw, layers
  over layers. Composing straight into the screen's buffers would save at
  most that quarter and cost a cache flush on every line, since the display
  does not snoop the processor's caches. So step 4b keeps the copy, into
  whichever buffer is not shown, and the render engine takes it away.
- **The desktop composed 514 frames a second** for a 60 Hz screen: every
  pointer report from the mouse is a pass, and every pass composes. Seven
  frames in eight were never seen. A flip latched at vertical blank is what
  gives the compositor a beat to keep - compose once a refresh, and the
  pointer's reports in between only move the cursor plane, which composes
  nothing since 3b. That is most of what 4b buys on this machine, before
  any pixel is drawn faster.

**Tests.** The gate's display suites read the reply at its new length; the
times themselves are the M700's.

## 18.662 Page flips on the M700 (`m700-2d.md` step 4b)

**Nebula, a write-combining region.** `SYS_MEM_CREATE` takes
`MEM_WRITE_COMBINE`: the region's pages are zeroed, cleaned out of the
processor's caches a line at a time (`mmu_clean_page`: `clflush` every 64
bytes and an `mfence`; nothing on AArch64, where `MAP_USER_FB` is
`MAP_USER_RW`), and every mapping of it in a process is `MAP_USER_FB`, the
screen's memory type. A display engine does not look in the processor's
caches, so a buffer it scans out cannot be write-back - and Mesa's buffers
will want the same. Not with `MEM_ON_TOUCH` (`SYS_ERR_FLAGS`, -114, a new
code, in the duplicate-case check).

**The driver** makes GPU buffers (`GPU_OP_BUFFER_NEW`): contiguous and
write-combining, entered in GTT slots past the cursor's, a megabyte
aligned, handed out as a region beside the reply. Buffer 0 is the
firmware's framebuffer. `GPU_OP_FLIP` writes the plane's stride and then
its surface, which the display takes at the next vertical blank, and is
answered at once; `GPU_OP_FLIPPED` reads `PLANE_SURFLIVE` and
`PIPE_FLIPCOUNT` and says which buffer is being scanned. The GTT is now
mapped once, all 8 MB of it: it was a page mapped per entry and never
unmapped, which four cursor pages could afford and a screen's 4838 cannot.

**The window server** asks for a screen-sized buffer when it takes the
screen, and from then on composes into its back buffer as before, then
copies into whichever of the two the display is not showing - what was
composed since and what the other one was given last time, the back buffer
always holding the whole frame - and flips. It touches a buffer only once
`FLIPPED` says the display has left it; until then what was composed is
owed, and the receive loop looks again a tick later. When the window
manager goes, the firmware's screen is flipped back for the console, and
the cursor plane hidden. With no Intel GPU - QEMU - nothing changes.

**The M700, 17 October**:

    intelgpu: buffer 1, 3440x1440 at GTT 01400000 = memory 00064dd000, write-combining
    windowserver: page flips, between the firmware's screen and buffer 1
    intelgpu: pipe A plane 1: ... surface at GTT 01400000 = memory 00064dd000

The first try made no buffer and said nothing: the window server sent the
width and not the height, and the driver refused a buffer of no rows. A
refusal other than "no GPU here" is said now.

**Diego, at the monitor: "m700 desktop works perfect", "Desktop works perfectly on m700".** Full gate 94/94 in 9:26.

**Tests.** The gate holds the copying path, which every QEMU machine
takes. The flips have no test but the M700.

## 18.663 One frame a refresh (`m700-2d.md` step 4b, pacing)

`WS_OP_COMPOSE` takes `WS_IF_READY`: with a flip still on its way, the
window server answers `height` 1 at once and composes nothing, and the
window manager keeps its damage for a later pass - asked again within a
tick (`sleep_for`), so the last of a drag is not left for the next mouse
report. Only composed frames are counted by `frames`.

**The first try was slower, and Diego felt it** ("it feel sloweer now the
dragging", "much slower than before"): 36 frames a second, but 10 million
pixels composed in each on a screen of two and a half - 18 ms a pass. The
window manager kept every rectangle it was given, and while a frame waited
each mouse report added the dragged window's old and new places, all
overlapping. **Now overlapping damage is merged** before composing (`merge`
in `wm/compose.lua`): two rectangles that overlap become their bounding
box when it is no larger than the two together.

**The M700, 17 October, a window dragged in circles for 30 seconds**
(1720x1440 this boot - the firmware chose it):

| | flips only (18.661, 3440x1440) | paced, merged |
|---|---|---|
| frames composed a second | 514 | **60** |
| busy, of 30 s | 29.6 s | **5.2 s** |
| mean pass | 1916 us | 175 us |
| worst pass | 4.66 ms | 3.62 ms |
| a composed frame | 1.37 + 0.45 ms copy | 0.82 + 0.38 ms copy |

Every frame composed is one the screen shows, and the desktop uses a sixth
of what it did. Diego: "it feels faster now".

**Tests.** The gate's display suites hold the QEMU path, where nothing is
held back and the merge composes the same pixels; the pacing has no test
but the M700.

## 18.664 The GPU says what it is doing (`gpumonitor.md` G0 and G1)

**G1, the driver.** `GPU_OP_STATS` answers in a shape of its own,
`struct gpu_stats` (64 bytes and a row of 24 for each buffer): the device
id; the clock now, `GEN6_RPSTAT1`'s CAGF in 31:23 at 50/3 MHz a step, and
its range from `GEN6_RP_STATE_CAP` (the MCHBAR mirror's 0x5998: RP0 in
7:0, RPn in 23:16, 50 MHz a step on Skylake); `GEN6_GT_GFX_RC6`, 1280 ns a
count; `PIPE_FLIPCOUNT` and `PIPE_FRMCOUNT`, so the refresh is measured;
the underrun bit; what the desktop takes from it; and every buffer the
driver made, with the process that asked for it (`SYS_SENDER`) - the
cursor's too. Each unit is i915's own: `intel_rps.c` and `intel_rc6.c` and
`intel_mchbar_regs.h`, fetched from Linux 6.12 into `build/downloads/i915/`.
`gpu.lua` reads it (`gpu.stats`, `gpu.since`), and `gpustat` prints it.

**Nebula, the GPU's power.** RAPL's graphics plane, `MSR_PP1_ENERGY_STATUS`
(0x641), read beside the package's each tick and added up in microjoules
- in `sysinfo`'s spare word, wrapping at 32 bits, so the struct did not
change size; `heat_known`'s `HEAT_GPU_ENERGY` says it is measured. **Only
on a list of client processors**, Sandy Bridge to Comet Lake: an MSR a
processor does not have is a fault in ring 0, and the kernel has no safe
read, so the list rather than a try.

**G0, the label**, and `neofetch`'s row: the version line at the bottom
right ends with `GPU:` and what draws the desktop. A screen buffer counts
as flips from the moment it is made - the label is asked before the first
frame, and the first try said only "cursor plane".

**The M700, 17 October:**

    HD Graphics 530 (8086:1912)
      clock      asleep, of 350 to 1150 MHz    (RPSTAT1 00000000)
      asleep     100% of 2.0 s in RC6
      power      0.00 W
      display    1720x1440, 60.0 frames a second, 3.5 flips a second
      desktop    HD 530 - cursor plane, page flips
      0    the firmware     1720x1440    9.5 MB  scanned out
      1    windowserver     1720x1440    9.5 MB  scanned out
      -    wm               64x64        0.0 MB  cursor plane

    GPU        HD Graphics 530, 350 to 1150 MHz, 19 MB in buffers;
               the desktop: cursor plane, page flips              (neofetch)

    ... | PC x86-64 | GPU: HD 530 - cursor plane, page flips      (the desktop)

**What it says.** The range is the HD 530's own; the refresh is measured
at 60.0; the GT sleeps through the whole of an idle desktop - RPSTAT1
reads 0 in RC6, which `gpustat` prints as "asleep" - because the display
engine, which does all the GPU's desktop work so far, lives outside it.
The power reads 0.00 W idle; whether PP1 moves is for G2's window to show
when an engine has work.

**Gate**: 93 of 94, then 94 - `x86-udp` missed its "ready" word at 576
s into the run, with every datagram check passed, and passed alone in 19 s:
the late-gate shape the Telnet suites have shown before.

**Tests.** Under QEMU there is no Intel GPU: `gpu.stats` answers "no
Intel GPU", `neofetch` has no GPU row, and the label says `virtio -
cursor` or `none - software`, which the display suites see in the corner.

`gpumon.lua`, as `docs/gpumonitor.html` draws it and Diego agreed ("go

**The display**'s flips against its frames, and **who holds its memory**;
down the right the facts as Windows lists them, and "Desktop drawn with"
in the label's words. One `gpu.stats()` and one `sys.info()` a pace,
Network Monitor's sampling and pace menu, and no state of its own beyond
the last reading.

**The M700, 17 October** (0.11.266, netbooted): HD Graphics 530, 350 to
1150 MHz, asleep 100%, 19.0 MB in 3 buffers - the firmware's screen, the

**That boot took four tries**, and the reason is worth keeping: this Mac's

**Tests.** `x86-gpumon`, new, 4 checks in 28 s: under QEMU `gpustat` says
